In the window Save As is usable for a drawing from a flat file as for any other (the command's own `enabled`, `command_enabled`): the Save dialog starts from the `.odg` the drawing is saved as and offers what the engine writes, never `.fodg`. A flat template (`-template`) is refused as a template is, and a flat file that is hostile (a DOCTYPE, UTF-16, another kind of document, a tree past the depth cap, a file cut off) is refused in words by the kind of trouble with nothing of the file in them and the open drawing as it was. The window keeps no list of recent files.
* After a save the session's file is the bytes the save made and its index is the one the writer gave, with the model's pages as the save had
  them; the next save compares the drawing with those and the file is not read again to find out. **The same drawing saved again is no edit and writes the same bytes** (`edited:
  false`, and a note is said once, not at every save), for every kind of edit (a move, a resize, a turn, a restyle, a retext, a delete, a reorder, a new shape, a connector, a page
  resized and a page split).
* Memory, `odgfile/hold.rs`. The writer's gate counts the drawing it is given, the file read again beside it, the package it makes and the model's growth since the read. It
  cannot see what the engine holds beside the drawing, which the save counts and takes from the memory it may use: **the undo and redo steps** (earlier versions of the drawing), **the pages the
  last save gave the writer** (the copy with its new shapes flattened), **the shapes the last save flattened** (and the model's shape each was made from) and **the shapes of the model that the
  copy replaced**. They are **measured**, never priced by a share of the model's cost over a count: every allocation is reached by a pointer from a version of the drawing, so what is counted
  is the pages, chunks of shape lists and shapes that the drawing given to the writer and the versions counted before do not hold, each once whoever holds it, **the members of a group
  walked as the shapes of a page are** (a group edited is its members, not one shape), each shape new to the walk priced by what it holds (its cells, rows, sections, text and kept attributes;
  a formula many cells share is priced once, a formula nobody shares at the tree's cost, 25 times its text). The walk stops as soon as the sum passes what a save may hold, so its cost is that
  of the drawing once, the new shapes and one look at each chunk of each version. A refusal for memory names the limit a save has (never what is left of it) and what the engine holds beside
  the drawing when that is much; a drawing whose history holds more than a save may hold is refused before anything is made. **A mass delete is no such case**: the history of a drawing
  of 4,000 rectangles with 3,990 deleted holds 4,000 rectangles, which is a few megabytes. The estimate is of the size of the model's own types and the text it holds, and it stands
  within a factor of three of the reader's own figure for what a model costs (a test holds it there); whole-drawing edits of 350,000 shapes are refused after one or two, by this count.
* `odgfile/flatten.rs`. The writer writes a new shape as a native element, and the engine's new shapes are not that: `shape.drop`
  makes an instance of a master that holds only its pin, a stencil shape links to its style sheet, a shape whose text was formatted holds `Character` and `Paragraph` rows, and
  `connector.add` writes neither route cell the writer reads to tell a connector from a line. The save hands the writer **a copy** of the drawing in which each shape the file does not
  hold is its flattened form; the engine's model is not changed, and `.vsdx` is written as before. A shape an earlier save flattened is **given again** (its copy of that save, at a
  step) when nothing it was made from has changed: the shape, the styles, themes, colours and sheet of the document, its master, whether a connector is glued and how a connector is drawn;
  else it is flattened again. A flattened shape **keeps its links to its master** (`Master` and `MasterShape`: the master is written into DiaCraft's document file, so a file read again has the shape linked to it) and has the three links of the root style; the frame cells, and the fill, line, vertical alignment and margin cells the
  writer has an attribute for, as constants of the values the shape resolves to (found through the master and the styles, a themed colour worked out, a palette index as its RGB);
  its `Geometry` sections, and the `Connection` section of a 2-D shape, merged with the master's, with the formulas the writer reads a basic shape by; for a connector (glued, or with the
  `DiaCraftRoute` marker, or with a route cell) `ShapeRouteStyle` and `ConLineRouteExt` as the route style it is drawn in; its plain text; and no id of the file's (`xml:id` and `draw:id`
  of `raw` are never copied, and a duplicate or a paste drops them from the copy). A group is copied with its frame as constants, its own other cells and sections as they are, and each member flattened where it is in the group. **Every master of the model is the copy's**,
  the file's own and the ones a drop added: the writer writes them into the document file, and a master stays in the model when its instances are gone. **`DrawingSizeType` is left out of the copy of a page of a flat drawing** (no attribute holds it, and a flat file has no document file; a save into a package keeps it, which DiaCraft's document file carries, as the model writer does)
  and **a colour a person chose (`RGB(r,g,b)` of the value the cell shows) is a constant in it**, since the writer refuses a formula in a style cell; **a new shape is the exception: it keeps its formulas, a fixed colour's `RGB(r,g,b)` among them, beside the value**.
  **Nothing on a new shape is dropped without a word, and almost nothing is dropped at all.** The copy **carries everything the shape holds itself**, as it is: rounded corners, a shadow (a shape that has one from a style sheet is given the cells as constants), a text block that is not the whole shape (a block moved with `text.block_move`), shape data (`Property` and `User` rows beside the route marker), the layer (`LayerMember`), the text's background and direction, the `Character`, `Paragraph` and `Tabs` rows, the markers of runs and the fields of the text, and any other cell or section: the writer carries them in DiaCraft's own data on the shape's style, so the file read again is the same picture. What the master holds is kept by the link. **Two kinds of loss are left, classified and said** (how many new shapes lost it and the first; said again only for a shape that loses something new): **text formatting** that **a style sheet** gives the text (the rows of the shape's own `TextStyle` link, its master's, and each sheet along the chain but the root style, whose rows are the defaults of every shape), and **the link to the Theme style** of a shape whose three links are not that one style. Inert is `ResizeMode`, which the engine writes by itself and the file does not need, and the place of a label on a line or a connector that holds no text and stands for no master, which the copy leaves out (carried, it is written into the style of every connector and made the second save of the drawing an edit); **the label cells of a line that is an instance of a master (or a member of one) are carried** (left out, a line read again takes them from the master with the values it has at its own size and scale, a text block 1.5 long in a line of 150 drawing units at 1:100). What the writer refuses in a new shape (a link to different style sheets for its three families, a picture that is turned or flipped, **A shape read from an `.odg` is written back as it was read** when the drawing goes through `.diacraft` and is saved as an `.odg` (the model path): a `draw:rect` stays a `draw:rect`, on the style name the file gave it, with its lengths in the units the file wrote them in; a moved one stays a `draw:rect` with a new `svg:x` and `svg:y`, and keeps its style name while the style's own cells are as they were; the layer and the text style name are written only where the file had them. This is no loss of the engine's own copy: what the copy carries is as before.
  a group that is turned or flipped; a dash, a gradient, a hatch and a turn or a flip are written now) stays a refusal, in its words, and says the way out (see "What is refused"). The work is counted (a step for each shape visited, cell resolved and audited, and row and cell of a
  section) and held to 6,000,000 steps, about 74,000 new rectangles in one save, before it is done, in words; and **each copy is charged to the memory a save may hold before it is
  made** (the shape the model keeps beside it, and the copy), by what the shape holds (`hold.rs`, `shape_bytes`).
* A new shape copied from a shape the reader read can hold attributes and elements of the file's own that the model has no field for, shape data
  (`Data1` to `Data3`) and foreign data. The save is not refused (copying a shape is common); a warning says how many attributes and elements and which of the two other kinds the new
  shape held that the file does not, once (`SaveNote::NewShapeUnwritten`). The attributes and the geometry element the writer writes itself are not counted. What the model holds in cells, sections and text that the writer does not write is told.
* An edited save writes a PNG of the drawing's first page, of at most 256 pixels on its long side, on white paper, as the window draws it (a frame's
  own limits hold), as the package's thumbnail; an unedited save keeps the file's own, byte for byte. A drawing that cannot be drawn leaves the file's thumbnail and says so in `warnings`.
  **The first save of a drawing that has no file yet** (a new drawing, or one started from a template: `OpenFile::is_named` is false) also writes the picture when nothing was changed, into a package that has no thumbnail, with its manifest row and no other change (`WriteOptions::first_save`); a package that has one keeps it. A drawing that has a file and is not edited is saved as the file's bytes whatever the session says of changes. **It takes effect once a new drawing can be saved as an `.odg`:** on main no command makes a drawing with no file and an `.odg` package (a new drawing's save as an `.odg` is refused), so a test that makes one is what runs it. A first save whose picture cannot be made writes none and says so in `warnings`; an edited save writes no second manifest row for a thumbnail the manifest lists already.
* An object DiaCraft cannot draw and has no picture of is drawn as its frame's outline, a pale fill, a cross and its name (a table, an embedded object, a 3-D scene, a dimension line, a callout, a form control, fontwork; the name is the cell `User.ODFObject.Value` the reader gives it), the label is left off when the frame is too small to read it in, and the status bar's list says "N objects DiaCraft cannot draw, shown as labelled boxes". The labels have a layout budget of their own, beside the file's text (`Limits::max_label_chars`, `Limits::label_time`). **A copy of one, or one an undo brought back after a save deleted it, is refused in words when the drawing is saved as an `.odg`** (its element and the files that go with it are not copied yet; the way out is to delete it). **A copy of an object that has a picture, of a text box that holds the frame of an object, or of a new group that holds either at any depth, is refused in words the same way** ((B1, owner); odg-shapes).
* A signed drawing keeps its signature parts as they are, and an edited save says it no longer matches (`warnings`); an unedited save says nothing.
* A new line is a line feed: the text commands refuse a carriage return (a control character other than a line break and a tab, `BadParams`). A model that has one by
  another road (code that builds a model) is refused by the save, in the writer's words.
* Milestone-1 class F1. A save keeps to the version the part declares in `office:version`, and never raises it. A part of ODF 1.0 or 1.1 (or one that declares none, which the schemas
  of those versions read) is given **no `xml:id`** (a shape a new connector is glued to gets `draw:id` alone, `id` and the next number, and glue is by `draw:id`) and **no `svg:d` and no `svg:viewBox` on a `draw:connector`** (a new
  or routed again connector is its `svg:x1` to `svg:y2`; an `svg:d` or `svg:viewBox` such a connector already holds goes when it is routed again, since it describes a route the ends no longer say, and its draw:line-skew goes with it, as it does in every version). The save says so: one note for each such connector, naming it and its page (class route_dropped_for_version), also when the file held no path for it, since the route DiaCraft has is not in the file. The saves of every kind of edit
  of the first milestone, in documents of 1.0 and 1.1, were checked against OASIS's RelaxNG schemas of those versions with `xmllint`, and each part is valid. A part of 1.2 or later is written as before. **The rule is for the connector and the `xml:id`**: a `draw:path`'s `svg:d` is ODF 1.0's own markup (the schemas of 1.0 and 1.1 give `draw:path` the attribute `svg:d`, required, and `draw:connector` none), so a new one-dimensional shape of a geometry of its own with a cubic row is a `draw:path` with its `svg:d` in a part of 1.0 or 1.1 as in a later one, and the writer's fuzz target counts `svg:d` on the start tags of `draw:connector` alone (class F1), `xml:id` over the whole part.
* Class F2. An edit routes again only the connectors glued to the shapes it changed; every other connector keeps its bytes. The line-jump rebuild (`draw/jumps.rs`) reaches every connector whose
  legs cross the old or the new route of one a command routed, and it rewrote the rows of each, in the form the engine writes them (a route a file made, a point on a leg, other formulas), though the connector needed no jump: the
  model's connector changed and the save wrote its `svg:d` again. A connector no command routed is now rewritten by that rebuild **only when a hop is made or taken away** (its rows or its new path are not a `MoveTo` and `LineTo`
  rows only). A hop is a decoration the `.odg` has no place for: the save keeps the file's own path for such a connector and says it could not write the route. A save compares a connector's route with the route the file holds by its corners on the page, hops taken out, so rows that only spell the route another way, or a hop taken away again, are no new route and the connector keeps its bytes and its draw:line-skew. After a save that kept the file's path, the route the file holds is that path, and a later save writes the model's route once its hop is gone (a change of the page's height keeps `PinY`, so every end moves down the page by the change and the file's path goes with it: a connector no edit touched keeps its own path shifted by the change, its draw:line-skew and `svg:viewBox` as they were, a route with a hop included, and the kept corners are the same whatever the height). A route kept with a word is named once, in the save that kept it, until it changes, and **a change of the page's height does not name it again** (a path with two subpaths is no hop, and is shifted and never said). A path the reader reads that begins with no move has `M 0 <shift>` put in front of it, so that it moves exactly, and a number that moves keeps four places, or the places it had when it had more.
* Class F4. A colour set, or a gradient turned off, on a shape whose edit says nothing of `FillPattern` writes `draw:fill="solid"` when **the model's fill pattern** is 1: the pattern of the
  shape's own sheet, else the one its style sheets give (the first that holds one, ending at the root). The model's gradient (`FillGradientEnabled`) is found the same way, the shape's own cell first and then the style sheets', and
  when it is on nothing is stated, since the colour is not the fill. So a solid colour set on a gradient, a hatch or a bitmap fill leaves no `draw:fill-gradient-name`, `-hatch-name`, `-hatch-solid` or `-image-name`, and one set on a shape
  whose styles state no fill mode states `solid`. A pattern of 0 is never stated by an edit that does not change it (the reader reads `none`, a bitmap and a hatch that is not solid as 0): the colour is written alone, and the fill the
  file states stays, with its image or hatch name. Where the shape's own style already states the same, nothing changes.
* Class F5. A turn or a resize of a shape that is flipped writes the turn of its frame **without the flips the file holds** (they are `draw:mirror-horizontal` and
  `draw:mirror-vertical`, which stay), so a shape flipped both ways reads back at the angle asked, and **beside exactly one mirror the turn written is minus the model's**, as it is for a new shape flipped on one axis: LibreOffice
  26.8.2.2 draws a single mirror after the turn. A change of the flips is not written, on one axis or on both (two flips of a shape turn its frame half a turn, which the mirrors do not follow), and nor is a turn of a shape whose
  `draw:transform` holds a negative scale: each is a refusal, in words. A new shape with `FlipY` is written with `draw:text-rotate-angle="180"` (LibreOffice turns the text of a vertically mirrored shape half a turn more, and the
  text then reads as the session's), a new connector glued to point 1 or 3 of a shape with exactly one flip names LibreOffice's point 1 or 3 on the frame it draws (rows 1 and 3, not 3 and 1), and a new connector whose route has
  line jumps is written as the corners of its route, its rows (the hops) carried in DiaCraft's own data. **A turn of a shape of the file that a connector is glued to at a
  `draw:glue-point`, or at a standard point of a polygon, a polyline or a path, is refused in words**: LibreOffice places those points on the box the shape takes up
  on the page, which a turn moves elsewhere than the model's rows, and the writer has no inverse of that placement yet; a resize is saved, the rows being sums of the shape's size,
  and a turn of a shape glued only at a custom shape's standard points or listed points is saved. A frame's `draw:glue-point` is one of those points (LibreOffice
  places it as a custom shape's), so a turn of a frame glued at one is refused too, and a move or a resize of it carries the end glued to it. A new shape whose connection points are not the four side middles is written
  with them as its geometry's own glue points (`draw:glue-points`, their ways out as `draw:glue-point-leaving-directions`) and `diacraft:glue="own"` on its style, and a new
  connector glued to its row *r* names glue point *r* + 4 (LibreOffice draws such points with the geometry, mirrored and turned with it), as does one glued to a shape of the
  file whose style says so. A move of a shape whose `draw:transform` gives its translation as plain numbers (hundredths of a millimetre, as LibreOffice reads them) writes
  the translation back as plain numbers.
* A page written as an empty element (`<draw:page .../>`, which LibreOffice writes for a page with no shape) is opened and closed round what is put in it; a `content.xml` with no
  `office:automatic-styles` gets the element, empty, before `office:body` and after `office:font-face-decls`, with the new style in it (written only when a style is put in it); and a manifest with the OpenOffice.org document type
  declaration (an external id and no internal subset, which the reader reads and ignores) is scanned by the save as the reader scans it, so deleting a frame that holds an object, or any save that adds a manifest row, is not refused for it.
* `BeginArrow`, `EndArrow`, `BeginArrowSize` and `EndArrowSize` are written as `draw:marker-start` and
  `-end`, with `-width` and `-center`, on a new connector and on an edit of an arrow cell or the weight of a shape of the file, by the restyle rules (a shared style is cloned, an orphan taken out).
  **Every number from 1 to 45 is written, in every size class from 0 to 6.** The marker is DiaCraft's own, a `draw:marker` in `office:styles` of `styles.xml` (added after the last element), named
  `DiaCraft_20_end_20_<n>` for a mark with no band (2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 39, 42) and `DiaCraft_20_end_20_<n>_20_t<k>` for a mark drawn with a band (a hollow or open part is a filled band one
  line weight thick, so the marker follows the band class k = round(100 w / `S`), 1 to 99), with the display name (`DiaCraft end 16 t23`) always written, since LibreOffice builds a marker's name from it. A marker the
  file holds under a name is used as it is, whatever it draws: it is DiaCraft's by its name alone, and a program that saves our file rewrites its path and rounds its curves; only the markers
  the file lacks are written. **A marker of DiaCraft's name that the save left no style naming is taken out**: of those the styles of `content.xml` named before the save and no longer name,
  not one a common style or a style of `styles.xml` still names, and never another producer's; a marker no style named before is left alone. The width is the spread (the for the numbers it
  does not measure) times `S` of the size class at the line's weight (class 6 is the base, 18 pt), written in points to four places (`6.54pt` for number 13, class 2, 0.75 pt); a disc or a square, solid or hollow, and the slanted stroke through the vertex (9, 10, 11,
  20, 21, 42) are centred on the vertex (`-center="true"`). A size cell that is not there is class 2, a weight that is not there 0.75 pt. A number of 0 writes the empty marker name (the style then draws
  no end whatever its parent does) and takes the width and the centre out. A change of the line's weight writes again the name and the width of the markers of DiaCraft's own that the shape's own style names (a
  marker of another make keeps the width the file gives it). **The art is ours**: each marker is one path of the union of the mark's pieces, drawn in whole thousandths of `S` with holes running against
  their outer contour, so that LibreOffice's even-odd fill and the nonzero rule give the same mark (`marker_art.rs`; every number at every band class is built and checked against its pieces by a test, the work is
  counted: 3,475 markers in all, the largest needing 2,736 steps; **the 1,024-byte bound on a path is on the markers the writer draws only (the longest is 499 bytes): a marker the file holds under our name is used as it
  is, whatever its path, and the part's own limits are the only bound on it**). **The custom end and what has no art** (R32 refused them until tier 2 was written): the custom end (254) is written as **number 4's marker** at the cell's size class (`DiaCraft_20_end_20_4` at 6.54 pt
  for class 2 and 0.75 pt) and **its cell is carried** by DiaCraft's extension on the shape's own style (the formula, `USE("...")`, and the value 254), since the reader rebuilds 4 from the marker, so the model reads back as it
  was; a new picture has no extension to carry it, so a picture with a custom end is refused in words. A number past 45 and a size class outside 0 to 6 have no art: the save writes no marker for them and the extension carries
  the arrow cells (a marker written for a size past 6 would be read back as 2). **A line end on a line whose weight is more than a million points** (13,888 inches: the width of the marker follows the weight and would be `inf` or hundreds of digits) has no marker either: in a new line the end is carried with no marker and its cells in tier 2, as for a size past 6; **in a weight edit of a line that names a marker of ours, and in an end set on a line the file holds, it is refused in words**, and a size cell that is no class is refused in a weight edit too, and not taken for 2. The engine's copy of
  a new connector carries its line ends. **A line end another program changed is told (the third sentence):** the custom end 254 is drawn as number 4's marker and its cell is carried with a fingerprint of the marker as the file has it; when another program sets the end to another marker (`Arrow` in a LibreOffice run) the reader gives the stand-in 4 and no 254, and a rewrite of the marker's width (LibreOffice's 0.231 cm) is no edit and keeps the 254. **DiaCraft's own filled diamond is the one custom end with a marker of its own**: `DiaCraft_20_end_20_254`, read as number 4 and the class its width gives, the cell carried the same way. **The inside of a hollow mark**: ODF's marker is a path painted in the line's colour, a hollow mark is that path with the hollow part cut out of it, and ODF has no fill for the inside of a marker and no way to attach one, so **the shape's fill that DiaCraft paints inside a hollow mark is not in the marker**. It rides where the fill of every shape does, in the shape's own style: **the fill of a 1-D shape is written** (`draw:fill`, `draw:fill-color`, `draw:opacity`, and the gradient, hatch and stipple forms), which the writer left out for a line or a connector until then, so a connector's fill is part of the file and DiaCraft reads it back (`crates/engine/tests/it/endfill_roundtrip.rs`: a new drawing saved as `.odg`, `.vsdx` and `.diacraft` and opened again draws as the session did; a fill set on a connector of an `.odg` is saved in place and comes back). **What another program does** (the Save As compatibility note; measured with LibreOffice 26.8.2.2, headless, on copies of the files DiaCraft wrote: a connector with a red fill and the same with none draw the same picture): LibreOffice draws the inside of every marker empty and uses no fill on a connector, so a hollow end that DiaCraft shows with a colour inside shows with nothing inside there; nothing is dropped from the file, and the save's `checked` says no more than it did (the formulas of the colours `shape.format` typed, which ODF holds as colours).
* **A line pattern of 2 to 23 is a dash of DiaCraft's own in an `.odg`**: `draw:stroke="dash"` and a `draw:stroke-dash` named `DiaCraft_20_dash_20_<n>` (and `_20_flat` after the number for the form a flat cap draws) in `office:styles`, its lengths in percent of the line's weight, for a new drawing, a new shape, a pattern or a cap set on a shape of a file and a style sheet written whole; a pattern past 23, a custom one and a fraction have no dash and ride in DiaCraft's data. **A line the file says is dashed keeps the dash the file draws it with, through every save that does not set the pattern** (the owner's ruling of 2026-11-27, "Keep the file's form"): a style that says `dash` and names no dash takes its dash from its parent that names one, or from none (the program that reads the file draws its own), and the model writer (a Save As, and the trip through `.diacraft`) writes the stroke as it read it and **names no dash of DiaCraft's own beside it**, so the dash the line draws with stays the parent's, or none, and another program draws what it drew for the source; a dash of another make that the line's own style names is written as held, and so is a dash of DiaCraft's that the file names when the cells cannot say the same name again (a style that says no stroke, or a flat form under a cap that is another style's); a dash of DiaCraft's that the cells do say again is written from them, as for a new shape. DiaCraft draws its own default dash (the pattern 2) for a line that says `dash` and names none, until the pattern is set. **A pattern the person sets after the read is written as writes it**, over the dash the line took from its parent or named in its own style (the stroke's stamp goes stale and the cells write the new pattern's dash, and the dash the style named goes with it). The splice writes only what an edit changes, so an edit of something else leaves the dash as the file has it. Tests: `crates/engine/tests/it/odg_dashes.rs` and `odg_dash_chain.rs` (the chains of styles, the edits and a property test of random chains), `crates/odg/tests/it/held_dash_chain.rs`.
* A text is compared with the file's paragraph by paragraph: by the characters,
  the cells of the `Paragraph` row and the cells of the `Character` row of each run, **never by the `IX` of a row** (the engine numbers the rows of a text anew when it formats part of
  one), and a plan keeps the paragraphs that are the same, edits those that differ and inserts or takes out the rest. A kept paragraph keeps its bytes, and **a paragraph written again keeps the `text:span` of each run that is unchanged** (the run lies in the head or the tail the two paragraphs share, in the same place and with the same row, and its span is one element that covers it: ownership R8), with its `xml:id` and whatever else it holds. An edit inside one run of raw text
  of a paragraph whose runs and row are the same is still spliced in place (a span keeps its bytes, a bookmark or a soft page break stays). Any other edit, across a run, at the
  edge of one, a changed row, the whole label replaced, writes the paragraph's content again from the model: a run with a row is a `text:span` whose automatic text style is the span's
  own for the row when the paragraph had one, else a style the part holds with exactly the row's attributes (a style of no parent whose one properties element is of the kind and which
  names nothing else), else a new one named by R27 (the prefix most of the file's text styles use and one more than the largest number of either part: `T13` beside `T9` and `T12`); a
  paragraph's own style changes only when its row does, by the same rule (`P`). A text style whose last span goes is taken out as an orphan. The attributes are inverted
  (`fo:text-align`, `fo:margin-*`, `fo:text-indent`, `fo:line-height`, `style:writing-mode`; `fo:font-size` in points, the bits of `Style` as the weight, style, variant and the two
  complex ones with the underline, the strike-through and the overline from their cells, `fo:text-transform`, `style:text-position`, `fo:color`, `fo:letter-spacing`, `style:text-scale`,
  and a face as the `style:font-name` of the part's own `style:font-face` for it, **declared in the same file's `office:font-face-decls` when the part has none for the family** (the model's table of faces is no field the save compares)), a palette index of a `Color` as its RGB (`#rrggbb`: every colour the writer writes, `fo:color`, `draw:fill-color` and `svg:stroke-color`, is a `#` and six hexadecimal digits, as the schema of the format has it), **and a colour a person chose (`RGB(r,g,b)` in a row of the model) as `fo:color`: the engine's copy makes it a constant, as it does a shape's colours.** An inserted paragraph is a `text:p`; **beside a list item whose row it has it is a new `text:list-item` of that list**, with that paragraph's style; a paragraph taken out takes its list item when it is the item's only child. **Where no neighbour has its row it goes outside any list**: after the outermost list the paragraph before it is in, or before the one after it is in (the reader skips a `text:p` that is a child of a `text:list`, and so does LibreOffice), and between two items of one list it is refused in words (the specification does not say how a list is split). **The paragraphs put in at one place are written in the model's order:** one that has the row of a list item beside it would be a new item of the list, which can be ahead of a paragraph already put in after the list, and is written after that paragraph and outside the list instead; one that would fall between two items of one list (it is after a paragraph that is a new item at the start of a list) is refused in words. **Refused, in
  words:** a link or any element or reference the writer does not map (a change mark, an index mark; a bookmark, a reference mark, a soft page break and a text field are put back); a tab stop marker or a piece of markup of another format the model keeps among a text's parts (**a page number, page count or file name field is kept **: its shown text is among the paragraph's characters and its element stays where the file has it, as any field's); a format that cuts through the characters of a field; a paragraph put between two items of one list where neither has its row; a list item whose paragraph settings change; a text format set where no character is (an empty shape, or an empty paragraph the edit leaves with a row of its own or the characters of a formatted run deleted from the end of a paragraph: the cells of a row that no character uses are not written, and the file would read as having none; a row that no marker holds in force, or that only a stretch of no character amid characters does, is no format a person sees and is saved); a bullet that is more than one character (`BulletStr`) or a bullet's font that is a number other than 0; a list item that holds more than its paragraph, a list header, or another list, next to a paragraph added or taken out; a font that is a number of the document's table other than 0, or a family that cannot be a name; a cell of a row
  that has no attribute here (`Locale`, `Tabs`, a formula); a shape whose file holds no `text:p`. The new shapes' own text keeps its formatting told, not written. The work is counted: each
  paragraph and run of each model is walked once, the plan is linear, **each paragraph of the file is tokenized once however many paragraphs are put beside it** (the bytes are charged
  before they are tokenized, `WriteWork::tokenized_bytes`), a text of more than 2,000,000 paragraphs or 16 MiB is not rewritten, **the lists the retext makes of the paragraphs (about 250 bytes each) are charged to the memory a save may hold before they are made, the names of the faces are indexed once, and the package made is read again through the reader, once, when a paragraph was put in, taken out or made a list's, to count the paragraphs of each shape that changed** (`WriteWork::read_back_bytes`).
* A paragraph whose `Paragraph` row has a list's cells (`Bullet` not 0) and that no neighbour has the row of is the item of a
  `text:list` the save makes, with an automatic `text:list-style` of one level named by R27 (`L` and a number when the file has no list style): `text:list-level-style-bullet` with the character of
  `Bullet` 1 to 7 (U+2022, U+25C6, U+25AA, U+25A1, U+2756, U+27A2, U+2713) or `BulletStr`, the face (`style:font-name`, declared as above; the number 0, the text 0 and nothing name none) and size (`fo:font-size`) of `BulletFont` and `BulletFontSize` (**a `BulletFontSize` of -1, "same size", which is the cell's default and what gives a bulleted paragraph's row, names no size**; any other share below 0 is refused in words), and the label's `fo:margin-left` and `fo:text-indent` of `IndLeft` and `IndFirst`; the other cells of the row are the paragraph's own style. The items that come so in a row at one
  place are the items of one list (two bulleted paragraphs and a plain one are one list and a paragraph), and a plain paragraph of the file that is given such a row is wrapped in a list of its own. A
  `Bullet` of 8 or more with no `BulletStr` is refused in words.
* The review to 3, to 4. **Style sheets in a saved `.odg`.** A style sheet the
  model adds is an empty common `graphic` style at the end of `office:styles`, its sheet is an entry of DiaCraft's document file, and a shape that names it as its three links has it as
  the `style:parent-style-name` of its automatic style. **A style sheet of the file is named by the name its own markup gives it** (`style:name`, as the read kept it), and not by the
  `NameU` the document file may have restored to the model (a `My Theme` the file holds as `My_20_Theme`): a parent written by the model's name named no style, and a second style of
  that name was saved over the first. The characters of the name are the ones XML 1.0 gives an `NCName`; `ª`, `µ`, `²` and `½` are written `_AA_`, `_B5_`, `_B2_` and `_BD_`. **What is
  written is read back**: the style sheets added, taken out or carried, and the links of each shape whose parent was written (a parent the file does not hold is a refused save, never
  a shape read back on the root); a package of more than 16 MiB is not read back, as the checks of the paragraphs and of tier 2 leave one unchecked. **A style sheet the model no longer has** (an undo of a saved `theme.apply`) **is taken out of the file** when it is the last of the file's and its
  markup is an empty common style: the element, its entry of the document file and the parents that named it; any other (a style whose markup holds a property) is refused, and the
  words say that an undo took it back, so that the way out is a redo. **The cells of an empty common style the file holds** (the `Theme` style after another program's save, which keeps
  the empty style and drops the document file) **may be filled in again**, and the document file carries them as it carries a new style's; `theme.apply` fills such a `Theme` style in
  (its answer's `style_added` says so) and the shapes that name it follow the theme. A change of any other style sheet of the file is refused. **An `.odg` is opened one way**
  (`diacraft_engine::odgfile::read_odg`, which `file.open` and `diacraft-cli export` both use): the themes the document file carries are read, and one that cannot be read whole is a
  warning of the report (`theme_unreadable`, `theme_entry_unreadable`, `theme_list_capped`, as a VSDX file's are) with its bytes kept.
* A bookmark, a reference mark (a point, or the two ends of a range), a soft page break and a text
  field the model holds as plain text (a fixed date or time, the title, the author, the file's other fields of the standard that show only their characters; not the page number, the page
  count and the file name, which are `Field` rows: a text that holds one is refused whole, as before) **stay in the file when their paragraph is written again whole**, with their own bytes.
  Where each goes is a rule of the text and not of the bytes: its offset in the model's text (the characters before it, as the reader counts them; a mark between two spaces that collapse
  is after the space) is carried, block by block, across the edit. A block is the run of steps the plan edits (not in place), puts in or takes out between two paragraphs it keeps; a
  paragraph kept, and one edited in place (an edit inside one run of raw text, the runs and the row the same), keep every element where it stands. In a block, the common prefix of the
  old and the new text (length p) is taken first, then the common suffix of what is left (length s): an offset up to p stays, one from the old length less s on moves by the change of
  length, any other goes to p (the suffix first would give another place for V21). A block that puts in no paragraph sends its elements to the start of the next paragraph
  the plan keeps, or to the end of the last. The elements at one offset stay in the order they stood in. In the paragraph written, an element stands at the top level at the
  paragraph's start or end and between two runs of different rows (before the next run's `text:span`), and inside the `text:span` of a run, which is not split, when the characters on both
  sides belong to that run. **A field is kept when its characters lie wholly in the common prefix or the common suffix**, inside the span of the run its characters are in
  (a format that cuts through its characters is refused in words: the specification does not say how one cut in two is kept); a field whose characters changed is written as the new
  characters, with no element, and the save says so once ([`SaveNote::FieldWritten`], V19: `Ann` retyped as `Bob`; **once for each kind of field in a shape, however many of that kind changed**, so a
  shape has at most 42 notes). **Memory:** the tokens of a paragraph (the token of each piece and four bytes for each character room of a text or a field) are held to the memory a save may hold while the paragraph is
  planned, and given back after it; a paragraph whose tokens do not fit is refused as a limit (`write_limit`, "memory for the paragraphs of a retext"). A retext of a paragraph of 1,300,000 bookmarks (the most the reader's cap
  of 4,000,000 items allows), of 600,000 paragraphs that each hold one, and of 50,000 changed fields saves under `ulimit -v 3000000` (peak resident 0.8 GB at the most), tested in child processes. A range
  that is not in the text, or a tag of a paragraph that is not text, is a fault (`write_mismatch`) and never a paragraph with no element in it. **White space** in a paragraph with elements is written in one pass
  over its characters: a space is a plain one unless it would not read back as one (after another space with only elements between, at the start of the paragraph after elements alone,
  after a field, and at the end), where it is `text:s`; no `text:span` of the file is copied as its bytes in such a paragraph. A soft page break between paragraphs
  (a direct child of the shape or of its text box) is **an anchor at the start of the paragraph after it and follows the block mapping (items 1, 3 and 5), as a bookmark does**:
  while the plan keeps that paragraph, or edits it in place, the break stays where it stands, and a paragraph put in before it goes before the break; when the paragraph is written whole or taken out, the
  break is carried over with its block's prefix and suffix and written where it lands: between the paragraphs when it lands on a paragraph's start (at the start of the paragraph's list item when that is
  a list item's: a list holds no soft page break between its items), else inside the paragraph at its offset (inside a run's span when the characters on both sides are the run's), so a break before the last
  paragraph, taken out, goes inside the end of the paragraph before it, and breaks before paragraphs taken out go before the next paragraph kept, in their order. The break's own bytes are copied, the white space before it included
  where it is written between paragraphs.
  **The paragraph written is read again from the bytes made and holds exactly those elements, each at its offset with its bytes** (the check of the bytes made; a paragraph that kept its
  bytes holds the ones put in at its start and its end). **Refused in words:** a link (`text:a`: the placing does not cover one), a change mark or an index mark (R10 places the
  elements it names only), any other element the writer does not map, a format that cuts a field, and a zero-width element that would be put where the namespace prefixes its bytes use are
  not those in force. The work is counted (`WriteWork::zero_steps`: the elements listed, carried and put in, the bytes of a paragraph taken out looked at for a tag, and the characters of
  the block comparisons; `WriteWork::checked_zero`: the paragraphs read back for the elements put in them), the elements and the spans kept for the second pass are charged to the memory a save may hold before they are listed, and each is linear: n and 4n elements in one paragraph, at one offset, as fields, in n paragraphs written whole, in n paragraphs taken out, and in n spans cost n
  and 4n. **Two faults in the code the elements share were found and fixed**: an edit spliced into one run of raw text read the white space after it another way when it took the text before a
  plain space (the check of the bytes made refused the save), and a `text:span` that began or ended with a space was copied as its bytes where the text before it had changed.
* A new shape and a reorder of the page in one save are written (they were refused as "a new shape on a page whose shapes are put in another
  order in the same save"). Where the order is the document's, one plan puts the shapes that move and the new ones in the model's order: the shapes that stay are a longest run that
  keeps its order, and the rest go after the one that stays before them in the model's order, a moved unit and a new element made in turn. Where the page's shapes carry
  `draw:z-index`, no element moves: a new shape is written with the value of the shape before it in the model's order (the least value for one that is first) and its element is put
  after that shape's, so the reader, which sorts by the value and then by the place, finds it there; a shape of the file with no value, which the reader numbers by its place (a new
  element moves it), is given the value the order needs; and the order the reader will read is worked out and must be the model's, or the page is refused in words (values that repeat).
  A new shape on a page that carries `draw:z-index` is written with the attribute (it was refused). The second and the third save are no edit.
* Design decision 8. The answer of `file.save` and `file.save_as` for an `.odg` has `notes`: an array, empty when the drawing holds nothing a LibreOffice save would drop, else one `{class: "libreoffice_would_drop", words, cross_shape_formulas, shape_data}`. It is judged on the drawing as the file holds it (the copy the writer is given), by shape: a cell holding a formula that names another shape (by `Sheet.<ID>` or by the name of a shape: fix round), a `Property` row (the section the model keeps shape data in) or a `User` row but the `DiaCraftRoute` marker; the ends and triggers of a connector (its glue) are not counted. **A shape that is an instance of a master is no trigger** (2026-11-17: a shape dropped from a stencil is one in every session, and its link and its master are carried by the document file). It is **not a warning**, it is given on every save (an unedited one too), and the window shows its words once in a session, in the banner, which a person dismisses. The count is held to the flattening's step bound.
* **A new custom shape's outline is written as the path it draws**, in sets: the sections that fill go in one set (with `S` when none of them strokes), the sections that only stroke (`NoFill`) in a set with `F`, and the sections that are not shown (`NoShow`, or `NoFill` and `NoLine` both) in a set with `F` and `S`; each run of a section (a `MoveTo` starts one) is a subpath, closed with `Z` where it ends where it began. A fill-only section beside one that fills and strokes, or a section that fills and is several runs not all closed, cannot be written as separate sets without the fill changing, so one set holds every section that fills as one ring (inner moves as lines) with `S`, and the next the runs of every section that strokes with `F`. **Arcs are exact at the size written:** an `ArcTo` is `A` (bow above 0, counterclockwise as seen) or `W` on the circle's box with the pen and the end as the two rays, and a bow of 0 a line; an `EllipticalArcTo` with `C` 0 and `D` above 0 is `A` or `W` on the ellipse through the pen, the middle point and the end (three points on a line are their chord); a section of one `Ellipse` row with its axes along the frame's is `U` from 0 to 360 degrees. **A coordinate** that is a share of the frame (`Width*k`, the bare name, the constant 0) is that share, and one whose formula names another cell or calls a function (`MIN(Width,Height)*0.12`) is the share its value is at the size written; a length beside the size (`Width*0.5+0.25`) and any other row are still refused (the equation is not written yet), and the shape then keeps the stand-in rectangle, with the warning that says so. **What the reader gives back:** it makes a section of each subpath, so a shape whose sections are in the order of the sets, one run each, with plain flags and rows in the forms the reader writes carries no tier 2; any other carries its rows as before, and a program that reads only the outline sees the outline written. An outline of more than 8,184 subpaths or 100,000 rows is refused (the reader stops at 8,188 sections) and keeps the stand-in. Before it, thirteen masters of Basic Flowchart Shapes and Gane-Sarson's Process and Data Store were written as that rectangle; none of the fifty-eight is now (LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 draws their outlines: inferred-from-sample, not the reference app). **An outline edited in a shape of the file is still written only in the forms the reader gives back as the same rows** (no set, no arc), with the words of the first rule above.
* A group of new shapes is saved as a `draw:g` holding its members (placed on the page by the groups round them; no `draw:z-index` on a member), read back as the group the session has, and saved again as no edit. A group is written when it is unturned and unflipped and has no text of its own (R45 writes a group's text as one more member, and keeps its angle and flips in the document file with its members written turned: neither is written yet, and **a text on a group, new or of the file, and a group that is turned or flipped are refused in words**, not dropped). **A group's frame is judged against the box of its members at a millionth of an inch** (the cells a save is given are at nine places, which a turned member's box carries to a few parts in a hundred million, so a group of members turned by any angle is the box and is written with no note; the writer held it to 1E-12 before, and refused every group with a turned member), **and a group whose frame is not that box** (a size it was held to by `LockCalcWH` after a member moved out, a margin, a pin set away from the middle) **is written as its members all the same, with one note for each such group naming it and its page** (a `draw:g` has no frame of its own, the file holds the group as its members, and read again it is the box of them; a group in a group is judged by the box of its leaves, and not by the frame of the group inside it; **a group of the file that a save changed something under (a member's pose, a member taken away, its own pose) is judged the same way and told when it is not the box**, as a `LockCalcWH` group is whose member turned after it was saved; **a connector glued to the group itself is named in the note**, since the reopened group has its connection points on the box and the connector's end stays where it was in the file; the precision is a millionth of an inch or a billionth of the group's largest length, whichever is more). **A picture that is a member of a new group is written where the group's map puts it** (it was written at its place in the group's frame, as if that were the page), **and a new picture or a new line or connector that holds members is refused in words** (a picture would be left out of a `draw:g`, and a one-dimensional shape's ends are nobody's there). A group's own cells beyond its frame, its sections, its `ID` (when another shape's formula or glue names it) and its link to a master are carried by DiaCraft's document file as `group` entries, **found by the group's `draw:name`, which is unique among the page's groups**: a group made in DiaCraft with no such name is named `Group_<ID>` (`Group_<ID>_2` when a group of the page has that name) in the copy a save writes, so its element and its entry say so, and the entry has no `nth`; **a group a file had that holds no data of its own** (no cell beyond its frame, no section, no `ID` another shape names, no link to a master, and the four connection points the reader gives every shape) **has no entry to find and is written with no name, as the file had it**; an entry for a group with no name, an empty one or one another group has says its place among the groups of the name in `nth` (always, the first too), keeps no `ID` alone, and is written only when the file holds it already, so that data given to an unnamed group of the file is refused in words (the entry would be found by a place that another program can change) and no program that reorders, adds or takes away groups moves a group's data to another. **The refusal has words of its own, and none of them says to undo**: it names the group that needs a name (`the group with no name numbered 2 on the page "Page-1"`, the number among the groups with no name of that page) and the three ways out that hold whatever was done last, to name the group, to put its data on a shape beside it, or to use Save As to save the drawing as a `.diacraft` file, which holds it, and says that nothing was written; for a flat file it says so. The cause is the group's and not the last change: a second save, a save after another shape was moved, and the undo of that move leave it as it was, and the way out of every other refusal, "Undo the change (edit.undo) to save", sent a person to take back what they had not done. The words are short, since the window shows the first 300 characters of a refusal, and name the page cut at 40 characters. **A group that holds no connection points says so in its entry**: the reader gives every group the four standard connection rows, so the entry of a group with no `Connection` section (a group of a VSDX file, one made in DiaCraft) says that the section is gone, and the group comes back with none, where it came back with four and the check after the save named them; a line and a connector with none say the same on their own style, and a line's or a connector's outline that holds a flag of its own (`NoFill` 1, as `connector.add` makes it) is carried whole, since the reader gives a segment's outline none; a group with no key of its own (no name, or one another group has) is given no entry for its connection points alone, and comes back with four. **What a group's own markup gives it is no data of DiaCraft's**: a group of the file with no name whose data is still what its markup gave it (its own graphic style, `draw:style-name`, and its own glue points, `draw:glue-point`, which are more than its frame and the four standard connection rows) needs no entry, since the reader builds that data again from the markup, so a save that rewrites the document file for something else (a window setting turned) leaves the entry out and is no refusal, and keeps the item of the group's VSDX data (`docs/diacraft-format.md` 7.3), which is no entry the markup gives; the same group given data in DiaCraft is still refused in words. **What the markup gives is judged up to the rounding of a save**: a move writes the members again, and the file read again has the group's box a few units in the last place from the session's, so the cached value of a `Connection` row that the box makes (`Width*0.5`, in the entry of a group with glue points of its own) differs from the entry of the file read again in its last places; a number of a cell's value within a trillionth of an inch and of its own size (`write::lengths::same`, the rounding the lengths a save writes are held to) is the same number, so a group of the file with no name and glue points of its own that is moved and saved is saved again, where the second save was refused in words for data nobody gave (and a group with a name saved again with nothing changed was written once more); **the cached value of a cell that holds a formula** (the same formula) **is not judged at all** for a group whose entry is left out, since the reader makes it again from the markup it reads, so a group with glue points of its own that is resized is saved too (its first save was refused in words for the new values of the rows its box makes); a name, a formula, a unit, a place the markup gives and every other attribute must be equal, and the same group given a cell, or a glue point moved by more than rounding, is still refused. **A group of the model is the file's by the element it is in, and never by its `ID`**: a shape put last, taken out or added in a save changes the `ID`s the reader gives the shapes after it, so a group found in the file read again by the `ID` the session has was another shape, and a drawing saved and saved again was refused in words for a group with no name whose data was the markup's own (a flat drawing on its second save, a package on a save that wrote the document file again, a setting turned); the two indexes of a save say which element each of the model's shapes and each of the file's is, and the group is looked for by it. The reader reads the entries before the pages; **an entry no group of its page takes (the group was renamed or taken away in another program) is warned of, once** (`diacraft_group_unclaimed`), and a page that has none is warned of (`diacraft_group_unknown`). **An entry with no `nth` binds to a group only while exactly one group of the page has that name**: a copy of the group put in the page, or another group given the name, leaves the entry unread, with one warning (`diacraft_group_name_shared`), where it was read for the first group of the name before, and so no group takes data or an `ID` that is not its own. **The `ID` of an entry no group takes is given to no other group of the page**, so a formula that names it reads no shape and never another. **A copy of a group that holds an object is refused in words as a copy of an object on the page is** (the members of a new group that the file does not hold are looked at, with or without a replacement picture; a member the file holds is a shape put into the group, which is refused in its own words). A group dropped from a master of several shapes (an instance of it) carries its links to the master (`master`, `master-shape`) in its entry too, and a file read again has them. A saved group is moved, given data and deleted; a **shape of the file put into a group, a group of the file taken apart, a member added to a group of the file and a group's rename are refused in words**. **A flat drawing has no document file, so it keeps none of a group's own data**: a User-defined Cell, Shape Data, a connection point of its own beyond the ones the markup gives, alt text (a title and a description), and any other cell or section the markup does not give a group, **given to a group of a flat drawing, with a name or with none, new or of the file, is refused in words that name the group and say that a flat file keeps none of it, with nothing written and no "Undo" in them** (the data goes on a shape beside the group, or the drawing is saved with Save As as a `.diacraft` file, which holds it; `edit.undo` takes it back, and the save is then no edit); the save answered `edited: false`, left the file as it was and marked the drawing saved before, with the data held in the session alone, and a new group's first save dropped its data and said it was an edit. What the markup gives a group (its own graphic style, its glue points, a title and a description as the file has them), a group moved or resized, data on a member of a group (a member has a style of its own), a new group that holds none, and a master link (refused in words as it is in a package) are as they were. A group made in DiaCraft comes back from a flat file with the four standard connection points the reader gives every group, as it always has, and that is no refusal. A Data Flow's label is written as the text of its connector, with its place carried, and the route of a connector that moved is written again.
* Parked items. A connector of the file glued to a shape an undo put back (a delete of both ends, a save, then the undo) is
  **saved with the shape and the glue**: it was refused with a redo or a second delete as the way out, since the undo is the change and undoing again goes round.
  `connector.style` with no `ids` changes the page's own cells, which DiaCraft's document file carries: it is saved and says nothing of the page, and a curved style says nothing either
  (a curved connector is written).
* Our rule (the rows for `draw:start-shape`, `draw:end-shape` and the glue points). **A drawing opened from an
  `.odg` is saved in place after the glue of a connector changed**: `connector.reconnect` to another shape or point, `connector.reverse_ends`, an end dropped on a shape or taken off one, a
  glued shape moved or deleted, and an undo of any of them. Save and Save As an `.odg` used to refuse every end glued anew, in words, and Save As `.diacraft` held it; the splice writes it
  now, end by end, for the connectors of the file (`write/compare.rs` `glue_edits`: the connections are matched by the elements they join, so a save that numbered the file's elements anew is
  no change). **What an end is written as:** the shape it is glued to by its `xml:id`, else its `draw:id`, else an id the writer gives it once for the page; the glue point by the number the
  shape has for it (the standard points by the map, beside one flip as the reader numbers them, a custom shape's own points and the ones its geometry lists as a new connector's end is, and
  `diacraft:glue="own"` four on), none for the whole of a shape, which LibreOffice places itself; both attributes are taken off an end that is free. The ends and the path go as for a connector that
  moved. **The cells of a glued end are not carried in DiaCraft's data**: they are what the reader rebuilds from the file's glue, and a copy would name a shape by the `ID` it has in the session.
  **Refused in words, with nothing written:** an end glued to two places, a line glued to a shape (a `draw:line` has no attribute for it), a shape that is not the first holder of its name on the
  page or whose name is empty, and a formula of its own on the end of a connector whose glue did not change. **The file made is read again** and each end glued is held to the glue the model has
  (`check_glue`): a save that would number a point otherwise is refused. A connector glued to a connection point that the shape's rows hold and its file does not declare (the doubling
  adds such points) is saved naming the point's number, and CPDOUBLE.ODG writes the point as a glue point of the file ("Connection points: double and halve (CPDOUBLE)" below). Tests: `crates/engine/tests/it/odg_glue_edit.rs`,
  `crates/odg/tests/it/write_glue.rs`.
* **What a style's attributes cannot say is carried, not refused**. A dash, a gradient, a hatch, a palette colour, a shadow, a transparency past 1 and a formula in a
  style cell (a theme's, say) are saved: the style keeps the attributes it had, DiaCraft's extension (`diacraft:` attributes on the shape's own automatic style) carries the cell,
  and the file reads back as the model holds it. A program that is not DiaCraft shows the style's own attributes. A user cell, a section the writer does not write and a handle's
  section are carried the same way, **and so is a formula set on a pose cell whose value stays the same** (`shape.pin` puts the pin at another place of the box with formulas on `LocPinX` and `LocPinY`; the shape draws where it did and the file reads back with them), **except on the end of a connector**: its ends are rebuilt from its glue, so a formula or another attribute of its own on an end with the glue as it was is refused in words. A shape that a LibreOffice paste made (its style repeats another shape's `ID`) is read as a copy with none of that shape's data; an edit that adds a cell to it gives it an `ID` and data of its own, and what any edit writes of tier 2 is read back, so a duplicate `ID` is a refused save and never a lost edit. A change to a group's own cells is carried by the document file's `group` entry (a flat drawing has no such file and refuses it in words); a group's rename is refused in words.
* **What is refused, in the writer's words, with nothing written and the session as it was** (`EngineError::Failed`, whose message the window shows as its banner, the CLI prints as
  `step N (file.save): ...` and the MCP server returns as an `isError` result): an arc or a NURBS in an outline a person edits in a shape of the file (a new shape's arcs are written); a text edit the
  list in names; a new shape put into a group of the file, a shape of the file put into a group, a group of the file taken apart; a page whose `draw:z-index` values repeat, when a new shape or a reorder cannot be read back in the model's order; a new shape of one of the three new stencils (all thirty of the original masters are saved: ten natively, and twenty whose connection points or outline are not the plain ones by DiaCraft's extension on the shape's
  own style, with a note that a program other than DiaCraft draws a rectangle for the outline, which none of them needs; the twenty masters of are written too: see the section below); a connector that is curved (the engine draws it as a quadratic B-spline, which the writer does not write); a page set to a preset
  size (the paper cells have no attribute); a text on a picture or an object frame (no spec says where a graphic frame's text goes in the file, and the reader reads none from it); a flip of a shape, or a turn of one whose transform holds the flip; and a carriage return. **Every refusal says the way out**: an `.odg` is saved only as an `.odg` until a later change, so the words end with "Undo the change (edit.undo) to save", and the undo is followed by a save (**but the refusal for a group with no name that holds data**, which has its own words and no undo); **a refusal for memory has its own words and its own way out, and one for a shape an undo put back says to redo**. **A curved connector is written** (the engine's quadratic spline is raised to cubic pieces, which is exact once it is split at the knots, and its own rows are carried), so the answer of `connector.add` or `connector.style` has no `warnings` for it, as for every master of the built-in stencils.

## Additional built-in stencils

The catalogue of the first batches has seven stencils and fifty-eight masters, which a new session opens, and the second batch (below) adds more that it does not, nine stencils and 116 masters so far, for sixteen stencils and 174 masters in all (the sixth is the Cross-Functional Flowchart Shapes, `cross-functional`: `xfunc.swimlane` and `xfunc.separator`, whose drop on a page with lanes inserts a lane or splits a phase; the seventh, the Organization Chart Shapes, has a section of its own: "The Organization Chart"). The original twelve Basic Shapes and eighteen Basic Flowchart masters keep their identities. New stable IDs are:

| Stencil | Master IDs | Count |
|---|---|---:|
| Decorative Shapes (`decorative`) | `decorative.star-5`, `decorative.star-6`, `decorative.star-8`, `decorative.burst`, `decorative.heart`, `decorative.lightning-bolt`, `decorative.cross`, `decorative.ribbon` | 8 |
| Arrow Shapes (`arrows`) | `arrows.right`, `arrows.left`, `arrows.up`, `arrows.down`, `arrows.left-right`, `arrows.up-down`, `arrows.four-way`, `arrows.bent` | 8 |
| Gane-Sarson (`gane-sarson`) | `gane-sarson.interface`, `gane-sarson.process`, `gane-sarson.data-store`, `gane-sarson.data-flow` | 4 |

Use the namespaced ID to distinguish the rounded Gane-Sarson Process from the legacy flowchart `Process`, whose unqualified lookup stays unchanged. `shape.drop` with `gane-sarson.data-flow` creates a real one-dimensional connector, initially horizontal with a 1.5-inch span centered at `x,y`; `connector.reconnect` attaches either end and `shape.set_text` labels the flow. Block arrows are ordinary two-dimensional shapes. Every node has one text block; no separate identifier editor is supplied. Existing templates retain their previous stencil lists.

VSDX save/reopen preserves these masters. An `.odg` save writes all fifty-eight (the two of the Cross-Functional Flowchart Shapes, and the six of the Organization Chart Shapes, with a warning for the two fields of a position's text; the gate that refused the twenty of this batch is gone): each master is dropped, saved, read back and compared by what it draws and where it connects, and saved again as no edit, and **the master is carried**: the shape keeps its link to it and DiaCraft's document file holds the master, so a file read again has the shape linked to its master. A catalogue-wide test holds all fifty-eight, **and none is written as a rectangle for other programs** (Gane-Sarson's Process is its rounded box, four arcs, and its Data Store its three sides in a set with `F`, where both were a rectangle with a note; so were thirteen of Basic Flowchart Shapes' masters); DiaCraft's extension still carries the rows that the outline does not give back exactly.

## DiaCraft's own stencils, second batch (STENCIL2)

The second batch gives the catalogue thirteen stencils of notation shapes (UML, BPMN, C4, network, cloud, crow's foot and Chen's) and fourteen templates, all drawn by the project in code. Built the foundation: the catalogue and the master format they grow in, and thirteen empty stencils and fourteen templates registered at once, so that the family tasks fill only their own files. **Nine of the thirteen are shipped**, with 116 masters (UML Class, UML Use Case, UML Sequence, BPMN Shapes, the C4 Model, Network Devices, Computers and Devices, Crow's Foot and Chen's), and nine of the fourteen templates are listed; UML Activity, UML State Machine, UML Component and Cloud Services and their five templates are not built. Every rule below is **ours**: the reference app was never taken apart. What the foundation holds:

* A stencil is listed when it has masters; ours. `ALL_STENCILS` registers twenty stencils: the seven above and the thirteen of this batch (`uml-class`, `uml-usecase`, `uml-sequence`, `uml-activity`, `uml-state`, `uml-component`, `bpmn`, `c4`, `network`, `computers`, `cloud`, `crows-foot`, `chen`), each with an id, a name, a category and the GUID series its masters will take. A stencil is **shipped** when it has masters (`StencilSpec::shipped`). `stencil::stencils()` is the shipped stencils in the order of the registration, made once, and it is the only list a command, a query or a window reads: `stencil.list` (its `stencils` and its `available`, which the More Shapes menu shows), `stencil.search`, `stencil.open`, `stencil.quick` and `shape.drop` reach a shipped stencil and no other, and `stencil.open` says of a stencil that is not shipped what it says of an id that is no stencil (`no built-in stencil ...`). Until a family task fills its stub the thirteen are in none of them. The categories are `Software and Database` (UML, C4, crow's foot and Chen's), `Flowchart` (BPMN) and `Network` (network, computers and cloud).
* The new stencils are closed by default; ours, owner 2026-11-25. A stencil is **open in a new session** when it is shipped and its `default_open` says so: the seven of the first batches are, the thirteen new ones are not. A blank drawing, a file that is not a template and a template that names no list have the seven open, as before; a template opens the stencils it names, and More Shapes and `stencil.open {id}` open the others. A search covers every shipped stencil, open or not.
* The master GUID form; ours. **A built-in master's `BaseID` is its fixed identity, `{D1AC<series as four hex digits>-0000-4000-8000-<ordinal as twelve>}`, and its `UniqueID` is another GUID, of its own** (`stencil/unique.rs`). The VSDX application keeps only the first three groups of a master's `UniqueID` (it puts a value of its own in the last two when it loads the file) and keeps `BaseID` as written (a tester's observation on the project's test PC, 2026-11-28, unverified until it is in the specs), so masters whose `UniqueID`s differ in the last two groups only were one master there: every drop from a stencil file of DiaCraft's gave the first master dropped, and a paste between two DiaCraft drawings gave the destination's master of that place. The `UniqueID` is a GUID of the version 4 form whose bits are a hash of the master's identity (series and ordinal) and of what it holds (the stamp of its part as the sheet codec writes it, with the `ID` 1 and no `UniqueID`): **the same built-in master has the same `UniqueID` in every drawing and file, a master built another way has another, and the first three groups differ from every other master's** (a test holds every master DiaCraft can make, the hidden line ends too, to it, and a stencil file of each built-in stencil). Drawings saved by 0.2.3 and the first builds of 0.2.4 hold built-in masters whose `UniqueID` is the `BaseID`'s text. **They are read as they are** (the drawing holds the ids the file had, and finds the masters by the `BaseID`, never by the form of the `UniqueID`), **and repaired when a VSDX file is written** (owner ruling, 2026-11-28: the splice into the drawing's own file, the model writer, a Save As, and every VSDX type, a stencil `.vssx` and a template `.vstx` too): a master whose `UniqueID` and `BaseID` are both exactly the text of one built-in master's `BaseID` (the form DiaCraft wrote, provably its own and known to read as one master with every other of its series) gets the `UniqueID` that master has today, keeps its `BaseID`, and is saved so; a hashed one of its own when the drawing holds a master with the first three groups of it already (`stencil::repair_old_ids`, which hands the writer the drawing with the masters repaired, so that the next save finds nothing more to change). **Every other master is written as it was read**: one that holds the text as its `UniqueID` and another `BaseID`, one in another spelling (lower case, white space, no braces), one the application that opens the file has passed through (its last two groups are its own), and every master of another program's file. A `.diacraft` and an `.odg` write the ids the drawing holds. Series 1 to 9 of the `BaseID` spell the text they always had, so no saved drawing loses its masters (finds them by it); series 10 and over are GUIDs of 38 characters where the old form was not (`D1AC000` and a two-digit series is nine digits). The series are 9 `uml-class`, 10 `uml-usecase`, 11 `uml-sequence`, 12 `uml-activity`, 13 `uml-state`, 14 `uml-component`, 15 `bpmn`, 16 `c4`, 17 `network`, 18 `computers`, 19 `cloud`, 20 `crows-foot`, 21 `chen` and 22 the hidden line-end masters. A test pins the cells the 58 masters of before build to (a stamp of each master's part as the sheet codec writes it, with the `UniqueID` it had then put back), so that the `BaseID`s and every cell are held. **A master of series 9 and up is at most 10 inches wide and tall** (a pool is 8 inches); the first seven stencils' masters stay within 3.
* A connector master keeps its look; ours. A one-dimensional master holds its **line ends, pattern and route as cells of its own shape** (`ConnectorLook`: the begin and the end, each none, a number, a formula of the shape's Shape Data with the number it gives, or a hidden master of ours; the line pattern 1 solid, 2 dash, 3 dot or 4 dash-dot, which the master may guard as `GUARD(n)` so that no format command changes it; the route straight, right-angled or the page's; a weight and a compound line), and **a shape dropped from it inherits them**: the instance holds `BeginX` to `EndY` and its frame, and no `BeginArrow`, `EndArrow` or `LinePattern`. The Gane-Sarson Data Flow is the look with no begin end and end 4, so it draws as before (its saved instance no longer holds `EndArrow`). `stencil.list` gives a one-dimensional master `ends: {begin, end, pattern}`, the numbers its cells resolve to (a master of ours that draws as a custom end gives 254), which the window draws a tile from. A connector the Connector tool makes (`connector.add`) is unchanged.
* An instance of a connector master holds no style link of its own; observed in the reference application on the project's test PC: the instances of the files it writes carry none, so style reaches an instance through its master shape. The Connector tool links a connector of its own to the root style for its three families, as a shape with no master needs, and a dropped connector master was that connector with the master named: it kept the links. **The reference application reads an instance's own `LineStyle`, `FillStyle` and `TextStyle` before its master's cells of those families** (our reading of its check): in that check every instance of a built-in connector master read the root's `BeginArrow` 0, `EndArrow` 0 and `LinePattern` 1, whatever the master held, plain numbers and formulas alike (the UML, BPMN, C4, crow's foot and Gane-Sarson lines lost their ends and dashes there). That the link is the cause is our reading, unverified until the application's check of this build. So `shape.drop` of a one-dimensional master takes the three links off the instance (`draw/shapes.rs`, `drop_connector`): it follows its master shape's styles, and its line ends, pattern and No Fill (the owner's ruling of 2026-11-27 that a connector's hollow ends are empty by default) reach it in every file a save writes, the model writer's, the splice's and a Save As from a `.diacraft` or an `.odg` drawing (an `.odg` gives the instance the look as cells of its own, and a link to the graphic style it read). DiaCraft draws it as before: with no link of its own an instance follows its master shape's (step 3). **`shape.change` drops a link that is the new master's own** (keeps every other): a link of the shape that names the style the new master's one shape links for the family, no link counting as the root's, is no formatting of the shape's, so a connector of the Connector tool changed to a connector master takes the master's styles; a link to the `Theme` style, or to any other, stays. A file's own instances are as they were. **On a page with a theme the master's shape takes the link, and not the instance** (the application's check of the earlier build read every instance of the connector masters as the style's `THEMEVAL()` after `theme.apply`, a solid line with no ends), so the instance keeps no link there either. `crates/engine/tests/it/master_line_cells.rs` reads the bytes each route writes for every one-dimensional master of the catalogue.
* A line end drawn from a master; and DD18, which replace the design's rule of a unit form drawn in number 22's box; what the documentation leaves open is ours. A `BeginArrow` or `EndArrow` of 254 whose formula is `USE("<name>")` (or a GUID in braces) names **a master pattern**: a master of the drawing whose `NameU` or `UniqueID` it is and whose `PatternFlags` holds 2 (256 keeps the end upright, 1024 scales it). The renderer draws it as the documentation says: **the master's pin** (`LocPinX`, `LocPinY`) **is put on the line's end point and the master is drawn pointing right**. An end that turns with the line points the way the line runs there, an upright one keeps the page's orientation. **An unscaled end is as tall as the line is heavy at Medium size**: the height of the master's alignment box (its top shape's `Height`) is the weight, and the drawing, which may be larger than the box, is scaled with it; a scaled end keeps the master's own size under the page's scale whatever the weight and the size class. It takes the line's colour and transparency (a section that fills is filled, one that outlines is stroked one weight wide; text and gradients in the master are not drawn), a turning end cuts the line where its drawing's back is, and an upright one does not trim it. **A file's custom end is drawn the same way**, where the design drew only DiaCraft's own form. **What the documentation leaves open is ours:** at size class *n* the box is the weight times the unit at class *n* over the unit at Medium (both at the weight), the line is cut at the back of the geometry, and at the **begin** the end points out of the line, away from its other vertices, as a numbered mark does. **Drawn as number 4 with the note, as before:** a `USE` that names no master, a master with no 2 in its flags, one with no geometry, more than one top shape, more than **16 sections, 256 rows, 32 shapes or 4 levels of groups**, and one whose box has no height. A weight of 0 is a box with no height and draws nothing, with no note.
