The master's rows are counted before anything is built (`custom_end::survey`) and charged as work (`WORK_PER_END_ROW` a row, `WORK_PER_DRAWN_SHAPE` a shape), so a page of lines that name one master is counted, and the line ends of the master's own shapes are not drawn (a `USE` among them is not followed). **The master `line-end.filled-diamond`** (the hidden list `stencil/line_ends.rs`, series 22, in no stencil, named Filled Diamond) is the first: `PatternFlags` 2, a square box (`Width` equals `Height`, `h`, 0.05 inch) with its pin at the middle of the right edge, and one filled section with no outline from the tip back **20 h** along the line with its sides **10 h** back and **5 h** across, so at the default weight of 0.75 point it is 15 points long and 7.5 across; its shape's own fill is black, for a program that draws a master by its own look. A connector that uses it names it in `More::brings`, so a drop copies it into the drawing first, and a `.vsdx` that holds it says `PatternFlags` 2 on its master row; no other master of the catalogue holds a flag. **`.odg`:** the writer knows DiaCraft's own diamond by the name `Filled Diamond` in the cell's `USE` and writes it as a marker of its own, `DiaCraft_20_end_20_254` (a box of 1000 by 2000 with the tip at the middle of the top side, as wide as ten boxes are tall: 7.5 points at 0.75 point and size 2, the size class read back from the width), with the cell carried as for every custom end, so another program draws a diamond where DiaCraft draws one; the engine's copy of a new connector keeps the `USE` of its custom end, so the line is still drawn from its master after a save and a reopen. **Not written to the `.odg`:** a master of another form (a custom end that names any other master is number 4's marker as before: a marker is one path in the line's colour scaled by one width, and a master may be a group of several fills), and the upright and scaled flags (a marker turns with its line and has no page scale); the cell and the master carry them for DiaCraft.
* A one-dimensional figure that is not routed; ours. A `Fixed1D` master draws its **own geometry** in the line's frame (x along the line as shares of `Width`, y across it in fixed lengths, which follow the page's drop scale) and is dropped horizontal with its ends the master's width apart, centred on the drop point. Its instance holds no route marker (`User.DiaCraftRoute`) and no route of its own, and the master's `ShapeRouteStyle` 16 keeps a reroute off it: its ends glue as a connector's do (`connector.reconnect`), and a move of a shape it is glued to carries the end and stretches the figure along the line, whose geometry is the master's. (The network's Comm-link and UML's Self Message are of this kind. In an `.odg` each is the polyline it draws while it is glued at no end, and a connector of the type `line` glued to its shapes when it is.)
* Geometry made by a function; ours. A master of the `Code` outline runs a function when it is built and gets its `Geometry` sections from the paths it returns, for figures with repeats. **A master is held to 64 `Geometry` sections, 1,024 rows and 128 connection points** (`stencil::caps_problem` says in words what goes past; the catalogue's test calls it for every master, and a build is cut at the caps whatever a function made). A coordinate of a path is shares of `Width`, `Height` and `MIN(Width,Height)`, a fixed length in inches, and one **corner radius** that gives way on a small box, `MIN(<r>,MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`, so a rounded box keeps its corners until the box is four of them across. **The fixed length and the radius are written times the factor of the page's drop scale** (`<length>*IF(DropOnPageScale>0,DropOnPageScale,1)`, `MIN(<r>*IF(...),MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`), so that a figure is the same on paper at every scale. A text block may lie **outside the box**: `LABEL_BELOW` is 1.6 times as wide as the figure and below it, its `Txt*` cells formulas of `Width` and `Height`. A section may be hidden (`NoShow`) or unstroked (`NoLine`) by a constant or by a formula of the Shape Data, which the build settles.
* What a master wears besides its outline; ours. A `Dress` is `orgchart::decorate` as data, for any master: a fill formula (`FillForegnd`, with `FillPattern` solid unless the dress says), a line weight and pattern, a text (placeholder text, or **fields** that show Shape Data, each in its own character format), the `Character` rows, the **Shape Data** rows (string, fixed list, boolean and number, typed as `shapedata.define` types a new row), `User` rows, protection cells (`LockHeight`, `LockRotate`, `LockTextEdit`), `SelectMode`, `IsTextEditTarget` and `ObjType` (1 for a shape people join: the dress of the masters of Basic Shapes, the Basic Flowchart and the Gane-Sarson shapes says it, and so does every two-dimensional master of the second batch's stencils that is shipped: each family's own dress says it; BPMN's masters hold it, its Pool and Lane hold 4, as do the Swimlane and the Separator of the Cross-Functional Flowchart Shapes, whose dress is the `Dress::NEITHER`), and a **role**: a plain shape, a **container** (typed `User.msvStructureType` `Container` with its heading side, margin, resizing as needed and no style row, so that a container command leaves the master's outline alone), a **part** of a structure (a drop of it goes into the structure) or a **pointless** shape that has no connection point (a title, a key). A shape dropped from a master keeps its **placeholder text as its own text**, as it keeps the text that shows fields, so that every format reads it back the same (an `.odg` holds no master to take a text from). Every formula in a dress has **no value in the table**: the master's build works the master out alone, in a scratch document, so that a cached value is what its formula gives at the master's default Shape Data and size. A master may also **bring** other built-in masters (`More::brings`: a connector brings its hidden line end), which `ensure_master` copies in first, and may be **hidden** from the window and the listings. The organization chart keeps its own code, which writes its `ObjType` 1 too.
* The figures and point sets the families share; ours, drawn in code from the notations' generic forms. Point sets: the four middles of the sides, three on each side (twelve), eight on an ellipse (a diagonal one leaves along the horizontal axis, since the router knows the four ways out and no more), a diamond's four vertices, five on each long side of a bar and one at each end (twelve), and the stem of a lifeline as pairs facing left and right at even steps. Figures: a dog-eared note, a document with a folded corner, a rounded box, a vertical and a horizontal cylinder, a stick figure, a diamond and a 3-D box. Each has a unit test that its points are on its outline.
* A master that is a group of members; ours; are its drop. A master of the `Group` outline has a top-level shape of type `Group` with **no geometry of its own** and its members as the shapes 6 and up (at most 32: the build stops there and the caps check of the catalogue says so), because a shape has one fill, one line pattern and one text, and a class's three compartments, a lifeline's head over its stem and a marker inside a body are each members with their own. The group holds the connection points, the Shape Data, the locks and the group properties. **A member's frame is four formulas of the group and of the members above it** (`Sheet.5!Width`, `Sheet.6!Height`), each in `GUARD` (a table writes the bare formula and the build wraps it, `MemberFrame::Formulas`), **a fixed length in one being that length times the group's factor of the page's drop scale, `0.1*IF(Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale>0,Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale,1)`**, so that a click or a drag moves only the group: `shape.move` of a member alone is refused in words (`` `PinX` is protected by GUARD and cannot be changed by a drag ``) and changes nothing. **On an instance a formula that names a master shape reads the instance** (`Sheet.5` is the group, whatever shape of the page has the `ID` 5, and `Sheet.6` is the instance's own copy of that member, so two instances on a page never read each other): the rebinding of `calc` and its dependency walk already took a member's formula that names the group, a member's that names another member and a top-level formula that names members, so no fallback rule was built (the risk the design named). **`shape.drop` of one** (`draw::drop_shape_above`, then `stencil/instance.rs`, which is the code of a stencil file's group master) drops an instance that holds only its pin and lists a member for each member of the master, each with an `ID` of its own above the instance's, its master's type and `MasterShape`, no cell of its own, a local copy of its master shape's geometry, and, for a member whose master shape's text holds fields, that text (the shown form of a field lives in the text that holds it, and `text.update_fields` brings it up to date when the group's Shape Data changes: an edit refreshes the fields of the shape it changes, which is not the member). The group follows the page's theme as any group's members do, and it is copied, duplicated, turned, flipped, saved and undone as any group is. **A text of the group's own is refused by an `.odg` save** (a group's text is not written yet), so a table puts the text on a member and its dress says `IsTextEditTarget` 0. **An `.odg` writes a group as its members at their places** (a `draw:g` has no frame of its own), so a group of compartments reopened from an `.odg` draws as it did and holds its size, where a `.vsdx` and a `.diacraft` hold the formulas and go on following their text. `MasterSpec::is_group()` tells a group master.
* Compartments that follow their text; ours; the design's section 4.4. A member whose frame is a **compartment** (`MemberFrame::Compartment { rank, min_in }`, made by `kit::compartments([0.35, 0.5, 0.5])`, one frame for each member of a table) is as wide as the group, as tall as its text needs, `MAX(<least>*IF(Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale>0,Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale,1),TEXTHEIGHT(TheText,Width))` with the least in inches (times the factor the group holds, 1 where it holds none: **the least height follows the page's drop scale, **), and stands under the compartments of lower rank (0 is the top, and equal ranks stand in the order of the members). **The rank says where a compartment stands and the order of the members does not**: the order of the table is the order of drawing and of typing, and the member last in the table is the one typing on the selected group goes to, so the name of a class can be its top compartment and its last member. The group's `Height` is `GUARD` of the sum of its compartments' heights, its `LockHeight` is 1 and its `IsTextEditTarget` 0 (a dress that says otherwise wins). So **a line typed in a compartment makes the group taller in the same undo step**: `shape.set_text` of the member works out the cells that read its text, the member's height, the group's and the pins of the compartments under it, and one `edit.undo` takes the line and the height back. **The group grows and shrinks about its middle**: its pin stays at the middle of its box, which an `.odg` save needs to keep a group's frame (the pin of a group set away from the middle is a note the per-stencil check refuses). A compartment's text is plain text, since a text that holds fields is not measured. The work of the edit is that of the cells of its own group, the same count of steps and of cells walked on a page of 60 groups as on a page of 2, and a text of 100,000 characters in a compartment gives a finite, very tall group and one undo gives it back. `shape.resize` with `id` and the window's handles size such a group along its width and leave its height to its text.
* A stack is not rounded piece by piece; ours; give the rule for one shape and none for a stack. A theme with rounded corners (Tidepool and Plumline: `rndg` 76,200 and 114,300 EMU) gives every shape that follows its `Theme` style a `Rounding` through `THEMEVAL`, and a shape rounds each corner between two straight sides, for its stroke and its fill. A class, an entity and the rest of the masters of **compartments** are pieces that stand against one another, so each piece rounded all four of its corners: a notch in every join, and white wedges where the fill of a keyword meets the fill of its name. **Each compartment holds a `Rounding` of 0 of its own** (a cell on a sheet replaces the inherited one), with no theme and under every theme and variant, and the stack reads as one box with square corners: the model has no rounding of the outer corners alone. **The package** (a tab on a body, one shape of two paths, each of which rounded all four of its corners and left a notch where they meet) holds a `Rounding` of 0 of its own as well. A shape of one piece is still rounded, the other members of a group master (a lifeline's head, a fragment's tab, a key's rows, which stand apart or inside one another) are as they were, and the parts of a swimlane structure are the same. `shape.format` with `rounding` on a class gives its compartments the radius a person asked for, each rounded by itself. **A drawing keeps the master it holds**: one made before this fix (a build of this version made it) has compartments, and lanes, that still follow the theme's rounding until each is given a `Rounding` of 0. Tests: `tests/it/stacked_rounding.rs` (each of the seven masters under every theme and variant reads 0, and the picture of each under Tidepool and Plumline is the picture of it with every `Rounding` written 0; so are a BPMN pool's lanes and a cross-functional flowchart's).
* A table of search words for each family; ours. The id of a master of the second batch is `<stencil id>.<name>`, and `keywords::of` asks the table of the family named before the first dot, so each family task edits its own file.
* The tile of a one-dimensional master and of a group master; ours: no specification says how a window shows them. **A one-dimensional master of the engine's own** (a connector, or a figure drawn along a line) **has a tile that is a short line with the marks its list gives it**: `stencil.list`'s `ends: {begin, end, pattern}` are the numbers its `BeginArrow`, `EndArrow` and `LinePattern` cells resolve to, and the window knows no master by name. **Each mark is the kind gives its number** (a head, a triangle, a diamond, a disc or a square, a bar, a fork, and the groups of them: crow's feet, discs with bars, double triangles), drawn in code in **the box (for the numbers no source measures)**: its tip on the end vertex and its body lying back along the line, turned along the first and the last segment that has a direction, on every open path of the figure (at most 16) and on no closed one. **A solid mark is filled with the tile's ink** (`stencil_ink`, the graphite of both themes), a hollow one is an outline whose closed part is painted with the tile's fill (`stencil_fill`, transparent in both themes as the body of every tile is) before the outline, an open one is strokes; the line stops short of a solid or hollow mark, 0.1 `S` under a solid one, and **the marks are never dashed**. The unit `S` is 0.09 of the figure's longest side whatever the line's weight (a tile is not a page: the Triangle, number 4, is 0.18 of the line long, as the Data Flow's head always was), made smaller where two marks would take more than 0.6 of a short line. **The line follows the pattern** (the marks and gaps in weights, each weight 0.75 of the tile's pen; a dot is a pen long; pattern 0 is drawn solid, so that a tile is never empty). **A custom end (254) is drawn as number 4**, as a page draws it today: the list gives the number and not the master, so a tile cannot show the master's own art. A number that is none of the 45 draws no mark. A master of a stencil file keeps its own outline and is given no ends. **The box of a one-dimensional figure holds its frame and its geometry together**, so that a loop that goes out farther than the line is long is not cut off. **A group master's tile draws the outline of each of its members at every depth, and the group's own geometry, and not the group's box**, which holds nothing of its own: at most 256 members and 20,000 points, in the order the group has them; a group set to select the group only (`SelectMode` 0) is drawn to its members too. **A tile draws only what the page paints of the shape**: a `Geometry` section that is hidden (`NoShow`) is left out, and so is a path the page neither strokes nor fills (a section's `NoLine`, or the shape's `LinePattern` 0, gives no stroke, and a section's `NoFill`, or the shape's `FillPattern` 0, no fill; the box a group's member holds its name in has no line and no fill), and so is the own geometry of a shape whose `DisplayMode` is 0. The rule is the renderer's (`SectionFlags::paint` of `diacraft-geom`, read through the same cells), so the markers that a BPMN gateway, event, task or data object hides at its default Shape Data are not in its tile, and a path that comes back to where it began, a circle among them, is an outline and not a line with a gap. The box a tile is fitted to holds the shape's frame and the paths it draws, and not the boxes of members that paint nothing. A figure with nothing to draw (a label with no line and no fill) is a box of the master's size, as before. The drag preview and the Pan & Zoom picture draw by the same rule. **The pointer reads the same cells** (a hit test ignores hidden geometry: a path that is shown and paints nothing is still the shape's): it passes over a shape whose geometry is all hidden and that is not a group and shows no text (a marker a group's member hides), and meets every other shape inside its shown outline, a text box or a shape with no line and no fill among them; a shape whose geometry is all hidden and that shows text (its own, or its master shape's) is met in its frame, which is its text block, as a shape with no geometry is. A text block is met wherever it lies.
* Templates are registered at once and listed when they ship; ours. `template::registered()` holds eighteen templates: the four of the first batches and fourteen of this one, in the order File > New lists them: `uml_class`, `uml_use_case`, `uml_sequence`, `uml_activity`, `uml_state_machine`, `uml_component`, `uml_deployment`, `bpmn_diagram`, `c4_diagram`, `basic_network`, `cloud_architecture`, `crows_foot`, `chen_notation` and `gane_sarson`. Each is a blank Letter page, landscape, with no theme, and its description names the notation and its version and says "based on" and what is not built. **A template is listed (`template.list`, `template::templates()`, `template::find`) only when every stencil it names is shipped**; `file.new {template}` of one that is not says it is no template. Today that is the **Data Flow Model (Gane-Sarson)** template (`gane_sarson`: the Gane-Sarson shapes and then the Basic Shapes) and the **Basic Network Diagram** template (`basic_network`: the Network Devices, the Computers and Devices and the Basic Shapes) and the **C4 Model Diagram** template (`c4_diagram`: the C4 Model shapes and then the Basic Shapes), so seven templates are listed. **The Crow's Foot Database Notation** template (`crows_foot`: the crow's foot shapes and then the Basic Shapes) **and the Chen's Database Notation** template (`chen_notation`: the Chen shapes and then the Basic Shapes) are listed too, so nine templates are listed. **The UML Class** template (`uml_class`: the UML Class shapes and then the Basic Shapes) **and the UML Use Case** template (`uml_use_case`: the UML Use Case shapes and then the Basic Shapes) are listed, **the UML Sequence** template (`uml_sequence`: the UML Sequence shapes and then the Basic Shapes) from and **the BPMN Diagram** template (`bpmn_diagram`: the BPMN shapes and then the Basic Shapes), so **thirteen templates are listed**: the four of the first batches and nine of this one.
* **Tests.** `stencil/catalogue_tests.rs` holds the catalogue's rules and the invariants every shipped master keeps (unique and namespaced ids, unique GUIDs, one series for each stencil, sizes, formulas that parse and values that are the formulas', paths that close where they fill, every connection point on the drawn outline and facing away from it, the caps, search words for every master of the second batch, and a connector master's ends), so that each family is held to them as it ships. `tests/it/stencils2_support.rs` holds the five per-stencil checks of the design (drop, edit and undo; render inside the box; round trips through `.vsdx`, `.odg` and `.diacraft`; glue; themes), and each of the thirteen `tests/it/stencils2_<stencil>.rs` files runs them (the checks of one shape pass over a master whose drop makes a structure, `MasterSpec::makes_structure`, BPMN's Pool) over `builtin_stencil(<id>)`'s masters: **while a stencil has no masters they pass on nothing, and the day it ships they run on every master**.

Each family task fills its stencil below and says what each master is, its fields and variants, the rules that are ours and what is not built.

### UML Class and UML Use Case

Two stencils of UML 2.5.1 shapes, drawn by the project in code, in the category `Software and Database`: **UML Class** (`uml-class`, GUID series 9, fifteen masters) and **UML Use Case** (`uml-usecase`, series 10, nine). Both are **shipped and closed in a new session**: the **UML Class** template (`uml_class`) opens the class stencil beside the Basic Shapes, the **UML Use Case** template (`uml_use_case`) the use case stencil, and More Shapes and `stencil.open {id}` open them anywhere else. Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/uml_class.rs` and `uml_usecase.rs`, with their tests in `uml_class/tests.rs` and `uml_usecase/tests.rs` (and `crates/ui-egui/tests/it/uml_class_text.rs` for typing on a class in the window). The notation spec (DD1 and DD19) wins over the design where they differ. The reference app was never taken apart; every rule below is **ours** unless it says it rests on the spec.

* The masters, in the Shapes window's order; ours, the design's tables. UML Class: `uml-class.class` Class 1.6 × 1.2, `uml-class.interface` Interface 1.6 × 1.24, `uml-class.enumeration` Enumeration 1.6 × 0.96, `uml-class.package` Package 2.4 × 1.6, `uml-class.data-type` Data Type 1.6 × 0.96, `uml-class.object` Object 1.6 × 0.8, `uml-class.note` Note 1.4 × 0.8, and eight lines 1.5 long: `association`, `directed-association`, `aggregation`, `composition`, `generalization`, `realization`, `dependency` and `note-link`. UML Use Case: `uml-usecase.actor` Actor 0.5 × 1.0, `use-case` Use Case 1.6 × 0.8, `subject` Subject 3.0 × 4.0, `note` Note 1.4 × 0.8, and five lines: `association`, `include`, `extend`, `generalization` and `note-link`. **The Quick Shapes are the first four that are no line** (the design's order, which puts the Package before the Data Type): Class, Interface, Enumeration, Package, and Actor, Use Case, Subject, Note. Every two-dimensional master holds `ObjType` 1 (a shape people join), so a route goes round it from the start. Each stencil has its own Note and Note Link, so that each is complete for its kind and keeps one GUID series.
* A classifier is a group of compartments; the spec's; are the mechanism. A class is a group master of three compartments: the **name** (bold, 11 points, centred), the **attributes** (`+ attribute : Type`) and the **operations** (`+ operation()`), each 10 points, **flush left and starting at the top** of its compartment (`HorzAlign` 0 and `VerticalAlign` 0). Each compartment is as tall as its text needs and at least 0.4 inch (on paper, at every scale), and stands under the one above, so **a line typed in the attributes makes that compartment, and the class with it, one line taller** (in the same undo step as the text) and a shorter text gives the height back. The class holds `LockHeight` 1: **a resize changes its width only**, and the compartments keep their heights. The class is selected first (`SelectMode` 1), and **typing on the selected class edits its name**: the name is the member last in the master's table, which is where typing on a group with `IsTextEditTarget` 0 goes, though it is the compartment at the top (rank 0 is the top and the order of the table is not the stack's). A double click on a compartment of the selected class edits that compartment. The text of a compartment is plain (a text with fields is not measured), and **its placeholder is the master's text until the compartment is typed in** (a member of an instance holds no text of its own until it is typed in), where the placeholder of a single shape (a use case, a package, a note) is the shape's own. **An interface, an enumeration and a data type have the keyword as a compartment of its own above the name**, `«interface»`, `«enumeration»` and `«dataType»`, in 9 point plain type and centred, so that the keyword is plain and the name beneath it bold, and **no line stands between the keyword and the name**: the two share a compartment, whose fill is drawn with no outline and whose line is the edges that are the classifier's own (the keyword has no margin under it and the name none over it, so that they stand close). An interface has attributes and operations (1.6 × 1.24 with the least heights 0.26, 0.3, 0.34 and 0.34), an enumeration a compartment of `LITERAL`, a data type attributes (1.6 × 0.96 each, 0.26, 0.3 and 0.4), and an **object** a name, `object : Class`, in bold type that is **underlined**, over its slots, `attribute = value` (1.6 × 0.8, 0.4 each). The design says an enumeration has `«enumeration»` over `Enumeration`, one text; the keyword is its own compartment so that the name typed on it stays bold and the keyword is edited alone.
* An abstract class has an italic name. The class holds a Shape Data row `Abstract` (a boolean, false). The name's `Style` is the formula `IF(Sheet.5!Prop.Abstract,3,1)`: bold, and bold and italic when `Abstract` is true (bit 1 of `Style` is bold and bit 2 italic), so setting the row (`shapedata.set {id, row: "Abstract", value: "yes"}`, or the Shape Data window) turns the name over and setting it false turns it back, in one undo step each. A format a person applies to the name replaces the formula, as any format does. Only the class has the row: an interface is abstract by nature, and an object, an enumeration and a data type have no such name.
* The package and the subject are containers; DD1. The package is one shape, a body whose top edge is a quarter inch under the top of the box (less in a box smaller than an inch: the tab's height is a corner-radius term, `MIN(0.25*IF(DropOnPageScale>0,DropOnPageScale,1),MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`, a quarter inch on paper at every scale, which an `.odg` writes as the value it has, where it has no place for a fixed length) and a **tab** over the left 0.4 of the box that stands on it, and its master has the container role (heading at the top, margin 0.25 inch, resizing as needed, and no style row, so that no container command makes its outline again): **a class dropped inside it joins it and a move of the package takes its members**, and `container.fit` and `container.margin` change its box and never its outline. **The name is typed at the top left of the box, which is in the tab at any size**: the text block is the whole box, flush left and starting at the top (the tab is kept always, DD1's option, so a package with no members shows its name in the tab). Its twelve connection points are on its outline and face away from it: one on the tab's top, two on the body's top beside the tab, and three on each of the other sides. **The subject** of the use case stencil is the same idea: a rectangle with its name at the top left, a container with a quarter inch of margin, twelve points (`GRID3`). **A container is no shape for the AutoConnect strip to offer**: the package and the subject stay Quick Shapes where they are, and the strip passes over them (`stencil.quick`'s listing says `autoconnect: false`).
* (the lines; the spec's and its V1; the design's section 6.1). Each line is a connector master that holds its ends, pattern and route as cells of its own shape, which a drop inherits; `stencil.list` gives each its `ends: {begin, end, pattern}`. Class: **association** none and none, solid; **directed association** none and an open head (3); **aggregation** a hollow long diamond (22) **at the begin, the whole's end** (DD19), solid; **composition** the filled diamond at the begin (the hidden master `line-end.filled-diamond`, which the connector brings into the drawing, `BeginArrow` `USE("Filled Diamond")` with the value 254); **generalization** a hollow triangle (16) at the end, solid; **realization** the same, dashed (2); **dependency** an open head (3), dashed; **note link** no ends, dashed. Use case: **association** none; **include** and **extend** dashed with an open head (3) and the keyword `«include»` or `«extend»` as the line's own text, in 9 points; **generalization** a hollow triangle; **note link** dashed with no ends. The class stencil's relationships are **routed at right angles** (`ShapeRouteStyle` 1, as the class diagram's are) and its note link is straight (2); every line of the use case stencil is **straight** (2: a use case diagram's lines run between figures at any angle). **A line's label is its own text**, typed on it. Multiplicity and role names at the ends of a line, and a navigability cross, are not built: type them in the label.
* The use case shapes. **Actor** is the kit's stick figure, 0.5 × 1.0 inch, with its name in a block under it (`kit::LABEL_BELOW`, 10 points, centred): a head, a body, arms and legs. It has **five connection points on the figure**, the top of the head, both hands and both feet, each facing away from it (the design says four, with the middle of the feet; the legs part, so the middle of the feet is not on the figure and each foot has its own). **Use Case** is an ellipse with its name inside and eight points round it (`RING8`). **Subject** is above. **Note** is the dog-eared box of the class stencil with the same plain text, flush left and starting at the top. A note's four points are the middles of its sides.
* Search words; ours, plain English. Every master has words, and the names a drawing of the reference app carries for these figures (the inventory's C67, C69 and C75: Member, Composite, Inheritance, Interface Realization, Package, Subsystem, Use Case, Actor, Association, Include, Extend, Generalization) each find the master that serves the purpose: `Subsystem` finds the subject, `Inheritance` the generalization, `Interface Realization` the realization, `Member` and `Composite` the class.
* What grew for these masters. A dress sets **row cells** (`RowCell`): one cell of one row of a section the dress holds or makes, as a number or as a formula with no value in the table (the build settles it): the paragraph's `HorzAlign` of row 0, and the formula in the name's `Character` row. The shape-level cells a text block needs (`VerticalAlign`, and the margins `TopMargin` and `BottomMargin`, which a keyword and the name under it set to 0) are written through the dress's `locks` list as before. A dress holds at most 16 row cells.
* What a save does. A drop saves and reopens in a `.vsdx` and in `.diacraft` as the shape it is: the same drawing, the same connection points, the master link kept, and saved again as no edit (`tests/it/stencils2_uml_class.rs` and `stencils2_uml_usecase.rs` hold all 24 masters through the five per-stencil checks). **In an `.odg`, a drop is saved and read back as the session had it** (DiaCraft's extension carries the master), and **other programs see the outline each of the 24 masters draws, not a rectangle, and the save gives no note for it** (a test holds it for each; LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 drew all 24 as their figures on 2026-11-26). Other programs see the figures a group is made of, the members at their places: a class is its three compartments, each its own rectangle with its own text, and, as a `draw:g` has no frame, **a class read from an `.odg` by another program no longer follows its text** (the compartments keep the heights they had when it was saved); a `.vsdx` and a `.diacraft` keep the formulas. **Three things other programs do not carry** (LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 drew each so): a dashed line (the realization, the dependency, the note link, the include and the extend) is drawn **solid**, since the writer writes the line patterns 0 and 1 and a dash needs a `draw:stroke-dash` of its own (did not change the writer: every dashed line of any drawing is drawn so); the keyword of an include or an extend is written in the line and not visible; and the actor's name, whose text block lies outside the shape's box (which an `.odg` has no place for), is drawn inside the box, across the figure's arms.
* **Not built.** The class's compartment of receptions, members as the rows of a list that stacks, grows and takes a dropped member (the compartments follow their text, and a member is a line of it: M4's lists), a stereotype as a property that a menu shows and hides (a stereotype is text, the keyword and the typed line above a name), multiplicity and role names at the ends of a line and the cross of a non-navigable end, a plain Dependency line in the use case stencil (the inventory's list has one; the include and extend lines are dependencies, and the stencil has a note link in its place), the actor drawn as a classifier rectangle with `«actor»` (allows it), and extension points in a use case.

### UML Sequence

The UML Sequence stencil (`uml-sequence`, series 11, in Software and Database, closed in a new session and opened by the UML Sequence template or `stencil.open {id: "uml-sequence"}`) holds **fourteen masters drawn in code**, in the order the Shapes window lists them: **Lifeline, Actor Lifeline, Activation, Combined Fragment, Destruction, Operand Separator, Interaction Use, Note, Message, Asynchronous Message, Reply Message, Create Message, Self Message and Note Link**. The figures and the notation are UML 2.5.1's (clause 17; DD2 and DD3, which win over the design where they differ); every rule below is **ours** where the standard leaves the form open. Every figure holds `ObjType` 1 (a line holds no 1: a message is routable, `ObjType` 2 of its own as every connector is, and the Self Message, a fixed figure, holds none), and the Quick Shapes are the first four that are no line: Lifeline, Actor Lifeline, Activation and Combined Fragment (so the Destruction stands after the fragment, where the design's table had it before).

* A lifeline is a head over a dashed stem. A **Lifeline** (1.2 by 3 inches) is a group of two members, the **stem** (a stroke down the middle of the box, `LinePattern` 2, as long as the height less the head: `MAX(0,Height-0.4)`) and the **head** (a rectangle of the group's width and 0.4 inch, which takes the style's fill and holds the placeholder `object : Class`, the member last in the group, so that typing, F2 and a double click on the selected lifeline edit it: `IsTextEditTarget` 0). An **Actor Lifeline** (1 by 3 inches) is the stem (from 0.85 inch under the top), the **figure** (the kit's stick figure, 0.4 by 0.6 inch at the top) and the **name** (an unfilled, unstroked strip of the group's width and 0.25 inch under the figure, holding `Actor`, the last member). `SelectMode` 1 selects the group first. **Both hold `LockWidth` 1** (a stretch of several lifelines keeps the width of each head, puts their middles where the stretch puts them and sizes each along its height; `shape.resize` of one lifeline by `id` writes a size that is a number, as it always did, so a head's width can still be changed by hand). The members' frames are `GUARD`ed formulas of the group, so the head and the stem follow its height and nothing but the group moves.
* Where a message glues on a lifeline. A lifeline has **43 connection points**: three on the head (the middle of its top, leaving up, and the middles of its sides, leaving left and right; an actor's are the top of its head and its two hands) and then **twenty pairs on the stem**, down the middle, **one pair at each twentieth of the box under its first 0.85 inch, from 0.95 of the way up to the foot**, one point of a pair leaving to the left and the other to the right (a pair is two points in one place, so that a message from the right of one lifeline to the left of another is straight). Each is a formula of the box (`Height*0.95-0.8075`), so **the points follow the lifeline's height**: a message glued to the same pair of two lifelines of one height is level (`BeginY` equals `EndY`, the message is not turned), and stays level when both move; a lifeline that is made taller moves the pairs apart. **The steps begin 0.85 inch under the top on both kinds of lifeline** (the height of an actor's figure and its name, and a lifeline's own head is 0.4 inch), so that a step is at one height on all of them, and a message between an actor and an object glued to the same step is level too; the object's stem is drawn from its head, and has no step in the 0.45 inch between. The design's `STEM(20)` has the pairs at the 21sts of the box from its top, which are not exact in decimals (a cell's cached value would differ from its formula's by the last place) and the first of which is inside the head, so the pairs are the twentieths and the last is at the foot, where a destruction goes. A head has three points and not four: the bottom of the head is where the stem begins, and its point would face into the shape.
* DD2. An **Activation** (0.16 by 1 inch) is a thin rectangle that **takes the style's fill (white), not the line colour**, and is dropped on a lifeline's stem; it holds twelve connection points, five at the odd tenths of each long side (a message meets the bar's edge) and the middles of its ends. Its label stands to the right of the bar (a block six times as wide as the bar), since the bar is too thin to hold text. A **Destruction** (0.3 by 0.3 inch) is **an X of two strokes** at 1.5 points, with its four arms' ends as its connection points and a label below it; it is a shape a person drops at a lifeline's foot, **not a menu item** of the lifeline.
* A combined fragment, an interaction use and an operand separator; DD3. A **Combined Fragment** (3 by 1.6 inches) is a **container** (`User.msvStructureType` `Container`, heading at the top; a shape dropped inside joins it, a move takes its members, and **it is not resized by Fit to Contents**, which passes over a group) and a group of three members: the **frame** (a rectangle with no fill, so that what lies under it shows), the **tag** (a pentagon 0.6 by 0.25 inch at the frame's top left, whose lower right corner is cut, in bold 8 point, with **a field that shows the Shape Data row `Operator`**) and the **guard** (a strip right of the tag, 1 inch wide at most and 0.25 inch tall, holding the placeholder `[condition]`, the last member, which typing goes to). **`Operator` is a fixed list of `alt`, `opt`, `loop`, `par`, `break`, `critical`, `neg`, `assert`, `strict`, `seq`, `ignore` and `consider`, `alt` at first** (DD3: the standard's default is `seq`, the design's `alt` is a choice of ours and stays). **The tag follows a change of the operator after `text.update_fields`, and not at once**: a field of a member reads its group's Shape Data and an edit of the group's data refreshes the fields of the group only. An **Interaction Use** (2.4 by 0.8 inch) is the frame with the style's fill, a `ref` tag 0.4 by 0.25 inch and the interaction's name over the whole box (`Interaction`, the last member). An **Operand Separator** (3 by 0.25 inch) is **a dashed line across the middle of its box**, with the guard `[else]` above the line in the left half of the box (the text block stands from the line to past the top of the box, so that the 12 point text is clear of the line), and four connection points: its two ends and its middle, once up and once down. A person drops it across a fragment: an operand is a separator, not a section the fragment adds (partial).
* The messages. The messages and the note link are **lines whose ends, pattern and route are the master's and which an instance inherits**, **straight** so that a message between two lifelines' points at one height is horizontal, with no begin end: **Message** (solid, the solid triangle 4, the placeholder `message()`), **Asynchronous Message** (solid, the open head 3, `signal`), **Reply Message** (dashed, open head, no placeholder), **Create Message** (dashed, open head, `«create»`) and **Note Link** (dashed, no end). **Self Message** (0.6 inch, with no placeholder text: see below) is a **`Fixed1D`** figure: a loop that goes **0.4 inch out across the line** (to the right when the message runs down, as the stem does) **and back**, with a solid head at the end; its two ends glue to two points of **one lifeline's stem** (the right-facing points of two steps), a move or a resize of the lifeline carries the ends and stretches the loop along the line (the far side is the line's length, the 0.4 inch is a fixed length), and no route is laid over it. A placeholder is **the line's own text** when it is dropped (`stencil::dropped_text`, as a dropped figure's is: an `.odg` holds no master to take a text from). **A line's label sits at the middle of the line, on it, in a block as wide as the line is long, and turns with the line**, as every line's does (the engine's rule: the text block of a line is its middle); a label beside the line, or above it, is not built. **So a Self Message has no placeholder** (the design's `message()`): its line is a few tenths of an inch between two steps of a stem and runs down, where the text would be wrapped to a letter or two a line and read sideways.
* **Not built (design §3).** A handle at the lifeline's foot (its length is its height, set as any shape's is: `shape.resize`, the window's handles and the Size & Position pane); a right-click switch of a message between straight, right-angle and curved (M4); connection points shown only while dragging; lost and found messages (DD5; the disc, 10, would draw the small circle); an operand added to a fragment by dropping on it (an Operand Separator is dropped across it); a destruction as a menu item of the lifeline; an activation that places itself on a stem and keeps its ends on it; a column of shapes that moves together with a lifeline. **For other programs**: the `.odg` save writes every master as the outline it draws (the groups as their members at their places), so **no master of this stencil is written as a rectangle for other programs**; the Shape Data, the tag's field (written as the text it shows), the container and the formulas are DiaCraft's own data, which another program's own save drops. **What LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 (the one black-box reader tried, on a drawing of every master and a diagram of them glued) shows of the `.odg`:** every outline as DiaCraft draws it, but **solid where DiaCraft draws a dash** (the stems, the separator, the reply, the create message and the note link: the writer does not yet write a dash for a new shape), **no label on a line**, **the self message as a straight arrow** (its loop is DiaCraft's data), the text larger than the page's, and the messages glued to stem points drawn at one height whatever their steps.

### BPMN

**BPMN Shapes** (`bpmn`, category Flowchart, GUID series 15, closed by default: a template or `stencil.open` opens it) holds nineteen masters drawn in code (`stencil/bpmn.rs`, the figures of its markers in `stencil/bpmn/markers.rs`), following BPMN 2.0.2 from the standard's public text; nothing of the standard's figures, the reference app's or another program's is traced or copied (`docs/provenance.md`). **The BPMN Diagram template** (`bpmn_diagram`) is listed now that the stencil ships: Letter landscape, no theme, opening `bpmn` and `basic`, described as based on BPMN 2.0.2 (it claims neither of the standard's conformance classes: the masters draw the figures and hold few of the attributes). The reference app was never taken apart. Every rule below is **ours** unless it says what the notation spec gives (and DD6 to DD12, which win over the design where they differ).

* The nineteen masters; ours. In the Shapes window's order: **Task** (1.4 by 0.9 inch), **Gateway** (0.6 square), **Start Event**, **End Event** and **Intermediate Event** (0.4 inch circles), **Sub-Process** (1.4 by 0.9), **Expanded Sub-Process** (3 by 2), **Call Activity** (1.4 by 0.9), **Data Object** (0.5 by 0.65), **Data Store** (0.7 by 0.6), **Message** (0.6 by 0.4), **Group** (2.5 by 1.6), **Text Annotation** (1.6 by 0.6), **Pool** (8 by 2), **Lane** (7.6 by 1.5) and the four lines, **Sequence Flow**, **Message Flow**, **Association** and **Data Association** (1.5 long). **The Quick Shapes are the first four that are no lines: Task, Gateway, Start Event, End Event.** The Pool and the Lane are parts of a structure, and the Expanded Sub-Process and the Group are containers, which the strip passes over for every stencil: all four stay off the AutoConnect strip. Every two-dimensional master holds `ObjType` 1, except the Pool and the Lane, which hold 4 as the reference's swimlane masters do (no route goes round them). Each master has search words, among them the inventory's sample names (Task, Gateway, Start Event, Sequence Flow, End Event, Pool / Lane, Collapsed Sub-Process, Data Store).
* Shape Data in the reference app's rows and words; ours where they say so. One stencil of base shapes, and a variant is a fixed-list or boolean Shape Data field that the Shape Data window sets (the reference app's right-click variants are Actions, M4, and a menu item will only write the same field): **Task** `BpmnTaskType` (None, Abstract, Service, Send, Receive, Instantiating Receive, User, Manual, Business Rule, Script), `BpmnLoopType` (None, Standard, Parallel MultiInstance, Sequential MultiInstance), `BpmnIsForCompensation`; **Sub-Process**, **Expanded Sub-Process** and **Call Activity** `BpmnLoopType`, `BpmnIsForCompensation`, `BpmnBoundaryType` (Default, Call, Event, Transaction: a thin, a thick, a dotted and a double border; Default, and Call for the Call Activity) and `BpmnAdHoc`; **Start Event** `BpmnEventType` (Start, Start (Non-Interrupting)) and `BpmnTriggerOrResult` (None, Message, Timer, Conditional, Signal, Multiple, Parallel Multiple, Escalation, Error, Compensation); **Intermediate Event** `BpmnEventType` (Intermediate, Intermediate (Non-Interrupting), Intermediate (Throwing)) and `BpmnTriggerOrResult` (None, Message, Timer, Escalation, Conditional, Link, Error, Cancel, Compensation, Signal, Multiple, Parallel Multiple); **End Event** `BpmnEventType` (End) and `BpmnTriggerOrResult` (None, Message, Escalation, Error, Cancel, Compensation, Signal, Terminate, Multiple); **Gateway** `BpmnGatewayType` (Exclusive, Exclusive Event (Instantiate), Inclusive, Parallel, Parallel Event (Instantiate), Complex), `BpmnExclusiveType` (Data, Event) and `BpmnMarkerVisible`; **Data Object** `BpmnCollection` and `BpmnDataRole` (None, Input, Output: ours, no reference row was seen); **Sequence Flow** `BpmnConditionType` (None, Expression, Default); **Association** and **Data Association** `BpmnDirection` (None, One, Both; a data association begins as One, since it is drawn as a directed association). **The intermediate event does not hold `BpmnDirection`**, which in the reference app's files is the association's direction. The rows the reference app also holds (`BpmnName`, `BpmnId`, `BpmnDocumentation` and the others) are not built. What separates None from Abstract in the reference app is unknown: **here both show no type marker** (ours).
* Markers; DD6 to DD9; ours in detail. Every marker is a `Geometry` section of its own whose `NoShow` is a formula of the Shape Data, **hidden unless the field holds exactly its word, so a word that is no item of the list shows the none marker** (a file can hold one; the Shape Data window refuses it). **A throwing or ending marker is dark and a catching one is hollow**: a dark marker is a member of the group that fills with **its own line colour** (`FillForegnd` is the formula `LineColor`), so it is as dark as the outline under any theme and follows the line colour put on the figure (a format is written in the members, and not in the group's own cells), and a fill put on the figure leaves it dark; a hollow one is outlines alone. An event shows a trigger only where Table 10.93 allows it for its kind, and **a trigger the table does not allow shows none** (a start event that is non-interrupting shows no error or compensation, an intermediate event that throws shows only message, escalation, compensation, link, signal and multiple, an interrupting intermediate event allows the union of the catching and the boundary triggers, since the master keeps no attachment). A task's type markers sit in its top left corner (a gear pair, a filled envelope for send and a hollow one for receive, a circled envelope for an instantiating receive, a head and shoulders, a hand, a small table, a page with lines); a gateway's markers are an X (shown by `BpmnMarkerVisible`), a circle, a plus, an asterisk, and the event-based forms (a pentagon in two rings, or one ring, and a plus in one ring); a data object shows a hollow arrow for an input, a dark one for an output, and three bars for a collection.
* The rings; DD8. A start event is a thin circle, an intermediate event two thin circles and an end event a thick one (3 points). **A non-interrupting event's ring is dashed** (pattern 2). **An event's name hangs under it**: the name is the text of the last member, whose box is the figure's and whose text block is below it (so that the group's frame is the box of its members, which an `.odg` save keeps), and typing on the selected group goes to it (`IsTextEditTarget` 0, `SelectMode` 1). A task's name and a sub-process's are inside; the Expanded Sub-Process's and the Group's are at the top.
* The borders of an activity; DD7. `BpmnBoundaryType` picks one: Default is thin and solid; **Call is thick** (2.25 points); **Event is dotted** (pattern 3, and not dashed: the reference's wording); **Transaction has a second border** just inside the first. In a Sub-Process and a Call Activity each border is a member of its own, since a member has one line weight and one pattern; in the Expanded Sub-Process, which is one shape, the thick border is two more outlines drawn just inside the first and the dotted one is its `LinePattern` formula.
* The markers along the bottom of an activity. A loop (a curled arrow), a parallel multi-instance (three vertical bars) or a sequential one (the bars turned a quarter), the ad hoc tilde, the compensation marker (two rewind triangles) and, on a Sub-Process and a Call Activity, the collapsed marker (a square holding a plus) stand in a row 0.2 inch apart **centred together**: each one's place is a formula of the Shape Data, so a loop alone is centred and a loop with a compensation marker is a centred pair. The Expanded Sub-Process, drawn as one shape, keeps each marker in a slot of its own (loop, ad hoc, compensation) and has no collapsed marker.
* The flows; the numbers and the guard are the reference app's masters'. **Sequence Flow** begins with no mark, ends with a solid head (4) and is solid, and its begin end follows `BpmnConditionType`: Expression 22 (a hollow diamond), Default 23 (a slash). **Message Flow** begins with a hollow disc (20), ends with a hollow triangle (16) and is dashed. **Association** and **Data Association** are dotted, and their ends follow `BpmnDirection`: None 0 and 0, One 0 and 3, Both 3 and 3. **A flow's `LinePattern` is `GUARD`ed in its master** (solid, dashed, dotted, dotted), so a format command that would change it is refused in words, which is the part of "BPMN refuses non-standard styling" that the ShapeSheet gives by itself; the other looks the standard forbids are not refused. A flow is routed as the page routes any connector, and the Connector tool and AutoConnect still start a plain connector (BPMN's default connector is not built).
* The Pool and the Lane are parts of the swimlane structure; DD11. **A Pool dropped** (`shape.drop`, `cmd/swimlane.rs`) **makes a structure**: a frame with its name in a strip on the left, 0.3 inch wide and **separated from what the pool holds by a line**, a list of lanes and one lane, 8 by 2 drawing units (inches on a page drawn 1 to 1, as every master's size is; **beyond the range of eight of the page's scale the pool keeps its size on paper**, 8 by 2 inches, every master do: the drop takes the rule where it is made, `cmd/shape.rs`; **the least of a lane, 0.4 inch, is held to the size in the unit it is in**, a drawing unit within the range and a paper inch beyond it, `draw::drop_scale::built_in_fit`, so a pool is dropped at every scale the page may have: at 1:8 it is 1 by a quarter inch on paper, and the least is not 0.4 times the page's drawing units to a paper inch, which at 1:6 to 1:8 is more than the master's 2 drawing units) centred on the point, the pool's name `Pool` and the lane's `Lane`; the answer is the frame's id with `master` null. **A Lane dropped on a pool is put into it**, as puts a Swimlane into a flowchart: before the lane it is dropped on when the point is in its first half and after it in its second, as thick as that lane. **A Lane dropped anywhere else, over a cross-functional flowchart included, is the shape the Lane master draws.** **A pool's lane has no line between its label and its contents** (the look of a lane in a box with a strip for its text, and not the cross-functional flowchart's lane with its divider), and the lane and the list of lanes of a pool hold `ObjType` 4 and the pool's frame 1, as the reference app's swimlane parts do. See the rule in "Swimlanes": the frame is the box of its lists and the strip, whatever lane is added, resized or moved, and turning the structure puts the strip on top. The pool survives a save and a reopen in `.vsdx`, `.diacraft` and `.odg` like any structure.
* What other programs see in an `.odg`; ours. An `.odg` save writes each master as the outline it draws, and DiaCraft reads its own back from the data kept with it. **The Expanded Sub-Process is the one master that other programs see as a rectangle** (the save says so in a note): its markers and the extra outlines of a thick or double border are fixed lengths, a form the writer does not write yet. The Text Annotation's bracket has arms of a share of its width for the same reason, so they grow and shrink with it. The Pool's drop is a structure of shapes (a frame, a list and a lane), written as the swimlane structures are.
* **Not built** (the design's section 3 and the spec): validation (a sequence flow refused across pools, a message flow within one, M8), the right-click variant menu and Set Connector Type (Actions, M4), a boundary event's attachment to its activity, BPMN's default connector for the Connector tool and AutoConnect, the full refusal of non-standard styling (only the flows' line patterns are guarded), the reference app's other attribute rows, and the starter diagrams. Where this differs from the design: the name of a gateway is under it (the design said beside it, where the connection points are), the Data Association's direction is a field (DD10) and begins as One, the Group's name is centred along its top (a dress has no paragraph alignment), and the Expanded Sub-Process keeps its markers in slots.
* **Tests.** `stencil/bpmn/tests.rs` holds the catalogue (ids, sizes, points, order, the Quick Shapes, search words), the Shape Data rows and words, `ObjType`, every value of every variant field showing exactly its marker and no other pixel (a table of sixty-one variants), a value that is no item showing none, the table of which trigger each kind of event shows, dark against hollow markers under three themes, the dashed, dotted, thick and double borders, the centred row, the flows' ends and guard, the Pool and the Lane (a structure, two lanes, a shape, a save and reopen in three formats, a turn), and the containers; `stencil/bpmn/markers.rs` holds the unit tests of the figures (inside the unit square, closed where they fill). The catalogue invariants and the five per-stencil checks (`tests/it/stencils2_bpmn.rs`) run on every master; the Pool, whose drop is a structure, is passed over by the checks of one shape (`MasterSpec::makes_structure`) and has the tests above.

### C4

One stencil of the C4 model's elements, drawn by the project in code, in the category `Software and Database`: **C4 Model** (`c4`, GUID series 16, twelve masters). It is **shipped and closed in a new session**: the **C4 Model Diagram** template (`c4_diagram`) opens it beside the Basic Shapes, and More Shapes and `stencil.open {id}` open it anywhere else. **C4 is an extra of DiaCraft's and has no parity row** (of the notation spec): the C4 model prescribes no notation, so the figures, the colours and the line are ours, and every rule below is **ours** unless it says it rests on the spec. Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/c4.rs` and `c4/tests.rs`. The notation spec wins over the design where they differ: the instance count is text, so that it can be a range, and the deployment node's label is at its bottom left with the boundary's (where the design said top left). The reference app was never taken apart.

* The masters, in the Shapes window's order; ours, the design's table with the sizes in inches. `c4.person` Person 1.4 × 1.5, `c4.software-system` Software System 2.0 × 1.3, `c4.container` Container 2.0 × 1.3, `c4.component` Component 2.0 × 1.2, `c4.database-container` Database Container 1.8 × 1.4, `c4.queue-container` Queue Container 2.2 × 0.9, `c4.boundary` Boundary 4.0 × 3.0, `c4.deployment-node` Deployment Node 4.0 × 3.0, `c4.infrastructure-node` Infrastructure Node 1.8 × 1.0, `c4.title` Diagram Title 4.0 × 0.6, `c4.key` Key 2.2 × 2.4 and `c4.relationship` Relationship 1.5 long. **The Component stands fourth**, before the database and the queue that the design's table lists first: the AutoConnect strip offers the first four masters that are no line, and the design says those are the Person, the Software System, the Container and the Component. Every two-dimensional master holds `ObjType` 1 (a shape people join; the boundary and the deployment node too, so that a route goes round one it does not start in or end in), and the relationship, a line, is a connector and holds no placeable flag.
* The figures; ours, plain geometry from shares of the box. A **person** is a round head over a rounded body, two closed outlines with a little room between them (the head's radius is 0.14 of the shorter side, 0.2 inch on the default size, standing on the top of the box); the **software system, container, component, deployment node** and **boundary** are rounded boxes (corners of 0.08 inch, 0.1 for the boundary, which give way on a small box); the **database container** is a vertical cylinder and the **queue container** a horizontal one; the **infrastructure node** is a plain rectangle (the model's examples draw an ellipse, which it allows to differ: DD13). The boundary is **dashed with no fill** (the model's examples draw it so; a choice, prescribe no border or colour), and the deployment node a light tint of the accent. Connection points: the person has four (the top of the head and the middle of each side of the body), the cylinders four (`SIDES`), the boxes, the boundary, the node and the infrastructure node twelve (`GRID3`, three on each side), and the title, the key and the relationship none.
* An element's text is three fields of its Shape Data; DD23. The **name** (bold, 11 points), the **type line** `[<Kind>: <Technology>]` (8 points) and the **description** (9 points), one over the other, each following its Shape Data row: a Container with the technology `Rust` shows `[Container: Rust]` under its name and one with no technology `[Container]`, with no colon; a blank technology is a technology, so it keeps the colon. A **person** and a **software system** have no technology: their type line is `[Person]` and `[Software System]`. The kinds are Person, Software System, Container (the database and the queue are containers: `[Container: PostgreSQL]`), Component and Infrastructure Node. A new shape shows `Name`, its type line and `Description`, which a person types over in the Shape Data window or replaces by typing on the shape. A text of 32,768 characters in a field is a value like any other, shown whole in the field and cut by the page renderer at 16,384 characters with a note, as any text is.
* The Shape Data; the design's rows. `Name`, `Technology` and `Description` are strings, and `External` is a truth value that starts false. The person and the software system hold `Name`, `Description` and `External`; the container, the database, the queue and the component `Name`, `Technology`, `Description` and `External`; the infrastructure node `Name`, `Technology` and `Description`; the boundary `Name` and `Kind` (a fixed list: Enterprise, Software System, Container, Group, which starts as Software System; Group is ours); the deployment node `Name`, `Technology` and `Instances` (a string, starting `1`, so that it can be a range such as `1-3`: the label shows `x 1-3`); the title `Diagram` (a fixed list: System Context, Container, Component, Deployment, Dynamic, System Landscape), `Title` and `Description`; the relationship `Description` and `Technology`. A fixed list takes only its items, so a kind or a diagram no item matches is refused in words and the shape keeps the one it had.
* The accents follow the theme; ours, design section 4.7. An element's fill is a formula of `THEMEVAL` with a default of ours, one base blue `#3A7FC0` and one grey: the **Container** (and the database and the queue) is the theme's `AccentColor`, the **Software System** a shade of it (`SHADE(...,25)`), the **Person** a darker one (`SHADE(...,50)`) and the **Component** a tint (`MSOTINT(...,50)`), and with no theme they are the blue, `#2E6698`, `#214A70` and `#9BBFE0`. **`External` true makes the fill the grey** `MSOTINT(THEMEVAL("Dark",RGB(0,0,0)),45)` whatever the kind and whatever the theme (a tint of the theme's dark colour under a theme, a neutral grey with none). **The text is light on the dark kinds** (`THEMEVAL("Light",...)`) **and dark on the Component** until it is external and grey. A format the person applies replaces the formula, as any format does. The deployment node is the lightest tint of the accent, and the infrastructure node keeps the style's fill. **A shape dropped into a page that has a theme has the theme's colours at once** (below): it is worked out as the shape is linked to the `Theme` style.
* The boundary and the deployment node are containers; ours, design section 4.4, the container masters. Each holds the container role (`User.msvStructureType` `Container`, the heading at the bottom and a margin of a quarter inch, resizing as needed, and no style row): **a shape dropped inside joins it, a move takes its members, and `container.fit`, `container.margin` and `container.auto_resize` change its box and never its outline**, which is its master's. `container.style` and `container.heading` refuse it in words. Deployment nodes nest, so a node dropped in a larger one is its member, and the boundary and the node hold what is dropped in them. **The label is at the bottom left**: a block over the lower left corner, 0.46 of the width and 0.2 of the height, with its text at the bottom of it (`VerticalAlign` 2): the boundary shows its name over `[<Kind>]`, the node its name, `[Deployment Node: <Technology>]` and `x <Instances>`. A dress has no paragraph alignment, so the text is centred in that block and not flush left.
* The title and the key. **No connector joins either**: each is of the pointless role and has no connection point. The **title** is text only, with no line and no fill, `[<Diagram>] <Title>` over the description (12 points bold and 9). The **key** is a group of five sample boxes, each named and filled with the colours of the masters it stands for (the same formulas, so a theme changes them too, and the External sample is the grey), and its own title `Key`. It holds `LockHeight` (its samples are boxes of a fixed height, so a resize changes its width only), `SelectMode` 1 and `IsTextEditTarget` 0: typing on the selected key edits its title, the member last in the table. Its members fill its box exactly, which an `.odg` save needs to keep a group's frame.
* The line. A one-dimensional master, **dashed, with a solid arrowhead at its end** (end 4) and none at its begin, routed as the page routes: the model prescribes no line style, so this is a choice it allows (DD13), and a format changes it as it changes any line. Its text is the **description over `[<Technology>]`** (9 points and 8), each following its Shape Data row, and a relationship with no technology shows no brackets. The label has a white background (`TextBkgnd` 2, which the reader takes as white) so that the dashes do not run through its words. **A line dropped from a master whose text holds fields keeps a text of its own** (changed `draw::drop_connector`, which gave a line none: the shown form of a field lives in the text that holds it, so a line with only its master's text could not follow its Shape Data). The text block of a line is as wide as the line, as for every connector, so the description of a short line wraps.
* Search words; ours, plain English. Every master has words for what the model calls it and what people call it: a person is also an actor or a user, a container a service or an application, a component a module, a database a data store, a queue a broker or a topic, a boundary a scope, a deployment node a host, the title a heading, the key a legend and the relationship a dependency. **No master has the words `arrow` or `process`**, which the window's searches of the first batches' masters pin (a search for them finds Arrow Shapes and Gane-Sarson, and the Basic Flowchart and Gane-Sarson). The Quick Shapes are the Person, the Software System, the Container and the Component.
* What a save does. A drop saves and reopens in a `.vsdx`, an `.odg` and `.diacraft` as the shape it is: the same drawing, the same connection points, the master link kept, and saved again as no edit (`tests/it/stencils2_c4.rs` holds all twelve masters through the five checks). **No master is shown to other programs as a rectangle in an `.odg`** (the person's head is two half circles). The key is a group, so an `.odg` writes it as its members at their places and a reopened key draws as it did.
* **Not built.** A legend that counts or finds the shapes a diagram uses, the model's code level, starter diagrams for each level (one template serves the context, container, component and deployment diagrams: the design leaves them to a later task), a boundary that sizes itself round its members as they are dropped (`container.auto_resize` does it when asked), a label flush left, and the dynamic diagram's numbered relationships.

### Network Devices and Computers and Devices

Two stencils of generic network figures, drawn by the project in code, in the category `Network`: **Network Devices** (`network`, GUID series 17, twelve masters) and **Computers and Devices** (`computers`, series 18, sixteen). Both are **shipped and closed in a new session**: the **Basic Network Diagram** template (`basic_network`) opens them beside the Basic Shapes, and More Shapes and `stencil.open {id}` open them anywhere else. The Cloud Architecture Diagram template waits for the Cloud Services stencil. Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/network.rs`, `computers.rs` and `network/` (`glyphs.rs`, the glyph kit; `fields.rs`, the Shape Data; `tests.rs`). The notation spec wins over the design where they differ (DD17: the design's five fields became the reference app's three groups, and the label shows the network name over the address). The reference app was never taken apart; every rule below is **ours** unless it says it rests on the spec.

* A device is a pictogram in an icon box; ours, drawn in code. Each device is a front-view pictogram inside an **icon box** whose size is the master's, built by the functions of `network/glyphs.rs` from rectangles, circles, arcs and strokes: a low box with a row of ports (router, switch, load balancer, modem), a wall of bricks in a frame (firewall), five arcs over a flat base (cloud), a low rounded box under three signal arcs (wireless access point), a globe of two meridians and two parallels (internet), a bar (Ethernet), a thick ring (ring network), a tower with drive bays and a power dot (server), a screen on a stand (desktop), an open lid over a base (laptop), a tower with a small badge of its role (a cylinder, a globe, a folder, an envelope, a window or a printer: the database, web, file, mail, application and print servers), a 2U box with bays and vents (rack server), a rounded slab with a screen and a button (tablet), a taller one with a speaker slot (mobile phone), a handset arched over a base of keys (telephone), a box with a sheet coming out of its top (printer), a box with three rows of drive slots (storage) and head and shoulders (user). **No vendor's mark, no icon set and no letter in a maker's style is drawn, and no master carries a vendor's or a product's name** (a test holds the words of ids, names and search words). The body is one or more filled sections that take the style's fill, and the details (ports, bays, bricks, arrows, badges) are stroke-only sections in the line colour, so a device follows every theme and every format a person applies; the one fill of ours is the Ethernet bar's, `THEMEVAL("Dark",RGB(0,0,0))` (the theme's dark colour, black with no theme). A coordinate is a share of the box written to nine places (so a cell's cached value is what its formula gives), an arc is an arc of an ellipse whose axes follow the box (a circle at the default size), and **everything lies inside the box**, at the default size and stretched to twice the width and half the height (`every_glyphs_strokes_lie_inside_its_icon_box`). **A section drawn later does not hide the line of one drawn earlier** (a shape has one fill and one line, and the fills are laid first): a badge over a tower's edge would show the edge through it, so a badged tower's fill draws no line and its outline stops where the badge begins, and a printer's sheet starts where its body ends.
* The masters, in the Shapes window's order; ours, the design's tables with the sizes in inches. Network Devices: `network.router` Router 1.0 × 0.6, `network.switch` Switch 1.2 × 0.5, `network.firewall` Firewall 0.9 × 0.8, `network.cloud` Cloud 1.4 × 0.9, `network.wireless-access-point` Wireless Access Point 0.9 × 0.8, `network.load-balancer` Load Balancer 1.0 × 0.6, `network.modem` Modem 1.0 × 0.5, `network.internet` Internet 0.9 × 0.9, `network.ethernet` Ethernet 6.0 × 0.12, `network.ring-network` Ring Network 2.0 × 2.0, `network.comm-link` Comm-link 1.5 and `network.link` Network Link 1.5. Computers and Devices: `computers.server` Server 0.6 × 1.0, `computers.desktop` Desktop 1.0 × 0.9, `computers.laptop` Laptop 1.1 × 0.75, `computers.database-server`, `web-server`, `file-server`, `mail-server`, `application-server` and `print-server` 0.8 × 1.0 each, `computers.rack-server` Rack Server 1.2 × 0.35, `computers.tablet` Tablet 0.6 × 0.8, `computers.mobile-phone` Mobile Phone 0.4 × 0.75, `computers.telephone` Telephone 0.8 × 0.6, `computers.printer` Printer 0.9 × 0.7, `computers.storage` Storage 0.9 × 0.8 and `computers.user` User 0.6 × 0.8. **The Quick Shapes are the first four that are no line**: Router, Switch, Firewall, Cloud, and Server, Desktop, Laptop, Database Server. Every two-dimensional master holds `ObjType` 1 (a shape people join), so a route goes round it from the start.
* The Shape Data; the spec's: the reference app's row names in its three groups, with labels and the order of ours. Every device holds the **equipment** group, nine rows: `Manufacturer`, `ProductNumber`, `PartNumber`, `ProductDescription`, `AssetNumber`, `SerialNumber`, `Location`, `Building` and `Room`. Every device but the firewall holds the **network** group after them, eight rows: `NetworkName`, `IPAddress`, `SubnetMask`, `MACAddress`, `AdminInterface`, `NumberofPorts`, `CommunityString` and `NetworkDescription`. The servers (all seven), the rack server, the desktop, the laptop and the tablet hold the **computer** group, four rows: `CPU`, `Memory`, `OperatingSystem` and `HardDriveSize`; and these and the two backbones (Ethernet and Ring Network) hold `Department` last (gives it to the computers, the samples show it on backbones too). So a router holds 17 rows, a firewall 9, a server 22 and the Ethernet bar 18. Every row is text, and every row starts empty but `NetworkName`, which starts as the device's kind (`Router`, `Database Server`). **The labels are ours**: the row name in spaced words (`Network Name`, `IP Address`, `MAC Address`, `Number of Ports`, `Hard Drive Size`). The two lines hold no device data. The mobile phone, the telephone, the printer, storage and the user hold the equipment and network groups as the spec's rule says ("every network device and computer but the firewall"); the spec's "five badged towers" is six masters here, as the sample names are (database, web, file, mail, application and print servers).
* The label. A device's label is **two fields of the master's text, `NetworkName` over `IPAddress`**: a switch with `core-sw-01` and `10.20.30.40` typed in the Shape Data window shows them one over the other, a freshly dropped router shows `Router` with an empty second line, and an empty field shows nothing on its line (the text follows the data). The text sits **under the figure** in a block 1.6 times as wide (`kit::LABEL_BELOW`; the Ethernet bar's is as wide as the bar and starts 0.048 inch under it), as a formula of the shape's width and height so it follows the figure, and it is **top aligned** (`VerticalAlign` 0, written with the dress's cells): a second line never climbs onto the figure. 9 points for the name and 8 for the address, in the style's colour. **The firewall holds no network rows**, so its label is plain text that starts as `Firewall`, which a person types over. **A placeholder text is the dropped shape's own** (changed `dress::dropped_text`, which gave a shape no text of its own for plain placeholder text): a shape that left it to its master read back from an `.odg`, which holds no master to take a text from, with the text as its own.
* The connection points; ours, on the drawn outline and facing away from it, as the catalogue's test holds. The middles of the sides (`SIDES`) where the outline reaches them: the router, switch, firewall, load balancer, modem, desktop, towers, rack server, tablet, mobile phone, telephone, printer and storage. The cloud, the wireless access point, the laptop and the user have the four places their outline does reach: the top, the bottom, and the sides of the body (the cloud's end lobes a third of the way up, the access point's base, the laptop's lid, the user's shoulders). The globe and the ring have the eight of `RING8`. **The Ethernet bar has eighteen**: eight along the top at the odd sixteenths of its length from the left, one at the left end, eight along the bottom the same way, and one at the right end. The backbone's arms (the reference app's built-in connectors, dragged to the devices by control handles) wait for control handles (M4): today a connector is glued to one of the bar's points.
* The two lines; ours, the design's. **Comm-link** is a `Fixed1D` figure: a zigzag of five legs, 0.2 inch across the line (0.1 each side, by fixed lengths that follow the page's drop scale), with no line ends, solid. Its ends glue, and a move of a device stretches the zigzag along the line and never lays a route over it. **Network Link** is an ordinary connector with no line ends, a solid line and a right-angle route (`ShapeRouteStyle` 1). `stencil.list` gives both `ends: {begin: 0, end: 0, pattern: 1}`.
* Search words; ours, plain English. Every master has words. The names of the inventory's sample list (Server, Database server, Ethernet, PC, Router, Firewall, Printer, Web server, Application server, Cloud, Laptop, Switch, File server, Mail server, Print server, Wireless access point, Comm-link) each find the master that serves the purpose: `PC` is the desktop, `Ethernet` the bar, `Comm-link` the zigzag. A test holds the 17 names, and holds that a name that is one master's alone finds only that master.
* What a save does. A drop saves and reopens in a `.vsdx` and in `.diacraft` as the shape it is: the same drawing, the same connection points, the master link kept, and saved again as no edit (`tests/it/stencils2_network.rs` and `stencils2_computers.rs` hold all 28 masters through the five per-stencil checks). **In an `.odg`, a drop is saved and read back as the session had it** (DiaCraft's extension carries the master), and **other programs see the outline each of the 26 devices draws, not a rectangle, and the save gives no note for it** (LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 drew all 26 as their figures, on 2026-11-26). Two things other programs do not carry: the label's text block lies outside the shape's box, which an `.odg` has no place for, so they draw the label inside the box at its top, wrapped at the box's width and over the figure; **The Comm-link's zigzag and the Self Message's loop are polylines while they are glued at no end** (a new one-dimensional shape of a geometry of its own is a `draw:polyline` in the page's coordinates, a `draw:path` for a curve, in a part of ODF 1.0 or 1.1 as in a later one (the rule of those versions is no `svg:d` on a `draw:connector`), with its frame in DiaCraft's data), so other programs draw the zigzag (LibreOffice 26.8.2.2). **A glued one is a connector**: a polyline has no glue another program keeps, so a Comm-link glued at an end is a `draw:connector` of the type `line` glued to its shapes, which that program routes its own way, as the straight line between the glue points, and keeps glued when a shape moves; the zigzag rides in DiaCraft's data and comes back exactly.
* **Not built.** The backbone's built-in connectors and their control handles (M4), a legend that counts the shapes (the Detailed Network Diagram's), equipment data read from or written to a data source (M7), and the rows `ShapeClass`, `ShapeType`, `SubShapeType` and `BelongsTo`, whose purpose the spec could not find. Cloud Services is.
* **Tests.** `stencil/network/tests.rs`: the 12 and 16 masters (ids, names, sizes, points, series), every glyph inside its icon box, the label and the field groups, the 18 points of the bar in order, the Comm-link's zigzag and its glue, the Quick Shapes, the search words and the 17 names of C32, no vendor's name, the template, and what is drawn over what; and, for every master of both stencils, the catalogue's invariants and the five per-stencil checks.

### Cloud Services

Not built yet.

### Crow's Foot and Chen

Two stencils of entity-relationship notation, drawn by the project in code, in the category `Software and Database`: **Crow's Foot Database Notation** (`crows-foot`, GUID series 20, eight masters) and **Chen's Database Notation** (`chen`, series 21, eleven). Both are **shipped and closed in a new session**: the **Crow's Foot Database Notation** template (`crows_foot`) and the **Chen's Database Notation** template (`chen_notation`) open each beside the Basic Shapes, and More Shapes and `stencil.open {id}` open them anywhere else.
