Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/crows_foot.rs`, `chen.rs` and their `tests.rs`, and the double line's bands in `crates/render/src/frame.rs` and `dash.rs`. The notation spec (and DD14 to DD16 and DD24) wins over the design where they differ: Chen's derived attribute is dotted (DD15), and the reference app's Associative Entity, which the design lacks, is added by a project rule (DD16, below). The reference app was never taken apart; every rule below is **ours** unless it says it rests on the spec.

* The masters, in the Shapes window's order; ours, the design's tables with the sizes in inches. Crow's foot: `crows-foot.entity` Entity 2.0 × 1.2, `crows-foot.entity-with-keys` Entity with Keys 2.0 × 1.5, `crows-foot.note` Note 1.4 × 0.8, and the lines `crows-foot.relationship` Relationship, `crows-foot.one-to-one` One to One, `crows-foot.one-to-many` One to Many, `crows-foot.many-to-many` Many to Many and `crows-foot.note-link` Note Link, each 1.5 long. Chen: `chen.entity` Entity 1.4 × 0.7, `chen.relationship` Relationship 1.4 × 0.8, `chen.attribute` Attribute 1.2 × 0.6, `chen.key-attribute` Key Attribute 1.2 × 0.6, `chen.weak-entity` Weak Entity 1.4 × 0.7, `chen.associative-entity` Associative Entity 2.0 × 1.0, `chen.identifying-relationship` Identifying Relationship 1.4 × 0.8, `chen.multivalued-attribute` Multivalued Attribute 1.2 × 0.6, `chen.derived-attribute` Derived Attribute 1.2 × 0.6, and the lines `chen.link` Link and `chen.total-participation` Total Participation, each 1.5 long. **The Quick Shapes are the first four that are no line**: Entity, Entity with Keys and Note (the stencil has three), and Entity, Relationship, Attribute and Key Attribute (the design's text names these four, so the window puts them first and the weak entity and the identifying relationship, which its table lists beside theirs, after them). Every two-dimensional master holds `ObjType` 1 (a shape people join), so a route goes round it from the start.
* The entity; ours. An entity is a group master of **compartments**: a **header band** over its **attributes**, and the keys variant has a **keys** compartment between them. Each compartment is as tall as its text (at least 0.4 and 0.8 inch, and 0.4, 0.35 and 0.75 for the keys variant, so the masters are 1.2 and 1.5 inches tall, on paper at every scale), the group is as tall as its compartments, and its `LockHeight` makes a resize change the width only (an entity's width can be changed and its height follows its attributes). The header is bold, 12 points, and tinted with the theme's accent, `MSOTINT(THEMEVAL("AccentColor",RGB(58,127,192)),70)`: our blue tint with no theme and the theme's accent lightened under one; the lists are 10 points, top aligned (`VerticalAlign` 0) and **centred**, since a master's dress has no paragraph row yet (a list cannot be left aligned). The starting texts are `Entity`, `PK  id` and `attribute : type`, and **an instance's member holds no text of its own until it is typed in**: what shows is its master's. **The header is the member typing goes to** (it is last in the table and the group's `IsTextEditTarget` is 0), and the group is selected first (`SelectMode` 1). The points are the twelve of `GRID3` on the group's box. The reference app's Attribute, Primary Key Attribute and Primary Key Separator shapes are the compartments' lines of text and their borders: attributes are typed and not dropped as rows (List shapes are M4).
* The cardinality ends; the spec's. A relationship is a **right-angled connector** whose `BeginArrow` and `EndArrow` are **formulas of two fixed-list Shape Data fields**, `BeginCardinality` and `EndCardinality`, each of the four words **Exactly one**, **Zero or one**, **One or many** and **Zero or many**. The numbers are the ones the reference app's files hold: **25** (two crossbars), **30** (a crossbar and a disc), **28** (a fork and a crossbar) and **29** (a fork and a disc), and the mark nearest the entity is the maximum and the one farther along the line the minimum, at the begin and at the end alike. A text that is none of the four words draws no mark (the Shape Data window refuses one; a formula or a file can hold one). A new Relationship has **zero or many at the begin and exactly one at the end** (29 and 25); One to One starts with exactly one at both ends (25 and 25), One to Many with exactly one at the begin and zero or many at the end (25 and 29), and Many to Many with zero or many at both (29 and 29). `stencil.list` gives each `ends: {begin, end, pattern}`, so its tile shows its marks. The marks are the line's own line ends, at the size the line's `BeginArrowSize` and `EndArrowSize` give. The reference app keeps its ends as plain values that its menu writes, and `Identifying` in a `User` row; DiaCraft keeps the words as Shape Data, which a reference drawing does not hold, and each file carries its own masters, so nothing is lost. Right-click variants and Set Connector Type wait for the Actions (M4): the Shape Data window sets the same fields.
* Identifying or not; **a project rule**, and DD24. `Identifying` (a Boolean Shape Data field, true to start) makes `LinePattern` 1, a solid line, when true and **2, a dashed line, when false**: a convention of data-modelling tools, which the reference app's files do not show (all 38 relationships of its sample drawings are solid, so what it draws for one that is not identifying is not known). The cell is the formula `IF(Prop.Identifying,1,2)`, so a format a person applies replaces it, as any format does. Note Link is a straight dashed line with no ends.
* The figures; ours. Entity is a rectangle with the twelve points of `GRID3`; Weak Entity the same with a second rectangle **0.06 inch inside** it (a section of its own, `NoFill`); Relationship a diamond with its four vertices as points, and Identifying Relationship a diamond with a second diamond, 0.83 of it, inside; Attribute and Key Attribute an oval with the eight points of `RING8`, and **Key Attribute's text is underlined** (the underline bit, 4, in the style of its first `Character` row, so what is typed takes it); Multivalued Attribute an oval with a second oval 0.06 inch inside; and **Derived Attribute a dotted oval**, `LinePattern` 3 (DD15: the design said dashed). The inset of a second outline is the corner radius's rule, `MIN(0.06,MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`, so it never turns inside out on a small box. The text of a diamond is a block three fifths as wide and as tall as the diamond (the inner diamond's, half as wide and two fifths as tall), so a label wraps at its words. The figures hold no text of their own.
* The Associative Entity; **a project rule**, DD16. The reference app's Chen stencil has an Associative Entity, an entity that stands for a many-to-many relationship, and no source read gives its figure. It is drawn as it is often drawn: the entity's rectangle (2.0 × 1.0) with a **diamond inscribed in it**, the diamond's vertices at the middles of the rectangle's sides, and its text inside the diamond; the twelve points of `GRID3` are on the rectangle. The figure waits for a public notation page that settles it.
* The two lines; ours. **Link** is a straight, solid connector with no line ends, its label (`1`, `N` or `M`) typed on it as on any connector; the reference app's relationship connector holds no ends either, and the short arrow of a key constraint is a line end a person applies in the Format Shape pane. **Total Participation** is the same with a **double line**: `CompoundType` 1 on a weight of 3 points, so that it stays a routed connector, and the page draws it as **two bands of a point with a point between them**. An `.odg` carries the cell in DiaCraft's own data, and other programs draw one line.
* A compound line is drawn as its bands; the spec's; `crates/render`. **`CompoundType` 1 to 4 is drawn as two or three bands that share the line's weight** (it was one stroke, with a note): 1 is a band of a third of the weight, a gap of a third and a band of a third; 2 a thick band (0.6), a gap and a thin one (0.2 each), 3 its mirror, and 4 thin, thick, thin (a sixth, a sixth, a third, a sixth and a sixth). The first band is on the **left of the direction of travel**, so type 2's thick band is above a line that runs to the right and below one that runs the other way. Each band is a stroke of the path offset to its side: a line is moved by the band's distance, the corner between two lines is mitred to the stroke's own mitre limit (3) and bevelled past it, a curve is offset by the geometry library to a tenth of a pixel, a closed outline (one that says so, or whose last point is its first) is offset whole, and a segment with no length is left out. The work is counted before it is done, the offset (a unit for a line, 32 for a curve, for each band) and the dashes of each band beside it, so the frame's budget cuts a page of them. **What no source says is ours:** each band takes the stroke's dash list and cap, and the line end is drawn once at the line's full size with the shaft stopping behind it; a compound line with a dash pattern or a line end is noted in the frame (`CompoundApproximate`), and a plain one is not.
* Search words; ours, plain English. Every master has words. The names of the inventory's sample lists (C77: Entity, Attribute, Relationship, Primary Key Attribute and Primary Key Separator; C78: Entity and Relationship Connector) and the reference app's Chen list (Weak Entity, Associative Entity, Primary Key Attribute, Multi-valued Attribute, Derived Attribute and Identifying Relationship) each find the master that serves the purpose: `Primary Key Attribute` finds Entity with Keys and Key Attribute, `Relationship Connector` the Link.
* What a save does. Every master saves and reopens in a `.vsdx` and in `.diacraft` as the shape it is, and in an `.odg` as the session had it: the same drawing, the same connection points, the master link kept, and saved again as no edit (`tests/it/stencils2_crows_foot.rs` and `stencils2_chen.rs` hold all 19 masters through the five per-stencil checks). A changed cardinality survives a save in both formats that keep it (the words are Shape Data and the numbers are the cells a recalculation wrote). **No master is a rectangle for other programs in an `.odg`**: the save gives no note for any of them (writes their outlines as they are drawn), and LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 drew a page of all nineteen on 2026-11-26 as their figures: the entities' bands and compartments, the crow's foot marks at either end, the note's fold, the second outline of the weak entity, the identifying relationship and the multivalued attribute, the associative entity's diamond and the key attribute's underline. Three things other programs do not carry: an entity's compartments follow their text only in DiaCraft (an `.odg` writes a group as its members at their places), the double line is one thick line, and **a dashed or dotted line is solid** (the Note Link, a relationship that is not identifying, the derived attribute: the `.odg` writer carries a solid line and no line only, so a rectangle formatted dashed is solid there too; the pattern is in DiaCraft's data).
* **Not built.** The reference app's Attribute, Primary Key Attribute and Primary Key Separator shapes as shapes, a foreign key made by a relationship, attribute types shown or hidden, left-aligned lists (a dress has no paragraph row), the menu on a relationship that sets its ends, Chen's key-constraint arrow and thick line as masters and the multiplicity the reference app's connector can show.
* **Tests.** `stencil/crows_foot/tests.rs` and `stencil/chen/tests.rs`: the 8 and 11 masters (ids, names, sizes, points, series), the shipped and closed stencils and their templates, the four words and their numbers at either end, the defaults of a new relationship and of the three shortcuts, a word that matches nothing and one of 32,768 characters, the identifying pattern, the numbers a save keeps, the entity's compartments (the header last, the group as tall as its compartments, a line more makes it taller, a resize changes the width only, the header's tint under three themes), each Chen figure's geometry, the dotted and the underlined, the double line and its two bands in a frame, the Quick Shapes and the search words; `crates/render/src/dash.rs` and `tests/it/lines.rs`: the bands of each type, the offset of lines, corners, closed outlines and curves, and hostile paths and their counted work; and, for every master, the catalogue's invariants and the five per-stencil checks.

## Stencil files

`stencil.open` reads a stencil file, the session keeps it with the other **open stencils** (not part of the drawing, its history or its file, and kept when the drawing is replaced), and `shape.drop {stencil: "file-1", master: ...}` puts one of its masters on a page. Real files are not in the tests: every package they open is built in code. Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/` (`opened.rs` what a session keeps and answers, `bring.rs` the one matching and the copy, `instance.rs` the drop, `icon.rs`) and `cmd/stencils.rs`.

* The path rules; `file.open`'s, gaps A2 and A5. The file is read by `file::read_file_stamped`, the one reading path: a folder, a device and a pipe are refused before a byte is read, a pipe swapped in later is opened without waiting and refused, a file over the cap (what `file.open` takes) is refused from its size and from the bytes that came, and the reader's own limits apply (`diacraft_vsdx::read`, default `Limits`). **A link is read through to the file it leads to**, as `file.open` reads one; with the automation roots in force (A2: `--automation-read-root`) the path must lie in a read root, judged by its real path, and what is opened is that real path; with none a program names any path the user can read, which a read changes nothing by. A refusal says what is wrong in words and holds neither the path nor text of the file: no such file, not a file, not a drawing file, damaged, too big, and **not a stencil** (a drawing or a template, judged by the package's content type and not its name; the extension disagreeing is a warning). **Macros never run**: a `.vssm`'s project is a part the reader does not take, and nothing here looks at one.
* **Open stencils** are numbered `file-1`, `file-2`, ... for the session; **an id is not given again**, though its stencil was closed. The stencil's name is the file's name without its type. At most **16** are open, and **together they hold at most what the reader limits for one file** (`diacraft_vsdx::Limits`: 512 MiB of XML parsed, 12 million items kept, 512 MiB of pictures): each stencil is charged what the reader reports its model took (`Stats::xml_bytes`, `items`, `media_bytes`), **not the size of its file**, since a file of a few megabytes may inflate to hundreds (a refusal says so and names `stencil.close`; S6 of the review). **The same file opened again** (by the file a link leads to) is the stencil that is open (`already_open`), not read again. A command or batch that fails puts the open stencils back as it found them, so a batch that opened one and then failed leaves it closed.
* What a listing says. `stencil.list` gives the built-in stencils as before, each now with `builtin: true`, and then each opened stencil `{id, name, builtin: false, masters, masters_total}`. A master is `{id, name, width, height, connection_points, one_d, hidden, icon}`: `id` is its `ID` **as text** (as the built-in stencils' are text, so a window sends it back as `master`), `width` and `height` are the master shape's `Width` and `Height` in inches (for a master of several shapes the box that holds the first 8 of them; **at most 10,000 shapes of a stencil are sized**, and a master past that share is listed with 0 and 0: a drop reads the size from the master it drops), `connection_points` the rows of its `Connection` section, `one_d` (and `connection_points`, and the count of top-level shapes) are of the master's shapes that are not deleted (`Del`), as the resolver counts them; `one_d` is whether the shape has `BeginX`, `BeginY`, `EndX` and `EndY` (a line, a connector), `hidden` its `Hidden` flag (a window may leave it out; it is listed all the same), `icon` `null` or `{format, bytes}`. A master with an icon that is not base64 or that is too large has `icon: null` and `icon_refused` saying why. **At most 2,048 masters of a stencil are listed**: `masters_total` says how many there are, and a master past the list drops by its `ID` or name all the same. A master whose `ID` an earlier one of the file holds cannot be told from it and is left out (`masters_ignored` counts them). **A master's icon is answered as bytes by `stencil.icon`** (base64 text, kind and size), or in this process by `OpenedStencil::icon_bytes`; a window draws the master itself when there is none. An icon is looked at by its letters only (an icon over 400,000 characters of text is refused without a pass over it, one over 256 KiB decoded is refused, and a stencil's icons together are read to 32 MiB of text), and the file's `IconSize` is never read.
* Which master `master` means in an opened stencil. A whole number, or text that is one, is a master's `ID`; any other text is a name, in any case, with spaces, hyphens and underscores alike, matched against the master's `Name` and `NameU` (of two masters called the same the first). An `ID` wins over a name.
* Whether a drawing already holds a master; ours; `stencil::find_same_master`, the one place: the built-in stencils' `ensure_master` and a later paste from one drawing into another use it too. `BaseID` names a master across drawings and `UniqueID` names it in one. A master `M` of the stencil is **the same** as a master `D` of the drawing when (1) `M`'s `UniqueID` is on no other master of the stencil and `D` has it, and their `BaseID`s are equal where both have one; or else (2) `M`'s `BaseID` is on no other master of the stencil and `D` has it (the same master under another drawing's `UniqueID`; of several such the one with `M`'s `NameU`, else the first). **A copy keeps its `BaseID` and its `UniqueID`, and takes a `UniqueID` of ours (a hash of the one it had, of the version 4 form, which no master of the drawing starts as) when the first three groups of its `UniqueID` are another master's of the drawing** (the VSDX application keeps no more of a `UniqueID`), so no two masters a drawing gets from DiaCraft are one master there (the answer's `notes` says when the copy's was renewed; 0.2.3 renewed to `{D1AC0003-0000-4000-8000-...}` and by the whole text). A built-in master the drawing holds under the old form of the `UniqueID` (the `BaseID`'s text: 0.2.3 and the first builds of 0.2.4) or under a `UniqueID` the VSDX application changed is found by rule (2), whatever its `UniqueID` is: `ensure_master` and a drop from an opened stencil of either form use the drawing's master, and the `UniqueID` the drawing has is kept while it is open (a save of a VSDX file writes the one of today for a master of the old form, and the master is found by its `BaseID` as before). An id that two masters of the stencil hold says nothing about either (copies inside a stencil keep their `BaseID`), so a master whose two ids are both shared, or that has none, is matched by what it holds: a master of the drawing that shares an id with it (or has none, as it has none, and is called the same) and is exactly what would be added is the one, else a copy is added. The drawing's master is used as it is: whether it differs from the stencil's is not looked at, since `BaseID` is the identity, so a master edited in the drawing stays what the drawing made it.
* What is done with each thing a master refers to that the drawing may lack; ours. The master is copied under the next `ID` after the drawing's highest (one if there is none), with no relationship of the stencil's (the writer makes the part). A shape that nothing below changes is **shared with the stencil's model, not copied**.

  | What | Done |
  |---|---|
  | **Styles** (`LineStyle`, `FillStyle`, `TextStyle` of every shape and of the master's page sheet, and the links of the styles they reach) | Each style is looked for in the drawing **by name and by definition** (its sheet, with its own links mapped); one that is there is used, one that is not is added under a free `ID` (one above the highest), with the same name. A style with the same `ID` and another definition is not the drawing's own: V11. **Only the copy's links are rewritten, and the text of the old ones is dropped with them**: the model keeps a link, an `ID` or a `Master` that is not the plain text of its number (`LineStyle="03"`, `ID="05"`) in `raw`, which wins on a write, so a copy keeps no `ID` of the stencil's (not the master's, not a style's), no `LineStyle`, `FillStyle` or `TextStyle` text on a sheet whose link was rewritten, and no `Master` or `MasterShape` on a master's shape (a master part names no master). Saved, a copy is under the `ID`s the drawing gave it and its links are the ones it was given. **The drawing's styles of a name are hashed by definition once, and each style of the stencil's chain is compared with the one or two that hash as it does** (and not with every style of the name: 65,536 alike-named styles against a chain of 20,000 would be 1.3 billion comparisons). The root style (`ID` 0) is the drawing's root whatever either holds. A link to a style the stencil lacks is dropped, a cycle of styles is cut where it closes, and a chain of tens of thousands is walked without recursion. Names are not made unique: a drawing can end with two styles of one name |
  | **Colour table** (a colour cell that holds a plain whole number above 23: `FillForegnd`, `FillBkgnd`, `ShdwForegnd`, `ShdwBkgnd`, `LineColor`, `TextBkgnd`, `Color`, `GradientStopColor`, `GlowColor`, `BevelContourColor`, `BevelDepthColor`, in the shapes and in the styles) | The entry is found in the drawing by its colour; if it is not there it is added under the same number when that is free, else under the lowest free number up to 253, and the copy's cells are rewritten to it. A number the stencil's table does not hold is left as it is (it names nothing there either). **Both tables are indexed once** (a table holds up to 4,096 entries, and a master may name a million numbers). A cell with a formula (`THEMEVAL`, `RGB`) is not a table index and is not touched |
  | **Face names** (`Font`, `AsianFont`, `ComplexScriptFont` of a `Character` row) | Named by `NameU`, so no cell changes: a face the drawing lacks is added to its table with the attributes it had |
  | **Theme parts** | Not copied **(left it for the writer to be able to add a theme part, which it can; which part to bring is a later task; gaps F7)**: a master has no theme part of its own (a custom colour scheme rides in `User` rows of its shape, which are copied). Its themed cells read the drawing's theme, or the root style where the drawing has none |
  | **Pictures, objects, embedded packages and any other reference to a part of the stencil's file** (a shape's `ForeignData` with a relationship, and **anything the model keeps as the file had it that names a relationship**: an element or an attribute of a master row, a page sheet, a style, a shape, a section, a row, a cell, a text, a `ForeignData`) | **The master is refused (until the writer can copy related parts; gaps F7)**, in words that count them: a copy would name a relationship the saved drawing cannot write. **A relationship attribute is found by its namespace and not by its prefix**: a prefix bound by the kept text itself (on the element or above it inside the kept text) to the relationships namespace, **in either form of the standard** (`http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships` and the Strict `http://purl.oclc.org/ooxml/officeDocument/relationships`), makes every attribute under it a relationship, whatever the prefix is called (`rel:id`, `q:embed`), and a prefix bound to another namespace makes none. **The declarations of the elements above a kept node, within one sheet, are in scope for it**: the `raw` attributes of the shape (or style, or master) the sheet belongs to, of the sheet, a section, a row and a cell, in nesting order and each taken back when its element is left, so `<Shape xmlns:q="...relationships"><q:x q:custom="rId1"/></Shape>` is found, and so is a name outside the list in a cell's kept text under a prefix bound on its shape or section (a sibling's binding is not seen). A shape's own kept elements and text see its `raw` (and a `ForeignData` its own `attrs` after the shape's). **Those of the shapes above (a group a shape is in) and the part's root are not followed**. **These outer declarations only add**: the writer need not give an outer element's `xmlns:` back at the element, and a kept `r:id` under an `r` rebound there was found, in a saved drawing, to be written as `<Mystery r:id="rId1"/>` under the part's root, where `r` is the relationships namespace, and to dangle. So a binding on an outer element to the relationships namespace makes the attributes under it relationships, and **a binding there to any other namespace is not believed**: the prefix is judged as if unbound (`r` and the names the namespace defines stay relationships). Only a declaration on the kept element itself, or on one above it inside the kept text (both are copied verbatim), lifts the default; an element's own attributes are judged with its own declarations. **A prefix bound out of sight of the kept text** (on the part's root, which the reader does not keep, or on a group above the shape) is **judged closed**: `r`, which every part's root binds to the relationships namespace and which the part a copy is written into binds there too, makes every attribute under it a relationship whatever its local name; any other such prefix makes a relationship of each attribute whose local name is one the namespace defines, the ten of `shared-relationshipReference.xsd` of ECMA-376 Part 1 (`id`, `embed`, `link`, `dm`, `lo`, `qs`, `cs`, `blip`, `pict`, `href`; read 2026-11-07 in the Apache POI copy, <https://sources.debian.org/src/libapache-poi-java/4.0.1-4/ooxml-xsds/shared-relationshipReference.xsd>), so another namespace's attribute of one of those names, bound out of sight, is refused too. **Four more names, `topLeft`, `topRight`, `bottomLeft` and `bottomRight`, are refused the same way, pending a spec check** (the copy of the schema read is the first edition of ECMA-376; the check cites their source and that of the Strict URI, and task puts the list with the format specifications). **The work is bounded by what the kept text holds** (S7): the bindings in scope are one stack for a walk (an element's declarations pushed on entering it and taken back on leaving, so K declarations and N children cost K and N), looked up by a hash on the prefix, and capped at 64 declarations on one element and 256 in scope at once; past either the master is refused in words (`it holds text of the stencil's file that declares more namespace prefixes than a copy reads`), before anything is pushed. **Every node is charged to the meter when it is put on the walk's stack, and an element's children before they are stacked**, so a wide element is refused by the meter and not after its children are stacked. The `Connect` rows of the master and the `Raw` elements of a shape's text are looked at as well, walked where they are. The styles the master reaches are looked at as well as its shapes. The master's other shapes are not affected, and the drawing is as it was |
  | **Other masters named by `USE()`** | Not followed. The answer's `notes` says the master has such formulas, and the drawing's cells that name a master it lacks read as they do without it |
  | **Data connections and recordsets** of the stencil | Not copied; the shape's own data rows (a `Property` section, `Data1` to `Data3`) are cells and text and come along |
  | **The master's icon** | The text, as the file had it |
  | **Macros** | Never read, never copied |

* The instance; ours where no spec says. **Everything about the instance is read from the drawing's master it names** (the stencil's copy, or, when finds the drawing's own, a master that may differ from the stencil's in its pin, its members, or being a box where the stencil has a line): its pose, whether it is a line, its `Type` and its members, so that the shape lands where it is asked and its members name master shapes the master has. The master is brought in first, and a refusal after that (a master of none, a page too full) leaves the drawing as it was. The instance holds **only what differs**: `PinX` and `PinY`, and for a one-dimensional master `BeginX`, `BeginY`, `EndX` and `EndY` instead (a line is dropped with its ends where the master's are, moved so that their middle is the place; its pin and size follow by the master's formulas, and a pin the master holds as a number and not as a formula is set where the ends and `LocPinX` put it: `begin + (LocPinX / Width) * (end - begin)`, which is the middle only when `LocPinX` is half the width, and what reads the pin is worked out again). Its `Type` is the master shape's and its name is the master's with the `ID` (`Process.5`). **The place is the centre of the shape's box**, so the pin goes where the centre lands once the shape's `LocPinX`, `LocPinY`, `Angle`, `FlipX` and `FlipY` are applied; what reads a cell the instance holds is worked out again, so the cached results are right. A drop is **one undo step**, which takes the master and everything copied with it away too, and the id rule holds: the session's mark goes above the instance's `ID` and its last member's.**A master of none is refused**; a master of one shape that is a group is dropped with that shape's members; **a master of several top-level shapes is dropped as a group**.
* The members of a group master; ours. A file's instance of a grouped master lists every descendant of the master's shape, each standing for its own by `MasterShape`, in the master's order, and a reader that is not ours (LibreOffice, in the check that came with this change) draws nothing for a member that is not listed. So the instance lists them: a shape for each descendant, with an `ID` of its own on the page (above the instance's, depth first), its master's `Type`, `MasterShape`, and no cell of its own but a local copy of its master shape's `Geometry` (the instance itself holds none), and no size or pin (but for the members of a master of several shapes, whose pins are in the group's frame). **A master of more than 5,000 descendants (a group's whole tree) is dropped without its members below the top level listed** (MS-VSDX lets an instance omit them, and `Resolver::effective_members` and the renderer take them from the master): listing them would put as many shapes on the page for each drop.

* A master of several top-level shapes; ours. The specifications say what its instance is: **a `Group` with a member for each top-level shape of the master, each standing for it by `MasterShape`** (2% of masters, 293 files from 48 sources, have several); only the group's frame is left to us. **The frame is the joint box of the members on the master's page**, each member's box carried through its own pin, turn and flips (a turned member counts by its corners): the group's `Width` and `Height` are the box's, its `LocPinX` and `LocPinY` the middle of the box, and its `PinX` and `PinY` the place (the box's middle goes there; the group is neither turned nor flipped). A member's pin is in the group's frame, so it is its master shape's pin on the master's page less the box's lower-left corner, held as an override of the member (`PinX` and `PinY`, or the four end cells of a line), and **a member that is not a line holds its `PinX`, `PinY`, `Width` and `Height` as formulas of the group**; every other cell of a member is its master shape's. The members' own descendants are listed under them when the whole tree is within 5,000 shapes, and left to the master otherwise. A master of **more than 5,000 top-level shapes is refused** in words, since each needs a member of its own on the page to carry its override. A member that is a line has its four end cells as overrides, **and its pin checked once what reads the ends is worked out**: a master that holds the pin as numbers and not as a formula of its ends would otherwise leave the pin at the master's page (a line drawn offset by the box's lower-left corner), so a pin held as a number that is not where the member's ends in the group's frame and its `LocPinX` of its `Width` put it (the middle only when `LocPinX` is half the width) is set there, as for the instance of a single line, and a pin that is a formula is left to the recalculation that follows the ends. `connection_points` in the listing is the rows of the `Connection` sections of all the shapes at the master's top level, so a connector glues to a member of the dropped group (tested: glued to a member, the group is moved, the connector's end follows). The group moves, turns and flips as any group does, is sized by `shape.resize` as any group is (its members are formulas of it), and saves and reads back. A master shape that is deleted (`Del`) is not a shape of the master, as the resolver counts them.

**The window** reads `stencil.list` and sends `stencil.open`, `stencil.close` and `shape.drop {stencil}`: see "Stencil files in the window" below.

* The Shapes window and stencil files; ours: no specification says how a window shows them. **More Shapes, Open Stencil** shows the desktop app's native
  file chooser (`.vssx` and `.vssm`, and every file as a second filter) on a thread of its own and sends `stencil.open` with the path it answers; **it is quiet where the
  app has no chooser** (the web), and while one is on the screen. The stencil gets **a row of its own** named for the file and is **the one the Shapes window shows**; the same
  file chosen again is the same stencil. A refusal (`stencil.open`'s words: not a stencil, damaged, past a limit, no such file) is told in the status bar and nothing
  changes. **A close control at the right of the row of each stencil file** (the engine's own have none) sends `stencil.close`; the Shapes window then shows the first stencil
  if it showed this one, and a drawing that took masters from it keeps them. **A tile for each master that is not hidden** (`hidden: true` is left out), at most 2,048
  of a stencil (the engine lists that many), in the file's order. **A tile is drawn from the master's icon when the engine says it has one and it is an ICO, a PNG or a BMP**
  (`icon_image.rs`: sides to 256 pixels, every offset checked, an icon of any other kind or one that does not read is not used), **else from the master's own outline**, read
  in a session of its own that has the file open again by the path the window opened it from (so the person's drawing is never used to draw a tile), **else a box** of the
  master's size. **A built-in one-dimensional master's tile has its line ends and pattern, and a group master's tile its members**. Figures and icons are read for the tiles in view only. A tile is dragged onto the page or clicked as the built-in ones are and sends `shape.drop` with
  `stencil`; **a master the engine refuses** (no shapes, more than 5,000 at the top level, a picture or another part it cannot carry across: gap F7) **is told in the status
  bar in the engine's words and the drawing is as it was**. The window commands are `shapes.openStencil {path?}` (no `path`: the chooser) and `shapes.closeStencil {id}`.
* Our rule. **The file is read on the window's thread**: `stencil.open` is the engine's command on the window's session, and the engine has no way to give it a
  stencil read elsewhere, so a very large stencil holds the window while it is read, up to the most a drawing file may be (gap U22). **A drawing read from a file is a new
  session**, so the thread that reads it opens the stencils the window had open again in it, by the paths the window opened them from (a stencil whose file is gone, has
  changed into something else, or does not fit the memory a read may use beside the drawing just read, is not in the list afterwards, **and is said**: by name in the status bar, and in
  `stencil_notes` of the answer of the open; the ids are numbered again from `file-1`); a stencil that a program opened through the control channel is
  noted by its path as well, since the window runs every command it is sent.

## Dropping a master on a page of another drawing scale

A master carries a drawing scale of its own on its page sheet (`PageScale` over `DrawingScale`, both in inches), and the page it is dropped on carries another. (31 rules, 23 vectors; the sources are the reference app's documentation, read 2026-11-26, and the public corpus) settles what a drop does, and **points to it: the earlier project rule, which wrote the ratio at every difference of scale, is withdrawn.** Every master built into DiaCraft is drawn at 1:1 (the page sheet of each holds one inch to one inch); a master of a stencil file has the scale its file gave it. The reference app was never taken apart (AGENTS.md); the rules marked **ours** are where the sources are silent.

**The rule, the "range of eight"**. *r* is the master's scale over the page's, and *k* the greater of *r* and 1/*r*.

| The drop | Written on the new shape | Text size, line weight and other constants |
|---|---|---|
| Within the range (*k* up to 8) | nothing: it keeps the master's size in drawing units, so on paper it is the master's divided by *r* | nothing |
| Beyond it (*k* above 8) | `DropOnPageScale` = *r* (a plain value with all its digits, no formula, no unit), and `Width` and `Height` = the master's times *r*, so on paper it is the master's size | nothing: never written |

**Every way of dropping follows it**: `shape.drop` (the window's drag and click, the command line, the control channel and MCP), the master of a stencil file, a one-dimensional master, a group master, a master of several top-level shapes, the shape AutoConnect drops (`connector.autoconnect` with `master`), the master a template puts on its first page, and `snap::drop_preview`, the shape the window's ghost shows (a drop on a copy of the document: its size on paper and its connection points). **Paste, duplicate, a move and Change Shape are not drops of a master** and keep the cells a shape has; a later `page.scale` changes no shape's cells. One undo step takes the drop back whole.

* Our rule. The edge is eight inclusive, and a relative 1E-9 above it still counts as within, so that 1:12 against 1:96, whose ratio is 8 in exact arithmetic and a hair above it after the division, is within. `draw::drop_class_of` is total and divides nothing; a ratio that is not a finite number above 0 is within.
* Our rule. A scaled master on a scaled page is antiscaled as an unscaled one is, following the documentation's worked example (1:24 on a page at 1:240) over its cell page.
* Our rule. A size cell that a `GUARD` protects stays inherited and is recalculated; so does one that the shape's lock keeps (`LockWidth` or `LockHeight` set and the cell a formula: the height of a group of compartments, kept by a resize too); a plain value or an unguarded formula is replaced by the scaled value, as a resize replaces it. For a one-dimensional master only a plain `Width` or `Height` is replaced: a `Width` that is a formula of the ends follows them.
* **DROPSCALE-1D-1** (ours). A one-dimensional master's ends lie along its direction, its length times *r* apart, centred on the drop point; its `Width` follows the ends by its formula, and `DropOnPageScale` is written beside them.
* Our rule. Only the instance's top-level shape is written. The members of a group master follow by the formulas they inherit (`Sheet.<group>!Width*0.4375`, `Sheet.<group>!DropOnPageScale`); a member whose size is a plain value keeps it, and no member holds a factor of its own.
* Our rule. A master of several top-level shapes is dropped as a group whose frame (the joint box of the shapes, the local pin its middle) is the master's times *r*, and so is each member that stands for a top-level shape: its pin in the frame (or the ends of a line), its `Width` and `Height`, and its own `DropOnPageScale` *r*, so the offsets of the members from the group's local pin are the master's times *r* and the arrangement keeps its look on paper. The members' formulas tie them to the group as before.
* Our rule. A `PageScale` or `DrawingScale` of the master's page sheet or of the page that is absent, 0, negative or not a number reads as one inch, each by itself, and the cells are kept as they are (`draw::usable_length`).
* Our rule. Paste, duplicate, moves and Change Shape write no scale: Change Shape's trial instance of the new master is dropped with `Follow::Never` and the shape keeps its size (`draw::drop_shape_following`, `stencil::drop_opened_following`).
* Our rule. Changing a page's scale rewrites no shape's `DropOnPageScale`.
* Our rule. A master whose own shape holds a `DropOnPageScale` other than 1 is inherited as it is at its own scale, and beyond the range gets *r*, the factor of this drop, and not *r* times its own.
* Our rule. A ratio that is not a finite number above 0, or a written `Width`, `Height`, end, offset or factor that would not be finite or would pass `MAX_COORD` (1,000,000 drawing units), makes it a drop within the range: nothing is scaled, nothing is refused, and the answer's `notes` say in words that the master was dropped at its own size and why.
* Our rule, owner 2026-11-26. **The least height of a compartment follows the scale.** A compartment is as tall as its text needs and at least a least height, which was a constant in its formula, `MAX(0.4,TEXTHEIGHT(TheText,Width))`, so a drop beyond the range left it alone and, at 1:20 and 1:100, the least was 0.02 and 0.004 inch on paper and held nothing: a UML Class was 0.85 inch tall on paper and not the master's 1.2, a Crow's Foot Entity 0.59 and not 1.2 (measured; the text kept its 4-point margin). The owner ruled that the least height is scaled, and the formula takes the factor that R18 offers masters for the lengths they hold as constants: `MAX(0.4*IF(Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale>0,Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale,1),TEXTHEIGHT(TheText,Width))`, inside the member's `GUARD`. `Sheet.5` is the group, the master's top-level shape (`MASTER_SHAPE_ID`; a master's formula that names a master shape reads the instance's, as `Sheet.5!Width` does), because no member holds a factor of its own and every one reads the group's; the group holds *r*, the factor of a drop beyond the range, so the least is *r* times the master's. **The seven masters that have compartments are the ones that change:** UML Class's `class`, `interface`, `enumeration`, `data-type` and `object`, and Crow's Foot's `entity` and `entity-with-keys` (`group_master.rs` `frame_texts` writes the formula for every master of compartments, so a new one has it). Each of them dropped at 1:1, 1:20 and 1:100 is as tall on paper as the master and so is each of its compartments (1.2 inches for a class, 1.24 for an interface, 0.96 for an enumeration and for a data type, 0.8 for an object, 1.2 for an entity and 1.5 for an entity with keys; `tests/it/compartment_scale.rs`), and a compartment that its text makes taller is as tall on paper at every scale, since the text keeps its size and its margin: the least height decides only where the text is shorter than it. **Within the range and for a shape no drop scaled** the group holds no factor and reads the root's, 1, so nothing changes (the shape keeps its drawing size). **A drawing whose root holds no `DropOnPageScale`** (a drawing a build before a change made, or one that never had it) reads a cell found nowhere as 0, and the `IF` takes 1 there: such a drawing keeps the heights it had; and a master that a file holds is the file's, with the formula it holds, so a drawing from an earlier build keeps its masters' formulas. A shape that is changed to one of the seven (Change Shape) reads the factor of the shape, as its text does. The formula is a formula like any other: a save in `.vsdx`, `.diacraft` or `.odg` holds it, in the `.odg` among the cells of the second tier (the cells are the model, and the file's own markup cannot say `TEXTHEIGHT`), and a line typed after a reopen is worked out by it. **No other built-in master holds the least height of a compartment** (a grep of `stencil/` for `MAX(` and `MIN(` in a master's formulas finds only these); **the other fixed lengths of the masters' formulas are the lengths of a figure, and they follow the scale too (owner 2026-11-27)**. The least thickness of a lane and a phase is worked out in code on paper (`container/lists.rs`, `MIN_INCHES` times the page's scale).

* Our rule, owner 2026-11-27. **A fixed length of a figure follows the scale.** A figure is more than its box: the head of a lifeline, the figure of an actor, the tag of a fragment, the markers of BPMN, the label bands of a C4 key, the corner of a rounded box and the tab of a package were each a constant length in a formula of the master (`Width-0.2`, `MIN(0.4,Sheet.5!Height)`, `MIN(0.25,MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`), which a drop does not scale, so beyond the range of eight a lifeline's head was a hundredth of its size on paper at 1:100 and a Task's corner a hundredth of a tenth of an inch: a shape that looked right at 1:1 lost its head, its tab and its corners. The owner ruled that **a built-in shape looks the same on paper as it does at 1:1, so its fixed inner lengths follow the scale**. The master writes each such length as `<length>*IF(DropOnPageScale>0,DropOnPageScale,1)` (the factor the drop wrote, and 1 where the cell is found nowhere, since a cell found nowhere reads 0 and a factor of 0 would take the length away). **Where the factor is read.** A shape of one piece reads its own `DropOnPageScale` (a drop beyond the range writes it on the instance's top-level shape, which for a master of one shape is that shape, and for a one-dimensional master beside its ends: DROPSCALE-1D-1), and **a member of a group master reads the group's**, `Sheet.5!DropOnPageScale` (no member holds a factor of its own, and an instance reads `Sheet.5` as its own group); the top-level shape of a group, which holds the group's connection points, reads its own. **What is scaled** is a length, in whatever cell it stands: a fixed distance in a `Geometry` or `Connection` row (`Width-0.2*IF(...)`, `0.4*IF(...)` alone for a stroke 0.4 inch across a line), the radius of a corner and the height of a tab (`MIN(0.1*IF(...),MIN(Width,Height)*0.25)`, which still gives way on a small box), the frame of a member (`GUARD(MIN(0.4*IF(Sheet.5!...),Sheet.5!Height))`, `GUARD(MAX(0.1*IF(...),MIN(1*IF(...),Sheet.5!Width-0.7*IF(...))))`), the spacing of a row of markers (BPMN's 0.2 inch and 0.1 inch) and the margin a container leaves round what it holds (`User.DiaCraftContainerMargin`, 0.25*IF(...)). **What is not**: a share of the box (every vertex of a master whose outline is shares follows the box, and so does each one of the masters that are not named below), a ratio, an angle, a count, a text block (a share of the box), the size of a text, the weight of a line, the size of a line end and a text margin (on paper at every scale, so never scaled, and not scaled twice), and the figures that are made on paper by code (BPMN's Pool and Lane, the Cross-Functional Flowchart's Swimlane and Separator: `draw/container/swimlane.rs` works in `BAND_INCHES` times the page's scale, and the Pool is dropped at the master's size by the range of eight alone). **The masters that change** are 41, the 7 of not among them: UML Class's `package` (tab, margin) and `note` (dog ear), UML Use Case's `subject` (margin) and `note`, UML Sequence's `lifeline` (head, stem, the places on the head and the stem), `actor-lifeline` (figure, name strip, stem, the places), `fragment` (tag, guard, margin), `interaction-use` (tag), `note` and `self-message` (the loop 0.4 inch across), BPMN's `task`, `sub-process`, `call-activity`, `expanded-sub-process` (corners, second borders, markers and their slots), `intermediate-event` (the inner ring), `data-object` (arrow and bars), `group` (corner, margin) and `pool` (the strip's line), C4's `person`, `software-system`, `container`, `component`, `boundary`, `deployment-node` (corners, margins) and `key` (its rows, title and corners), Network Devices' `wireless-access-point` (the base's corner) and `comm-link` (the zigzag 0.1 inch to each side), Computers and Devices' `desktop`, `laptop`, `tablet`, `mobile-phone`, `printer`, `database-server`, `web-server`, `file-server`, `mail-server`, `application-server` and `print-server` (corners and badges), Crow's Foot's `note`, and Chen's `weak-entity` and `multivalued-attribute` (the second outline 0.06 inch inside the first). **Where the text is made**: `Co::formula` for the outline and the points of a master (`stencil.rs`: a coordinate's fixed length and corner radius), `scaled!` for a table of a member's frame (`bpmn.rs`, `c4.rs`, `uml_sequence.rs`) and `dress.rs` for a container's margin, with the one text of the factor in `group_master::drop_factor`. **A drop within the range, and a shape no drop scaled, hold no factor** and read the root's, 1, so nothing changes; **a drawing whose root holds no `DropOnPageScale`** (a drawing a build before a change made) reads 0 where the formula names it, which the `IF` turns into 1, so it keeps the lengths it had, and a master that a file holds is the file's, with the formulas it holds, so a drawing from an earlier build keeps its masters as they were. **Files.** The formulas are cells: a `.vsdx` and a `.diacraft` hold them and a shape read from either is worked out by them (a resize after a reopen keeps a corner of 0.08 inch on paper at 1:100); an `.odg` holds each master with its body in the second tier, formulas included (the file's own markup cannot say `IF`), and a shape of one piece read from it holds its own copy of them, which names no other shape and goes on following the factor the shape holds. **A group read from an `.odg` is its members at their places, shapes of their own**, **and the formulas their copies take from the master name the shapes of the page**: a formula found on the master says `Sheet.5` for the master's group, an instance reads it as its own group, and the copy holds it as the cell's own, so the save writes each `Sheet.<id>` as the `ID` of the shape of the instance that stands for it (`odgfile/flatten.rs`, `Flattener::rebound`, over `Resolver::rebind`; a shape of a page keeps its `ID` through a file, a group in the document file's entry for it), in the `Geometry` rows and the sections' flags (the factor of every length, the `NoShow` of every marker), in the text block and in the rows of the text (an abstract class's italic name, `IF(Sheet.5!Prop.Abstract,3,1)`). A formula that names a master shape nothing of the instance stands for (a member that was removed) is the constant of its value, and the save counts it with the formulas it writes as values. So after a recalculation the factor reads the group's, a marker shows and hides with the group's shape data, and the lengths are the same as in the drawing that was saved. **What is left of the limit**: a member's own frame (its `Width`, `Height` and place) is a value in the file, so a resize of the group stretches a member whose size is a length of the master's formula (a marker, a tag) as it stretches a plain shape. A shape dropped from the master after the reopen is made through the master and is right. `tests/it/figure_scale.rs` holds the ruling: every master of every built-in stencil, dropped at 1:1, 1:20, 1:100 and 20:1, has each length of its frame, text block, geometry and connection points (and the margin of a container), in the shape and in every member, as long on paper as at 1:1; at 1:2, 1:4, 1:8, 2:1 and 8:1 each length is the master's, in drawing units; and the pictures, rendered at paper scale, are the same.

* **Where the box lands.** The drop point is where the middle of the box goes. A master's local pin is its own formula, which follows the size, and the drop never writes it, so once the sizes are written and worked out the pin is put where the new box has its middle at the point: it holds for a pin at a corner, a plain local pin, a turn and a flip (`draw/drop_scale.rs`, `recentre`).
* **What reads the cells.** The cells written are worked out as any write is (`calc`'s `commit_changed` for the cells written and what reads them, through the master's formulas too): a connection point, a geometry row or a size that names `Width` or `DropOnPageScale` has its result, a constant in a formula stays what it is (the drop writes nothing but the factor and the sizes; a built-in master's fixed lengths are not constants, they are the length times the factor). A page too large to recalculate refuses the drop in words and leaves the drawing as it was.
* **The root style of a new drawing holds `DropOnPageScale` 1** (the coordinator's ruling, under the owner's rule that documented behaviour wins; `doc`'s `root_style`). The root style of every file of the corpus holds 1, so a shape no drop scaled reads 1 and a formula of a master that names the cell is the master's own size: in a drawing DiaCraft made, a connection point that is a length of the shape plus a length times the factor is not short of the factor when the shape is resized (it was, with no cell in the root: a cell found nowhere reads 0). **A root that comes from a file is the file's** and is never given the cell: a VSDX file whose root has none is saved as it is (the part that holds the styles is not rewritten) and saved as `.diacraft` with none, one that holds 1 keeps it, and one that holds another number keeps that. An `.odg` has no root style, so the root a reader makes of one is a new drawing's, with the cell, and no save writes the factor into the file (`tests/it/drop_scale_root.rs`). A drawing saved by a build before this, a `.diacraft` file included, has no cell in its root and reads 0 where a formula names it, until a drop beyond the range writes the cell on the shape.
* **The answer.** `drop_on_page_scale` (the factor written, only when one was) and `notes`; `width` and `height` are the new shape's size on paper, so beyond the range they are the master's.
* **What it costs.** What is written is the top-level shape's cells and, for a master of several top-level shapes, those of each member that stands for one: no walk of a group's members. A group master of 24 levels of 32 members is dropped (791 members listed) and so is one of 5,100 members (more than a drop lists), at the cost of the drop that was and one recalculation of the cells written (`tests/it/drop_scale.rs`).
* **Files.** The cells are cells: a drop saved and read back in `.diacraft`, VSDX and `.odg` has the same `Width`, `Height` and `DropOnPageScale`, to the bit, and a second save and read changes nothing. An `.odg` states a size for every shape, so a shape dropped within the range holds its size as a cell there and reads the same number.
* **The window's ghost is the shape the drop makes** (closing U49). A master is not dropped at the size it is listed at: beyond the range of eight it keeps its size on paper, and a group whose height is the sum of compartments that follow their text (the seven masters `uml-class.class`, `.interface`, `.enumeration`, `.data-type`, `.object`, `crows-foot.entity` and `crows-foot.entity-with-keys`) had the height of that text, because the compartments' minimum heights were constants in the formulas, which a drop never scales; **the least heights follow the scale and a drop of the seven is the master's size on paper, and the height of the text decides only where a compartment's text is taller than its least.** So the engine drops the master on a copy of the document (`snap::drop_preview(doc, page, DropMaster, centre)`: a stock master, or a stencil file's master by its id or name; a copy shares everything with the document, and the document is not changed) and reads off the shape it made what `shape.drop` reads off it: the box's size on paper (`DropPreview::width`, `height`, `rect_at`) and the connection points (`points_at`, at most `MAX_OWN_POINTS`). The window draws the ghost at that size, snaps that box and pulls those places, moved with the pointer: the box and the places are the same wherever the shape goes, moved by the distance. A master whose drop is no one shape (BPMN's Pool is a structure of swimlanes made by code) has its size by the range of eight alone (`draw::drop_scale::built_in_size`, which the command takes too), and a drop that cannot be made on a copy (a page that is full, a master with no shape) is drawn at the size the range of eight gives the master (`snap::size_on_paper`). `snap::dropped_points` and `dropped_points_of_file` are the places alone, and `tests/it/snap_drop_points.rs` holds them to the places of the real drop, for every master of every built-in stencil at the scales 1, 2 and 100 to 1, to a billionth of an inch (had let the seven masters off the height).
* **What the preview costs.** It is worked out **once for a drag** (`edit/tiles.rs`: the master, the page and the drawing's generation and revision are its key, so a change of the page's scale in the middle of a drag, which is an edit, makes it again) and never for a frame: each one made is counted (`snap::counts().drops`), and the window's test drags a tile over forty frames, still and moving, and has one. measured on beast on 2026-11-26 at a load of 35 to 55, in the development profile (optimised), the least of five for each of the 173 masters that make one shape, at 100 to 1: a median of 0.3 ms and at most 7.3 ms (`bpmn.intermediate-event`, a group of many members), 1.9 ms for a UML class, the same on a blank page, a page of 1,000 shapes, a page of 5,000 and a drawing that holds 174 masters, because the copy's page holds no shapes: a drop on a copy of a page that had them took 46,896 steps of calculation on a page of 500 shapes and 300 connectors, against 3,144 on a blank one, and the page's own is now left out (`tests/it/snap_drop_points.rs` counts it, and times it behind `--ignored`)
* **Compartments beyond the range** (measured, and nothing was changed there: **the least height it found to be a constant is scaled **, above, so a UML Class is the master's 1.2 inches on paper at every scale; the margin of the text, which this holds, is as it was, and the numbers that follow are what the build before a change gave). Found that the last line of a UML Class dropped at 100:1 "sits on the shape's bottom edge". **It does not:** the margins of a text are paper lengths (4 points above and below the block at every scale) and a compartment is as tall as its text and its margins (`TEXTHEIGHT`, divided by the scale), so on a drop of each of the seven masters of compartments (UML Class's `class`, `interface`, `enumeration`, `data-type` and `object`, and Crow's Foot's `entity` and `entity-with-keys`) the lowest ink of the last line is 12 to 18 rows of 1/200 inch (0.06 to 0.09 inch, the margin and the line's own air) from the bottom edge at 1:20 and at 1:100 alike. **What the scale changes is the least height of a compartment**, a number in the master's formula (`MAX(0.4, TEXTHEIGHT(TheText, Width))` for the class) and so a constant that a drop leaves alone: at 1:1 it keeps the last line 0.19 inch off the edge, and beyond the range it is 0.004 inch on paper and keeps nothing, so each compartment is as tall as its text and its margins, and a UML Class is 0.85 inch tall on paper and not the master's 1.2, a Crow's Foot Entity 0.59 and not 1.2 (the master's paper size, which the sum of compartments cannot keep: `Height` is a `GUARD`ed formula and stays one). The documented way for a master to keep a constant is a formula that names `DropOnPageScale`, and the built-in masters have none: whether the least heights should was a question for the owner, whose ruling is (`stencil/uml_class/tests.rs`, `the_last_line_of_a_compartment_keeps_its_margin_at_a_scale_beyond_the_range_of_eight`, holds the margin, and the height; a root with no `DropOnPageScale`, a file of a build before a change, reads the factor as 0 where such a formula names it, which the formula's `IF` takes for 1).
* **What is left.** The ghost is the drop on bare paper, as it was: a Lane let go over a Pool, a Swimlane or a Separator over its structure, and a position of the Organization Chart inside another are put in their structure or linked by the release, and the ghost does not show that. A master of a stencil file that is dropped inside a group is dropped on the page that holds the group, as the specification reads it; no command drops into a group.

## Search for shapes and Quick Shapes

`stencil.search` finds masters in every stencil by the whole words of their names and search words; `stencil.quick`, `stencil.add_quick`, `stencil.remove_quick` and `stencil.reset` read and change the Quick Shapes of each stencil, the masters above its divider, which feed the AutoConnect flyout. The reference app was never taken apart: what the specifications give is (the search box), R4 (Quick Shapes), the right-click menus and Reset Stencil. Code: `crates/engine/src/stencil/search.rs`, `keywords.rs` and `quick.rs`, `cmd/stencils.rs`, and for the window `crates/ui-egui/src/shapes_window.rs` and `stencils.rs`. Every rule below that is **ours** has a row in the check list (the check list, proposed in the task's report).

* (what matches; the words written out, with V1 as the test). A *word* is a run of letters and digits, and everything else parts words (`Pump-House` is two). A master matches a query word when the word is **a whole word, in any case,** of the master's name or of its search words: `Air Cond` finds no `Air Conditioner`, `air` does. With **AND** (`mode: "all"`, the default: Options, Advanced, Shape search, "All of the words") a master needs every word of the query, with **OR** (`"any"`) one of them. The same word twice is one word. The Shape search option that hides the box and the Options page that holds the AND/OR choice are not built: the choice is the window command `shapes.search {mode}` (not saved).
* Our rule. A stencil file's master has its name (`Name`, else `NameU`) and the text of its **`ShapeKeywords`** cell, read on the master's page sheet (files put it there) and on the sheets of its first eight shapes, as a `V` or as the element's text. The built-in masters are made in code and hold no such cell, so their words are a table by id (`stencil/keywords.rs`): plain English words for what the figure is called in other places or used for (a diamond is also a rhombus, a decision is a branch). They are written from the figures and from general knowledge of flowcharts and are not copied from any stencil; they are not written into a drawing. A master that is hidden is not found (the window leaves it out).
* (ours; R2 says "the shapes on the device"). Every **built-in stencil, open or not** (a template that left the flowchart closed does not hide it from a search, and the answer says `open`), and every **open stencil file**; the built-in stencils that are open first, in the window's order, then the others in the catalogue's, then the files. The Online group and Download of R2 are not built (a P2 row).
* The budget; a hostile stencil: 100,000 masters, names and search words of megabytes. The query is refused in words past 256 characters, 16 different words or a word of 64 characters (a word dropped from an AND would find more, not fewer). The search looks at **at most 100,000 masters and reads at most 16 MiB of names and search words**, each master **charged for the text it is read from before it is read**; a search word text is read to **4,096 bytes** and no further; a master stops being read when it is decided. **A search that meets either limit stops and says so**: `complete` is false, `searched` and `total` say how far it got, and a note in words says which limit; a limit that is reached never lets more through. At most **500** masters are listed (`listed`, `truncated`), and `matches` counts them all. The work is counted (`tokens`, `bytes` in the engine's `Outcome`) and tested on stencils of 120,000 masters, names of 1.5 million characters, search words of 1.2 MB and a word of a million letters.
* What the specification gives. Quick Shapes are the masters above the thin divider in a stencil, typically two to six, added by dragging across the divider or with Add to Quick Shapes and taken away the same way; a stencil called Quick Shapes gathers those of every open stencil, each stencil's group under its name when there are several; **the AutoConnect strip shows at most four**, the first four of the stencil that is selected; Reset Stencil gives the stencil its own back.
* Our rule, where are silent. **A stencil with nothing set has its first four masters that are not connectors and not hidden** (what offered before). **The group is the drawing's**, like the AutoConnect box: it is kept in DiaCraft's own extension data (a child `quick_shapes` whose attribute `v` is JSON: `[["b", "basic", ["rectangle", ...]], ["f", "Mine", ["5", ...]]]`, a built-in stencil by its id, a stencil file by the file's name, a master by its id), so **every format carries it** (`.diacraft`, VSDX, `.odg`) and no stencil file is written to; a drawing whose groups are all the stencils' own holds nothing of it. **It is no undo step and makes the drawing unsaved** (a setting: "Unsaved, not undo"), and undo and redo carry it across (`view::carry_settings`). The group is in the order the masters were added and a master added again moves to the place asked (`at`, from 0); the masters below the divider keep the stencil's own order; a group may be **empty** when the drawing set it so, and the strip then offers the stencil's first four masters, so that no stencil is one the arrows cannot use. **The strip offers the first four masters of the group that it may offer (no connector and no part of a structure), fewer when there are fewer** (the strip is not filled from the rest). A group names at most **24** masters, a drawing holds the groups of at most **32** stencils, a key is at most 128 bytes and the data at most 64 KiB; data past them, or that is not what this build writes, is **unreadable**: the stencils' own are shown, `readable` is false, the data is **kept as it is** and a change is refused in words. An entry for a stencil that is not open stays in the data, and one for a master that is gone is passed over when the group is read. Two stencil files of one name share a group. **What is written always reads back the same**. A file's name that a key cannot be as it is, one with a control character or past 128 bytes (64 characters of three bytes are), is kept with each control character as U+FFFD and cut at a character boundary at 128 bytes, so two names that differ only past the cut, or only in their control characters, share a group too. A key the data cannot hold at all (a file with no name) is refused in words, and so is a change whose data would not read back as it is held (past 64 KiB): the reader reads the text before it is written, and nothing is written.
* (replaces; ours where R3 is silent: it says the strip shows the first four shapes of the stencil that is selected and "not all stencils feed it (the Arrow Shapes stencil does not)", and no page says which others, or what the strip shows while such a stencil is selected). **A master feeds the strip** when it is no connector, **no part of a structure** (a Swimlane or a Separator, whose drop is put in a list of lanes or phases, and a stencil file's master whose shape is typed `Container` or `List`, and a built-in master of the container role, a package or a subject), and of a stencil that feeds it: **every built-in stencil but Arrow Shapes, and every stencil file**. **A built-in master that no connector joins** (the C4 Model's title and key, whose dress is the pointless role and which have no connection point) **feeds it nothing either**, since the strip adds a shape and joins it to the one it came from. Such masters stay Quick Shapes where they are (the group is the person's choice, and the Quick Shapes stencil gathers them), and the strip passes over them. **A stencil that feeds the strip nothing** (Arrow Shapes, the Cross-Functional Flowchart Shapes, a file of parts) **gives it what the first open stencil that feeds it offers**, in the window's order (the default R3 names: "the stencil that follows the Quick Shapes stencil"), and `stencil.quick`'s `offer.stencil` says which; with no open stencil that feeds it the arrows still show and a click on one still joins or copies, and no flyout opens. **What the window is told:** `stencil.list` marks such a master `part: true` and `autoconnect: false` (a built-in container master has `autoconnect: false` and no `part`: its drop is a shape of its outline), and a master of Arrow Shapes `autoconnect: false`. **A part that reaches the strip from a file** (a stencil file's container or list master, or a drawing's Quick Shapes data that names one) is passed over by the flyout and by the Quick Shapes stencil's strip; **let go on an AutoConnect arrow it is dropped as a drop of it is** (a Swimlane on a page with lanes is inserted in the list, on a page with none it is the shape it is drawn as) and joined to nothing; and **`connector.autoconnect` naming one is refused in words** with nothing changed ("a part of a structure ... drop it with shape.drop").
* **`stencil.quick`** (query, no drawing needed) `{stencil?}` → `{stencils: [{stencil, name, builtin, customized, masters}], offer: {stencil, masters}, readable}`. Without `stencil` (or as `quick`) it is **the Quick Shapes stencil**: the group of every open stencil in the window's order, and `offer` the first four among them that the strip may offer; with a stencil's id it is that stencil's group and the strip it offers. A master of a stencil file carries `stencil`, the id a drop takes.
* **`stencil.add_quick`** `{stencil, master, at?}`, **`stencil.remove_quick`** `{stencil, master}` and **`stencil.reset`** `{stencil}` (Reset Stencil) → the group as `stencil.quick` has it and `changed` (false for a call that changes nothing, which is no edit). The first change of a stencil that had nothing set copies its default group in, so that a change is a change of what is shown. A stencil that is not there, a master that is not in it and an `at` that is not a whole number are refused in words.
* **The window** (`shapes_window.rs`). **The box** at the top has the prompt **Search shapes** and a magnifier at its right: **typing narrows the masters of the stencil on view by name** as before, and **Enter or the magnifier searches every stencil** (`shapes.search {text, mode?}`, a window command: no `text` searches the words of the last search again, blank text clears the search). **The results are a stencil of their own**, `search`, with a row at the head of the stencil menu (a cross on it clears the search) and each stencil's matches under its name; the box keeps the words, taking them out resets the search and shows the stencil that was shown before it, going to another stencil keeps the results, and a refused query is told in the status bar with the results as they were. `window_state` has `shapeSearch` (`text`, `mode`, `matches`, `listed`, `complete`). **A stencil's gallery is its Quick Shapes above a thin divider and the rest below it**; a group the drawing emptied shows the hint **Drop Quick Shapes here**. **The Quick Shapes stencil** (`window.stencil quick`) has the groups of the open stencils under their names. **Right-click on a tile** is **Add to Quick Shapes** or **Remove from Quick Shapes** (the rest of that menu is not built), **a tile dragged and let go inside the window** changes its group (above the divider it becomes a Quick Shape at the tile it was let go on, below it it is one no more) and is not dropped on the page, and **Reset Stencil** is a row of the stencil menu (the rest of that menu is not built; reordering stencils, R6, is not, so the groups gather in the window's order). The flyout of the AutoConnect arrows offers the strip of the stencil on view (`StencilInfo::offer`, which a test holds equal to `stencil.quick`'s `offer` for sets of changes), and a gathering shows the first four it may offer; where the stencil on view feeds the strip nothing, the flyout offers the first stencil's of the window's list that feeds it (`DiacraftApp::autoconnect_offer`), and a part of a structure let go on an arrow is dropped as a drop of it is.
* **Files.** The choice is saved and reopened in `.diacraft`, VSDX (the model writer and a save into the file itself) and `.odg` (tests/it/stencil_quick.rs); a stencil file that is not open when the drawing is reopened has its entry kept. The search writes nothing.
* **Not built** (rows stay as the check list has them): the Online group and Download, the Options page for the AND/OR choice and the box's hide option, the drop-down arrow of the box (Q1 of the pane's spec), reordering stencils, the stencil title's right-click menu but for Reset Stencil, the rest of the master menu, and **the Document Stencil** ("Drop shape resizes to the drawing scale" is built: **Dropping a master on a page of another drawing scale**).

## Page setup

A page's size, orientation, drawing scale, printer paper and Auto Size, and the page list (delete, reorder). The rows are the checklist's "Page setup and drawing scale"
(presets and custom size, orientation, Auto Size: P0) and "Pages and page tabs"; the cells are the page's (`PageWidth`, `PageHeight`, `PageScale`, `DrawingScale`,
`DrawingSizeType`, `DrawingScaleType`, `DrawingResizeType`, `PaperKind`, `PrintPageOrientation`). Code: `crates/engine/src/draw/page_setup.rs` (what a page says, the writes), `page_fit.rs` (Auto Size),
`pages.rs` (delete, reorder), `paper.rs` (the tables) and `cmd/page_setup.rs`. The reference app was never taken apart: every rule below is **ours** and is listed in the report of the task for the check list.
Every length is in **paper inches** (`PageWidth` and `PageHeight` are in drawing units, and the command turns them with the page's drawing scale). `page` is optional on the setup commands and is the first page that is not a background.

| Command | Parameters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `page.presets` (query) | none; works with no document | `{sizes: [{id, name, group, width, height, paper_kind}], papers: [{kind, name, width, height}], scales: [{id, name, kind, family, paper, paper_unit, drawing, drawing_unit, units_per_inch}]}`: the Size gallery (portrait inches; `paper_kind` null when that size is not a paper whose code is known), the papers a printer paper can be, and the drawing scales (`paper` and `drawing` in the units named) |
| `page.setup` (query) | `page`? | `{page, name, background, back_page, width, height, orientation, size, drawing, paper, scale, auto_size, sheets}`: `width` and `height` the page on paper, `back_page` the `ID` of the background page it names or null, `size` the named size it is in either orientation (`{id, name}`) or null, `drawing` `{width, height, units_per_inch}` in drawing units, `paper` `{kind, name, assumed, width, height, orientation, orientation_set}` (one sheet as held; `assumed` when the size is a stand-in), `scale` `{preset, kind, family, paper, paper_unit, drawing, drawing_unit}`, `sheets` `{across, down}` how many sheets of the paper the page covers. Every command below answers with this |
| `page.size` | `preset`, or `width` and `height`; `page`? | a named size in the orientation the page has, or a custom size |
| `page.orientation` | `orientation` (`portrait`, `landscape`); `page`? | turns the page and the paper |
| `page.scale` | `preset`, or `paper` and `drawing` (`paper_unit`?, `drawing_unit`?: `in`, `ft`, `yd`, `mi`, `mm`, `cm`, `m`, `km`; inches when left out); `page`? | a drawing scale |
| `page.paper` | `preset` or `kind`, and/or `orientation`; `page`? | the printer paper and the way it is held; the page is not touched |
| `page.auto_size` | `on`; `page`? | Auto Size on or off |
| `page.type` | `type` (`foreground`, `background`); `page`? | makes the page a background page or a page that is not one; answers the page's setup and `unassigned`, how many pages named it as their background and name none now |
| `page.background` | `background` (the `ID` of a background page, or `null` or `none`); `page`? | gives the page a background page, or none |
| `page.delete` | `id` | `{id, name, pages, unassigned}`: `unassigned` is how many pages named it as their background and name none now; not enabled in a drawing of one page |
| `page.move` | `id`, `to`, `renumber`? | `{id, from, to, renamed}`; not enabled in a drawing of one page |
| `page.add` | `name`?, `like`?, `background`? | `{id, name}`. `name` has at most 31 characters, is not "page" and digits in any case and is not the name of another page, compared without regard to case; with no name the page is called `Page-N` for its id N, or for the next N no page is called by. `like` is the id of a page whose setup (its whole page sheet: size, orientation, scale, units, shadow offset, ruler and grid) the new page copies; `background: true` makes a background page, named `VBackground-N` for the first N no page is called by, put before the pages that are not backgrounds |
| `page.duplicate` | `id`? (default: the first page that is not a background) | `{id, name, from}`: a copy of the page right after it, with its shapes, connections, layers and page cells, named for it and a number that no page has the name of, within 31 characters; one undo step |
| `page.rename` | `id`, `name` | `{id, name}`: names the page; `name` has at most 31 characters, and a longer one is refused in words with nothing changed; a name another page has (compared without regard to case) and a name that is "page" and digits are refused the same way, and a page may be given its own name again; one undo step |

Each setup command is one undo step, and one that would change nothing (a size, an orientation, a state the page has already) is no undo step and does not make the drawing unsaved. A call that
fails (a page with no size, a number out of range, a cell protected by `GUARD`) changes nothing. What reads the cells written (`ThePage!PageWidth`, the scale cells) is worked out again and no cell else.

* The named sizes are held portrait (width at most height), and choosing one gives the page that size **in the orientation it has**: a landscape page (wider than tall, a page has no orientation cell) takes the size turned. A square page is portrait.
  A custom size is taken as given, from 0.1 to 10,000 inches each way (the files hold pages from 0.775 inch to 3,307). **No shape moves when the page changes size** (the page grows from its lower-left corner).
* A named size that is a paper of the table (`paper::PAPERS`; the Windows codes `PaperKind` holds, from the XlPaperSize page of Microsoft's Excel VBA reference and the DEVMODE page, both read 2026-11-07, because gives no list) also sets `PaperKind` and `PrintPageOrientation`, so that the page is one sheet.
  A custom size, and a size with no paper (A0 to A2, A6, the ARCH sizes), leave the paper alone. The sizes of the gallery are ISO 216 A0 to A6, the North American Letter, Legal, Tabloid, Executive and Statement, ANSI C to E and the ARCH sizes; which are offered, and their ids, are ours.
