The Size & Position pane's Width and Height are no longer quiet for a group; they are quiet only for a line. Before this the command said "a group cannot be resized yet".
* Our rule ("left, centre, right, justify and distributed"; `HorzAlign` 3 stretches every line but the last and 4 the last too). `text.format {align: "distributed"}` writes `HorzAlign` 4, and `shape.formatting` reads 4 back as `distributed` (before, it read 3 and 4 both as `justify`, so a distributed paragraph could not be told from a justified one, and a selection holding both showed one value). The text layout already stretched the last line for 4. **No ribbon button and no key**, as in the reference application (`ParagraphDistributed` is off the ribbon): the Text dialog's Paragraph tab offers it. An `.odg` carries 4 as `text-align: justify` with `text-align-last: justify`.
* Our rule (the Line section's Begin Arrow size and End Arrow size, Medium by default). `shape.format {begin_arrow_size, end_arrow_size}` writes `BeginArrowSize` and `EndArrowSize`, whole numbers 0 to 6 (very small, small, medium, large, extra large, jumbo, colossal) and refuses others in words; `shape.formatting` answers both (2 where a shape holds none, the root style's value). The renderer already draws the class. The Format Shape pane's Line section has the two lists beside the arrow lists, the Format Painter carries the sizes, and the cells are saved and read back in `.diacraft`, VSDX and `.odg`. A size is a class: the length of an arrowhead is not typed.
* The owner's ruling of 2026-11-26, which supersedes the last sentence that a hollow mark's inside is not the shape's fill; ours: no specification says what the reference application draws inside a hollow mark, and the project's list of assumptions to check lists it. **The inside of a hollow line end takes the shape's own fill.** A mark whose closed part is an outline (the hollow numbers 14 to 22, 29 to 34, 40 and 41 by the Paint column; one closed part for each disc, triangle, square or diamond, at most two in a mark) is painted inside, **before its outline**, with the fill of the shape that holds the line: its colour and `FillForegndTrans`, its pattern (`FillPattern`, with `FillBkgnd` between the marks) or its gradient (`FillGradientEnabled`, the `FillGradient` stops, the layout and the angle), by the same code that paints the shape's own fill. **The outline keeps the line's colour, transparency and one line weight**; a solid mark keeps the line's colour; an open mark has no closed part; a custom end (254) is drawn as it was (its outline-only sections stay empty inside); and a shape with no fill (`FillPattern` 0) stays transparent inside. **A gradient is measured over the mark's own box in the shape's frame**: the rule of the shape's own fill with the mark's closed part for the path, so the gradient turns with the shape unless `RotateGradientWithShape` is 0, and then it runs in the page's frame over the mark's box. A mark stays whole on a dashed line and so does what is inside it. **A connector DiaCraft makes has No Fill** (ours, the owner's ruling of 2026-11-26: `connector.add`, which the Connector tool and a drag from a connection point send, AutoConnect, the Organization Chart's connectors and every one-dimensional master of the stencils write `FillPattern` 0 on the shape they make, as a cell of its own; the root style's solid white and a theme's connector fill are left as they are, since shapes need them), so its hollow end is see-through, over what lies behind it, until a person picks a fill colour. A colour, a pattern or a gradient from Home > Fill, the Format Shape pane or `shape.format` gives it one and the inside takes it, No Fill takes it away again, and Use Default gives it its style's fill back (solid white in a plain drawing, so the inside is white, and a centred square or disc covers the edge of the box it ends on). The fill controls act on a connector as they do on a box, and the window's tests drive them. **A connector of a file from another app keeps the fill the file gives it** and shows it inside its hollow ends as the file says, and DiaCraft's own `.diacraft`, VSDX and `.odg` files keep `FillPattern` 0 and a fill picked later. No cell is new. **The work is counted** (`WORK_PER_END_FILL`, 4 units for each closed part, and the 24 bands of a rectangular gradient, charged before the fill is painted: a page of 10,000 connectors with hollow ends and gradients stays inside the preview's budget) and a mark wholly outside the view is not painted. **The SVG and PDF writers write the inside as one more path**, filled by the odd-crossings rule, before the mark's outline (a mark is a path in both files, so there is no marker to reuse; each closed part of a gradient fill has a gradient of its own in an SVG file). A line end casts no shadow (a shadow is the shaft and the outline of the shape, and always was), so the fill adds none. **The Shapes window's tiles and the Arrows menu's pictures** paint a hollow mark's closed part with `stencil_fill`, the tile fill of both themes, before its outline: it is transparent, since a tile has no body fill, and a theme that gave tiles one would fill the marks too. The `.odg` is the last sentences.
* Our rule (More Shapes "opens a menu of stencil categories similar to the template categories"). `stencil.list` names the `category` of each built-in stencil, open or in `available`: Basic Shapes, Decorative Shapes and Arrow Shapes are `General`, Basic Flowchart is `Flowchart` (the words of the template categories) and Gane-Sarson is `Software and Database`; a stencil opened from a file has none. **More Shapes** (the chooser at the head of the Shapes window) files every stencil under its category (the open ones first within it), puts a check mark on each that is open and shows the one on view highlighted; a click on one that is not open runs `stencil.open {id}` and then `window.stencil`, so a drawing made from a template, which opens only the stencils its kind needs, can open the rest. The stencils opened from files stand under their own heading, and a list with no categories (a stencil list the app was given) is plain. The menu is one popup of headed groups, not a flyout per category (R3 gives no layout).
* Our rule ("a blank page with basic geometric shapes and arrows"). **Basic Diagram opens Basic Shapes and Arrow Shapes** (Basic Shapes holds ten geometric shapes and no arrows); `template.list`, `file.new {template}`, a template saved from such a drawing and the model a new Basic Diagram starts with say so, and Decorative Shapes, Basic Flowchart and Gane-Sarson are one choice away in More Shapes. Basic Flowchart is unchanged: its stencil holds the shapes the row lists (Terminator, Process, Decision, Predefined Process, Document, Data, On-Page Reference and Off-Page Reference).
* Our rule ("picking a tile opens a dialog with its name, a description, preview thumbnails, a close button, Metric Units and US Units radio buttons, and a large Create button"). A press on a template's tile on File > New opens its detail in place of the gallery: the name, the category, the description, a larger picture of its page (drawn from `template.list`, as the tile's is), **Create** and **Close**. Create asks about unsaved changes as Ctrl+N does and then runs `file.new {template}`; a Cancel there leaves the detail as it was; Close and Escape go back to the gallery and make nothing, and a second Escape leaves the File view. **There is no Metric Units or US Units choice** (the engine has no unit choice at the start of a drawing: the P1 row "Choose metric or US units when starting"), and one picture and not a row of thumbnails. The Blank drawing tile makes its drawing at once, as before. The window command `window.templateDetail {template?, close?}` opens and closes it (`control-protocol.md`).
* The window's keys for zoom are **Alt+F6** (`view.zoomIn`), **Alt+Shift+F6** (`view.zoomOut`) and **Ctrl+Shift+W** (`view.fitPage`, Fit to Window), beside the window's own Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- (Command in place of Ctrl on a Mac, where `Cmd` is the platform's key). **On a Mac, Fit to Window is Command+0** (ours; `ui-egui/src/shortcuts.rs` `MAC_KEYS`): Apple's Human Interface Guidelines give Shift-Command-W to "Close a file and its associated windows" in their table of standard keyboard shortcuts and ask an app not to repurpose one ([Keyboards](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards), read 2026-11-22), so Command+Shift+W is left to the system there. Command+0 is in no row of that table, takes Command alone, sits beside Command+= and Command+-, and is the key the sibling craft apps give their own Fit in Window. Nothing in the window took Command+Shift+W before (winit's app menu binds Command+Q, Command+H and Option+Command+H, and egui binds no W): the clash was with the system's convention. No spec gives the reference app's keys on a Mac. **On a Mac, Command+Plus zooms in too** (ours; `MAC_ALSO`): with Command held the window takes the character from the layout's Command table, so the `=` that the Portuguese, Icelandic, German and Nordic layouts type with Shift+0 arrives as `0` (Fit to Window), while `+` is a key of its own there; the US and British layouts give `=` for Shift+Command+= as well. Each measured layout reaches one of the two keys, the Swiss ones only by the key at the US position of `=`. Before, Command+Plus was egui's own key for the size of the whole window, which it scaled instead of zooming the drawing; elsewhere Ctrl+Plus is still egui's (the shortcut list gives Ctrl+Plus to the web app only). The Ctrl+Shift click magnifier of the zoom page is not built (Ctrl with the wheel zooms).
* Our rule ("Shift with arrow keys moves it a pixel at a time"; Shift with an arrow key moves a pixel at a time). With one connector selected whose ends are both glued (a nudge of the shape would move nothing) and that has handles, **Shift with an arrow key moves the leg that key moves across** (Left and Right an upright leg, Up and Down a level one) **by one screen point**, with no snap, as one `connector.edit_path` and one undo step. **Assumed** (the specifications say "it" and not which leg): of the legs with a handle that the key moves, the one nearest the middle of the route (the first of two the same distance away). A connector with a free end is nudged as a shape, as before, and a plain arrow key leaves a connector with both ends glued alone.

**What the rows said that was stale** (re-scored with evidence, no code): Auto Size extends the page (the page breaks are drawn: `auto_size_grows_the_page_by_whole_sheets_and_the_page_breaks_show_their_borders`), Snap on or off (the drawing tools obey the switch: `the_snap_switch_decides_whether_a_drawing_tool_lands_on_the_grid`), Right-angle connectors (the grade is "Design's Connectors menu or the connector's own menu": the Design tab's menu does it), Basic Flowchart template (the stencil holds the shapes the grade lists) and Ribbon with tabs and groups (the grade is the structure of named tabs and groups, one set at a time, which the order tests hold; a control the commands do not stand behind is drawn disabled and belongs to its own row).

## The colour palette and the theme preview

What the Fill, Line and Font Color menus offer and write, the Colors dialog, and the page showing a theme while its tile is under the pointer. The rows are the checklist's Fill colour and Apply a theme (P0), and Custom colours by RGB or hex and Standard colours stay put (P1).
 Code:
`crates/engine/src/theme/palette.rs` (the palette and what a pick is), `theme/preview.rs` (the copy a preview shows), `formatting/shape_cells.rs` and `text.rs` (what a pick writes), `cmd/theme.rs`; the window:
`crates/ui-egui/src/ribbon/palette.rs` (the menu), `colors_dialog.rs` (the dialog) and `theme_preview.rs` (the preview). The reference app was never taken apart: every rule below is **ours**, on the list of what to compare with the
reference application.

| Command | Parameters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `theme.colors` (query) | `page`? | `{page, themed, theme_colors: [{column, slot, label, swatches: [6]}] (ten columns, `column` 1 to 10, the colour then its five shades; the third and fourth repeat the first two), variant_colors: [7], standard_colors: [10 {label, hex}]}`; a swatch is `{label, tooltip, hex, pick, tint, formula}`. With no theme on the page `themed` is false and the colours are the table `THEMEVAL` gives with no theme. Nothing is changed |
| `theme.preview` (query) | `theme`? (an id of `theme.list`, or `none`), `variant`?, `colors`?, `styles`?, `scope`?, `page`?, `ids`? | as `theme.apply` answers (`pages`, `changed_pages`, `shapes_linked`, `cells_rewritten`, ...) with `preview: true`, **worked out on a copy of the drawing: the session is not touched**, and for `ids` `shapes: [{id, fill, line, color}]` as the copy shows them. A page of more than `MAX_PREVIEW_SHAPES` (5,000) shapes, or one that takes more than a tenth of the steps of a recalculation, is refused in words |
| `shape.format {fill, line}` | `#RRGGBB`, `none`, `default`, `theme:<colour>[:<shade>]` | |
| `text.format {color}` | `#RRGGBB`, `default`, `theme:<colour>[:<shade>]` | the same for the text's `Color`, for the shapes or the characters of `start` to `end` |
| `window.colorsDialog {target, close?}` | `target`: `fill`, `line`, `color`, `stop_color`, `line_stop_color`, `fill_background` or `shadow_color` | the Colors dialog (`docs/control-protocol.md`) |

A `<colour>` is `light`, `dark`, `background`, `accent1` to `accent6` or `variant1` to `variant7` (the names `THEMEVAL` answers also work: `AccentColor2`), and a `<shade>` a whole number from -100 (darker) to 100 (lighter): the
`delta` of `MSOTINT`. A word that is neither is refused in words that name what is taken, and the answer to a refused word is short however long the word was.

* Our rule ("no source gives what applying a theme does to a cell under THEMEGUARD", and the specifications do not say what a palette pick writes). **A theme colour is a formula, so
  that it follows the theme.** The cell holds `THEMEGUARD(THEMEVAL("AccentColor2"))`, or with a shade `THEMEGUARD(MSOTINT(THEMEVAL("AccentColor2"),40))`: `THEMEVAL` answers the colour of the page's theme (and
  `VariantColor1` to `VariantColor7` those of its colour variant), `MSOTINT` the shade (above 0 the lightness rises by that share of the room to the top, below 0 it falls by that share of itself) and
  `THEMEGUARD` marks the cell as following the theme (it evaluates to its argument, and a later format replaces the formula, as it does a `THEMEVAL()`). The cell's value is the colour it works out to on the page; a
  theme applied afterwards (`theme.apply`, `theme.variant`) works the page out again and the value follows. **A colour from Standard Colors, Recent Colors or the Colors dialog is `RGB(r,g,b)`** and no theme changes it
  (`a_theme_colour_follows_the_theme_when_it_changes_and_a_standard_colour_does_not`). A pick on a shape that reads no theme (a shape with its own style, a pasted one) makes it read the page's: it
  follows the page's `Theme` style for the families that have no style of their own (an instance through its master's shape), and the scheme cells that send a shape to its page are written 65534 where it does not read them so (as a Quick Style does); a page with no
  theme needs neither, the formula answers the no-theme table (`#9DBB61` for the second accent) and a theme applied later links the shape and works the formula out again. A fill or a line colour is as say
  (a solid pattern, a gradient turned off). **Bounded:** a colour of the theme (or `default`) is put on at most `MAX_PICK_SHAPES` (10,000) shapes in one command, groups opened, refused in words before any work is done (a plain colour is held to the 20,000 shapes any format takes); the shapes named are made to follow the theme **in one pass over their places** (`theme::follow_page_theme_refs`: one planner, one resolver, no walk of the page to find a shape by its `ID`), and the passes are counted (`theme::follow_work`, tested in `theme_color_cost.rs` on a page of 100,000 shapes). **The shapes named are themselves found in one walk of the page**: `formatting::targets` asks `draw::find_named` for all of them at once, and the walk stops at the last one found, where a search for each by `Document::find_shape` walked the page from the top for each (4,096 names on a page of 30,000 shapes were 58 million visits, and the page a command works on was found the same way, so 117 million for one fill); `page_for` is `draw::page_holding`, which walks each page once for all the names. A shape not on the page is refused in the same words as before ("page 1 has no shape 999"), in the order the shapes are named. The count is tested in `formatting/tests.rs` (the visits of one walk, and none by `find_shape`) and in `theme_color_cost.rs` (a fill, a theme colour, a text colour and a Quick Style on 4,096 ids spread over a page of 30,000 shapes).
* "a top row plus five shade rows", the tooltip "Turquoise, Accent 6, Darker 25%"; the tints are those the sample files saved by the reference app hold in a page shape's own cells, `inferred-from-sample`. Each column is the colour and five shades: an accent and a variant colour are lightened
  by 80, 60 and 40 and darkened by 25 and 50 percent, the light colour (the first and third columns) darkened by 5, 15, 25, 35 and 50, and the dark colour (the second and fourth) lightened by 50, 35, 25, 15 and 5. A swatch's tooltip is the colour's name
  (`colour_name`, ours: a hue word, `Light` or `Dark` in front, the greys by lightness), its theme name and its shade.
* **The palette has ten columns**: **the first four are white, black, white and black in every theme
  state and the last six are Accent 1 to 6** (drew nine, with Background third, because no function names a tenth). **The third and fourth columns repeat Light and Dark** until a source settles what they are
  (no public file shows a pick of a third or a fourth column as anything but a `Light` or a `Dark` form): a pick of one writes the same formula as the same swatch of the first two (`THEMEGUARD(THEMEVAL("Light"))`,
  `THEMEGUARD(MSOTINT(THEMEVAL("Dark"),25))` and the rest), and `theme.colors` answers each column with its `column` (1 to 10), since two columns name the same colour. Background is no column of the palette, and `theme:background`
  is still a colour a command can name. The window names a repeated column's swatches `palette.fill.theme:light:-25@3`, the place after an `@`, so that no two elements of the menu share a name; its Use Default row shows the swatch of
  the column that picks Accent 1 (a fill) or Dark (a line and text), whichever place it is in.
* Our rule ("Standard Colors (ten swatches)"). The ten are our own (Dark red, Red, Orange, Yellow, Light green, Green, Light blue, Blue, Dark blue and Purple: `theme::STANDARD_COLOURS`), listed by `theme.colors`.
* Our rule ("Use Default's behaviour is not described"). `default` hands the cells to the theme: for a fill `FillForegnd`, `FillPattern` and `FillGradientEnabled`, for a line `LineColor` and `LinePattern`, for text
  `Color`, each as the call `THEMEVAL()` with the marker `Themed` (what the `Theme` style holds), so the shape has the colour its theme gives it and follows a theme applied later.
* Our rule ("Recent Colors (ten swatches)"). A colour chosen in the Colors dialog, or picked from the recent row, is the newest of ten that the three controls and the pane share; the ten Standard Colors are always on
  the menu and are not added, and a theme colour is not a colour to remember (it follows the theme). **They are kept while the window is open and not between runs**: the person's settings store has no field for them yet.
* Our rule ("Color model (combo; the image shows RGB)", "a palette of colour cells"). The Colors dialog's Custom tab has a colour field (hue across, saturation down), a lightness bar, a Color
  model of two, **RGB** (Red, Green, Blue) and **HSL** (Hue, Saturation, Lightness), a Hex box that takes `#RRGGBB` and is refused in words when it is no colour (and takes the keyboard with its text selected), and the New and
  Current swatches; the Standard tab is a grid of twelve hues in six lightnesses and a row of greys. OK sends one `format.shape`, `format.text`, `format.gradient` or `format.shadow` with the colour as `#rrggbb`; for the text colour, with a text box
  that was open, **the characters that were selected in it** (the box closes while the dialog is up, what was typed is sent, and the box opens again over the same characters when it ends). Cancel and Escape change nothing.
* Our rule ("pointing at a tile previews it on the page"). **A preview is made on a copy of the drawing** by the code `theme.apply` and `theme.variant` run (`theme::preview`), so the session is not touched: no
  command, no undo step, no revision, no unsaved mark, and the redo stack is kept. **Budget:** the pages of the copy hold at most 5,000 shapes (counted before anything is copied, stopping at the cap) and their recalculation at most a
  tenth of the steps of a document's (a rectangle is about 180 steps); a page past either is refused in words ("apply the theme to see it") and the window says so once for the tile. The window asks for the copy when a tile is under the
  pointer (`ask_theme_preview`), makes it once for the drawing, revision, page and tile, draws it on a render worker of its own in place of the page's picture, and **lets it go in the first frame with no tile asked for**; moving to another
  tile stops the picture being drawn and the picture of the one before stays until the next arrives. A tile that is the page's theme and variant already is not previewed. It is made on the window's own thread (about a fifth of a second
  for a page at the cap). Not previewed: Quick Styles, the layouts, Effects, Connectors and Embellishments (no engine setting behind them).
* Our rule (the `.odg` model writer, `odgfile/flatten.rs`). **Every drawing keeps the shape's own formulas of the cells the writer has an attribute for** (for a drawing from a VSDX file; **any other drawing **, which
  kept only the theme formulas before): the colour a theme pick gives is a value in the file's attribute with its formula (`THEMEGUARD(...)`, `THEMEVAL(...)`) carried in DiaCraft's data on the shape's style, and follows the
  theme when the file is read again, and so do **a fixed colour's `RGB(r,g,b)`** (a colour from Standard Colors, Recent Colors or the Colors dialog, and the fill and line the swimlane, pool and container stencils write: the
  check after a save said 18 formulas lost for the cross-functional flowchart, 6 for a BPMN pool, 2 for a container and 2 for a shape a person coloured), **a formula a person types in the frame or style cells** (the ShapeSheet
  window), and **the pin of `shape.pin`** (`Width*0`). A formula that names another shape (`Sheet.2!PinX+2`) comes back naming it, the shapes a formula names keeping their
  `ID`s, **and so does a formula the copy takes from the shape's master** (`Sheet.5` for the master's group is written as the `ID` of the group instance, in the geometry, the text and the style cells,
  `Flattener::rebound`); a structure read back from an `.odg` is worked on as one read back from a `.diacraft` file. **What the reader works out stays said**: the place of a member of a group (a formula of the group's frame) and the frame of a
  line (worked out from its ends) are written as their values: the check after a save names them for a drawing of any origin, and the save of a drawing from a VSDX file says how many. **The formula a style cell has from its master or a style sheet stays too**
  (the fill, line, line-end, alignment and margin cells the writer has an attribute for), like the shape's own (an ERD relationship's
  `IF(Prop.Identifying,1,2)` for its pattern and its line ends' formulas of its Shape Data), carried in DiaCraft's data while the attribute says the value it works out to. An inherited formula that is a bare number is a constant, and one that names
  the theme, or is longer than 1,024 bytes, or is a style sheet's and names a shape, stays the constant it works out to; **one that the master holds and that names another shape of the master
  (`Sheet.N`) is kept naming the shape of the instance that stands for it** (a member's line pattern that follows its group's shape data, and the constant when nothing of the instance stands for that shape), and a shape that follows the `Theme` style and holds a dash of its own holds the cap it resolves to, so the dash is named
  for that cap. **A text colour that is a formula is a run's cell with a formula, which a save in place into a drawing opened from an `.odg` does not write yet**
  (tier 2): Save refuses it in words and Save As keeps it.

## Shape operations

Union, Combine, Fragment, Intersect and Subtract build new shapes out of the geometry of the shapes named, or, for Subtract, change the first one. The rules are
a draft, and the choices it leaves to the project are SHAPEOPS-PROPS, -FRAME, -ROWS,
-NEEDS, -GLUE, -UNDO, -AREA, -COMBINE, -FRAGMENT, -INTERSECT, -SUBTRACT, -PRECISION, -CAPS and -PRIMARY in the check list. **The reference app was never
taken apart**: every behaviour below that the specification marks `unknown` is ours and
unverified. Join and Trim are **Join and Trim**, below, and Offset and Fit Curve **Offset and Fit Curve**; the Operations menu of the window is **The window**, below.

| Command | Parameters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `shape.union` | `ids` (two or more), `page`? | `{page, ids, deleted, kept}`: one new shape with the outline of all, one section for each boundary of the union (each outer boundary and each hole), in front, with the first shape's text and formatting; the originals are deleted |
| `shape.combine` | `ids` (two or more), `page`? | one new shape with a section for each shown section of each original, in selection order and then section order, so that where they overlap there is a hole (the sections share one fill); its rows are the originals' own, carried exactly |
| `shape.fragment` | `ids` (one or more), `page`? | one new shape for each region the shapes make together, in the order of R23, with the first shape's formatting and **no text**; open paths and `NoFill` 1 paths cut the regions and leave nothing of their own |
| `shape.intersect` | `ids` (two or more), `page`? | one new shape for the area **every** operand covers, with one section for each boundary; refused when no area is common to all |
| `shape.subtract` | `ids` (two or more), `page`? | the area of every shape after the first is taken from the first, which **stays the same shape** (id, name, master link, text, formatting, Shape Data, layers, glue, place in the drawing) and has only its geometry and frame changed; the others are deleted; refused when nothing of the first is left |

`ids` lists the shapes with the **first shape first** (SHAPEOPS-PRIMARY): the first id is the shape whose text and formatting a result takes, and Subtract's
first shape. The shapes must share one container: all on the page, or all members of one group. `page` is the page's `ID` (default: the first page that
holds all the shapes). `ids` in the answer names the shapes made, the last in front (SHAPEOPS-ORDER); `deleted` the shapes deleted; `kept` is Subtract's first shape and
`null` for the others. Each command is **one undo step**; a command that is refused changes nothing and adds no step (SHAPEOPS-UNDO). The made shapes get ids above
every one on the page and above the session's high-water mark. The commands are enabled whenever a document is open, as the other shape commands are: the selection
is the window's, so what each needs of its shapes is checked when it runs, in words (`draw::check_shape_ops` asks the same questions without running one).

**The path work is `craft-pathops`** (the Craft apps' shared library of path operations on `kurbo::BezPath`, here from the one-bit fork at revision
`533839399341547b29ababfb8ef030298b133914` (the head of its pull request, storytold/craft-libs#677, with upstream's main of 2026-11-23 merged in) until the pull request merges), and its `Limits` are its defaults, never raised. The calls are the
`try_` forms, so that a refusal reaches the person: Union is `try_unite_all_with`, Intersect `try_pathfinder_with(Intersect)`, Subtract `try_pathfinder_with(MinusFront)`
with the first shape at the back, Fragment `try_pathfinder_with(Divide)` over the fills and the cutting lines, and `try_area` tells whether a shape has area. A shape's
fill goes in as the rings of its sections that take the fill, filled by the odd-crossings rule. What the library refuses is said in words: `TooComplex`
as "the shapes have too many path elements, or their edges cross or meet in too many places, to be worked on in bounded time (the limits of the path library)",
`Degenerate` as "the shapes are too degenerate to combine (coordinates too large for the sweep, or a shape it cannot take)", `NonFinite` as "a shape's geometry holds a
number that is not finite"; each is a refusal that changes nothing (`Failed`, not `BadParams`). The library is not changed here.

**What is read of an operand** (`draw/shapeops/operand.rs`):

* The rows are the shape's effective ones (its master's and its own), read by the renderer's own reader of a row's cells and built by
  `diacraft_geom::build_paths_bounded`, so what is worked on is the curve that is drawn. Arcs, elliptical arcs, an ellipse, NURBS, splines and Beziers stay curves.
* The paths are carried **through the shape's own pose** into its container's coordinates: the page's, for a shape on the page, and the group's own frame, for a member
  The groups round a member play no part in it, so a result inside a turned group is as turned as the members beside it, and a turned or flipped operand takes
  part with its real outline.
* A section with `NoShow` 1 is not read. A section with `NoFill` 0 gives its fill ring, which closes an open path by a straight edge, whatever the
  shape's `FillPattern` says (SHAPEOPS-AREA). A section with `NoFill` 1, or one whose path is open, is a cutting line for Fragment (ours:
  R23 says "open paths and `NoFill` 1 paths"; a ring that is a cutting line is cut in two before it goes to the library, which takes a ring for a closed shape).
* **A guide, a group, a picture or an embedded object, a connector** (a one-dimensional shape with a glued end, or one of ours that keeps a route), **a container or a
  list, a shape with no shown geometry and a shape on a locked layer are refused** (SHAPEOPS-NEEDS). A container or list is a shape with `User.msvStructureType`
  `Container` or `List`, or whose `Relationships` formula holds `DEPENDSON(1, ...)` or `DEPENDSON(2, ...)`. A shape is on a locked layer when **any** layer its own
  `LayerMember` names, in the page's `Layer` section, has `Lock` set (ours: the specification does not say which of several layers
  decides; a page with more than 4,096 layers is refused in words). Union, Intersect and Subtract need a fill area in every shape, Fragment needs one shape with one,
  Combine and Fragment take lines for the rest. Plain unglued lines are accepted. **A section has a fill area** when it takes the fill (`NoFill` 0) and its fill
  ring is thicker than 1E-5 in some direction: a point, a line there and back (an open straight path with `NoFill` 0) and a run along one line have none. **That is judged from
  the ring, and by no sweep of the library**: the sweep of one operand costs what its crossings do, which no count here bounds, and it would be paid for each operand, again
  by a window asking about a selection. So a shape whose rings pass and cover nothing under the odd-crossings rule (two equal squares one over the other, as two sections) is
  let through by the check, and what a command makes of it is what the rule gives: where nothing would be made the command is refused by its own result ("no area to unite",
  "no area in common", "nothing of shape N is left", "no region"), in words and with nothing changed, and a Union of it with a shape that fills is that shape's outline (the
  one that fills nothing adds nothing, and goes with the rest).
* **The locks** (SHAPEOPS-LOCKS): a shape that would be deleted and has `LockDelete` refuses the command (Subtract's first shape is not deleted, so its own
  `LockDelete` does not refuse it); `LockVtxEdit` on Subtract's first shape refuses Subtract, and on any other shape refuses nothing (no vertex of it is edited: it is
  deleted); `LockFormat` refuses nothing.
* **The work is counted before it is done** (SHAPEOPS-CAPS): a command takes at most 4,096 shapes (the command's id limit), a shape of more than 1,024 `Geometry`
  sections (counted over the shape, its master and its styles) is not an operand, and all the operands together may hold at most 8,192 sections, 200,000 rows, 1 MiB
  of constructor text (a `PolylineTo`'s `A` and a `NURBSTo`'s `E`), as many path elements as the library takes in one operation (524,288) and 50 million
  multiplications of spline work. Each is charged from the sheet's own counts (`Resolver::rows_held`) **before any section is merged or built**, so a shape that
  inherits a huge master costs a count and not a merge, and every section looked at is charged, a hidden or an empty one too. What each shape made is given of the first shape's formatting (its cells and the rows and cells of its sections) and of its frame, times the shapes made, is charged as well (below). A command makes at most 10,000 shapes (Fragment, which stops building pieces when it meets the cap and says "more than 10000", not how many there were) and a shape holds at most 8,192 sections.
  **What is not counted is the library's own sweep.** One call of the path library (`craft-pathops`, its default limits, never raised here) costs what the crossings of its
  edges do, and its limits do not bound that: a shape of 2,001 vertices each joined to the one 1,000 steps on, which passes every limit, takes a sweep 15 to 20 seconds and
  several gigabytes. The engine runs that sweep **once for a command** (the checks before it are by no sweep) and neither lowers the library's limits nor counts crossings of its
  own: the bound is the library's, which `craft-libs` has as a pull request (#677) and DiaCraft takes when its pin moves to it. Until then such a shape makes a command slow,
  and a test of it is ignored (`shapeops_hostile.rs`, with the reason).

**What is written** (`draw/shapeops/rows.rs`, SHAPEOPS-FRAME and -ROWS):

* The library's contours are read as loops: vertices closer than 1E-5 merge, the vertices a straight run passes through are taken out (the library keeps its inputs'
  own anchors, and the union of four bars in a ring would otherwise list a vertex in the middle of each side), a region of less than 1E-8 of area is dropped, and the
  loops are turned so that **outer boundaries run anticlockwise and holes clockwise**. The unit of these tolerances is the cells' own, which is the inch on a page of
  the default scale and the drawing unit on a scaled page, the unit `geom` closes a path in. Curves stay within 1E-5 of the library's exact result, a tenth of
  the 1E-4 of R46; the library's refit precision is that.
* A loop is one section: `MoveTo`, a `LineTo` for each straight edge and one clamped cubic `NURBSTo` for each curved one (degree 3, knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, weights 1,
  `NURBS(1,3,0,0,x1,y1,0,1,x2,y2,0,1)` with the control points as shares of the box), each coordinate `Width*k` or `Height*k` with the share to
  **twelve places** (`Width*0.666666666667`, V2: a cell holds nine, which would be 1E-9 out), the constant 0 for 0, plain `Width` for 1, the constant 0 where the box is
  flat. A closed loop ends on the formulas its `MoveTo` starts with. The flags are `NoFill` 0 (every loop written is closed), `NoLine`, `NoShow`, `NoSnap` and
  `NoQuickDrag` 0. Rows are numbered from `IX` 1, as a file's are.
* **The frame of a made shape**: unturned and unflipped (`Angle` 0, `FlipX` and `FlipY` 0), a two-dimensional shape; `Width` and `Height` the box with sides along the
  container's axes that holds the geometry, **a curve counting by its true extent**; `PinX` and `PinY` the middle of the box in the container's coordinates, `LocPinX` the
  formula `Width*0.5` and `LocPinY` `Height*0.5`; the text block the whole shape (the seven text transform cells, as a text box's). A made shape has no master, no
  name and no `UniqueID`.
* **The work is done near the origin.** The container's coordinates are moved so that the middle of everything worked on is the origin, and the results are moved
  back for the pin, so that a small shape far out is as easy for the library's sweep as one near the origin (two squares at 1E8 or 1E12 unite to the shape V2 gives, with the
  pin as far out). A shape that really is that large is refused by the library (`Degenerate`) in words.
* **What a made shape takes from the first shape** (SHAPEOPS-PROPS, `draw/shapeops/look.rs`): its three style links as it reads them (its own or its master
  shape's); every direct cell of the three families the catalogue lists (Line Format, Fill Format with the shadow, gradient and effect cells, the theme and Quick Style cells,
  the Text Block Format cells) that the shape or its master holds, as formula and value; the `FillGradient` and `LineGradient`
  rows as the shape reads them; `LayerMember` (SHAPEOPS-LAYER); and, where the command gives text (Union, Combine, Intersect: the first shape's, or its master's), the text with its runs and
  the `Character`, `Paragraph` and `Tabs` rows its markers name. **Fragment gives no text and none of those rows** (a first shape may hold a thousand rows of each, and a Fragment may make 10,000
  shapes). **The sections are shared:** the shapes a command makes hold the same `Arc` of each section, not a copy for each, and what the sections hold (a row and each of its cells, a section
  and each of its cells), **with the cells the first shape holds itself (up to the 97 of the families) and the frame's cells each shape is given**, times the shapes made, is charged before
  any shape is built and refused in words past 500,000 in all (about a kilobyte is held for each cell by the recalculation that follows, which a million cells fill), for a file written from the drawing writes the sections for each shape. A
  section of more than 1,024 rows, or more than 8 sections of one name, is **refused in words** and not dropped whole. A value a style supplies is not copied, the link is. **Not carried:** Shape Data,
  User-defined cells, Hyperlinks, Actions, Action Tags, Controls, Connection Points, Scratch, Events, Protection, Miscellaneous, Glue Info and Shape Layout. A field
  becomes the text it shows, and a formula that names anything but a direct cell the made shape has (another shape, `Prop.Cost`, `TheText`) becomes its value.

**Fragment's regions** (SHAPEOPS-FRAGMENT): the fills of the operands and the cutting lines go to the library's Divide, which gives one face for each region any fill
covers, a face with holes as one path of several contours; a cutting line leaves nothing of itself. The faces are ordered by the top of each face's box, highest first, then
by its left side, leftmost first, the sides compared to a hundred-millionth as whole numbers so that the order is total; the last is frontmost.

**Combine's rows are carried, not computed** (SHAPEOPS-COMBINE, `draw/shapeops/carry.rs`): a pose is a move, a turn and flips, never a scale, so every row type
is carried by moving its points through the pose and writing its numbers again in the new frame. A point is moved; an `ArcTo`'s bow is a distance, which a turn leaves and a
flip of one axis **changes the sign of**; an elliptical arc's axis angle `C` is turned and reflected with the points and its ratio `D` stays; knots, weights and a
spline's degree stay; `RelMoveTo`, `RelLineTo` and `RelEllipticalArcTo` are written as `MoveTo`, `LineTo` and `EllipticalArcTo` with their shares as formulas, and
`RelCubBezTo` and `RelQuadBezTo` keep their kind with their shares worked out for the new box (ours); a `POLYLINE` or `NURBS` constructor is moved
point by point and written in the relative type. A constructor that cannot be read is carried as what it draws (a line to the end, a move), and an
`InfiniteLine` is left out. Each carried section keeps its own `NoFill`, `NoLine`, `NoSnap` and `NoQuickDrag`, and a section with `NoShow` 1 is dropped.

**Subtract changes the first shape in place** (SHAPEOPS-SUBTRACT): the work is done in the first shape's own frame, so its geometry is what it was. Its shown sections
that have a fill area (they take the fill, `NoFill` 0, and cover an area: not an open straight line with `NoFill` 0) are replaced by the boundary of its fill less the union of the others' fills; its
`NoFill` 1 sections, its open sections that cover no area and its hidden ones are kept as they were, and a first shape that keeps one keeps its frame (below).
On a master instance a replaced section it inherits is marked deleted on the instance (`Del`) and the new ones are local, numbered from the lowest `IX` that neither the
shape nor its master holds. The other operands are deleted whether or not they touch it. **The frame** is refitted to the box of the new geometry in the shape's own axes,
`Angle`, `FlipX`, `FlipY` and the formulas of `LocPinX` and `LocPinY` kept, and `PinX` and `PinY` moved by what the box's corner and the local pin moved, through the shape's
turn and flips, so that nothing moves on the page; the local pin follows its formula, so a centred pin stays centred. **A first shape that holds `LockCalcWH`, or keeps
any section of its own, keeps its frame exactly** and the geometry is written in it (R28 for `LockCalcWH`; ours, for the rest: a refit moves the origin
of the shape's own frame, and what is kept, written in that frame, would move on the page; the specification says kept sections stay "as they were" and does not say what
happens to the frame then). A first shape with no width or no height in that case is refused. Cells that follow `Width` and `Height`, such as connection points written as
shares, move with the box, and a connector glued to them follows; formulas that name a row of a replaced section are not kept.

**Glue, guides, containers and undo**: the originals go by the engine's own delete at the places one walk of the page found them: a
connector glued to one keeps that end where it is, unglued, its `Connect` row goes, and it is neither glued to the made shape nor deleted; a shape held to one by alignment cells
is released; jumps are settled. A made shape has no connection points. **A command that makes one shape puts it where the first shape was in containers and lists**
(SHAPEOPS-CONTAINERS, ours: only the first shape's ties of kinds 4 and 5, `DEPENDSON(4, ...)` and `DEPENDSON(5, ...)`, go to the made shape, and each
`Relationships` formula that holds `Sheet.<first>!` as a member, in a `DEPENDSON(1, ...)` or `DEPENDSON(2, ...)` call, holds the made shape instead); callouts' ties are not
carried and a tie to a shape that is gone names nothing, as a delete leaves it; a command that makes many shapes puts none in a container. The made shapes are appended to the end of
the container's list (the page's, or the group's members), so they are frontmost in it, and what was between the originals is behind them.

**What these cost**, measured by `crates/engine/tests/it/shapeops_hostile.rs` in the development profile (the times move with the load of the machine; each test holds the
whole call to 60 s, far above what it takes and far below a hang): 120 thin bars crossing in 3,600 places unite in 0.3 s to a shape of 3,482 sections; 300 bars turned about one centre
in 0.6 s; a pie of 256 slices (512 ends at one point, the library's limit) in 1.1 s, and one of 300 is refused in 2 ms; 2,000 and 3,000 squares nested unite in 0.1 s, a Subtract of
1,500 in 0.09 s, and an Intersect or a Fragment of 3,000 nested is refused in 0.1 s (the library's limit on the entries of its windings); 4,096 disjoint squares unite in 0.6 s;
a Fragment into 10,000 regions (99 lines each way across a rectangle, 199 operands) is made in 1.9 s and one into 10,201 is refused in 0.3 s; shapes 85 groups deep take 1 ms; a
union of 9,000 sections is refused by its count in 0.05 s and a section of 200,001 rows in 0.1 s. Two squares at 1E8 or 1E12 unite in 0.5 ms.

**What is not here:** a container for the many shapes of a
Fragment; the refit of a Subtract frame that keeps sections; a drawing scale's inches (the tolerances are the cells' units).

**The window (`crates/ui-egui/src/operations.rs`, `options_dialog.rs`).** The Developer tab's Shape Design group has the **Operations** menu (`OperationsMenu`) with nine rows. **The Draw tab has the same menu** (owner, 2026-11-25; a DiaCraft extra beyond the reference app, decision): its last group, **Shape Operations** (ours: the map has no such group), holds one button, **Operations** (`DrawShapeOperations`), whose menu is the same list of nine rows **and a tenth, Fit Curve** (after Offset: the reference app's ribbon lists it among the commands that are not on it, so the Developer tab's menu does not have it), so it runs the same commands, with the same enabled states and the same words for a quiet or a refused row, and the Developer tab keeps its entry with the map's id, for parity. **Union, Combine, Fragment, Intersect, Subtract, Join and Trim** run the window's `operations.union`, `operations.combine`, `operations.fragment`, `operations.intersect`, `operations.subtract`, `operations.join` and `operations.trim` (no parameters; `engine.commands` lists them with the engine's), each of which names the shapes selected and the page they were selected on (refused in words when that page is not the one shown) and sends the engine's `shape.*` command, and **clears the selection when it succeeds** (nothing stays selected, and a Subtract's first shape stays but is not selected). **Offset** opens its dialog (`operations.offsetDialog`) and, on the **Draw tab's menu only**, **Fit Curve** opens its (`operations.fitCurveDialog`): see **Offset and Fit Curve**, below. **Update Alignment Box** is drawn and quiet, with the tooltip "Update Alignment Box (not available yet)", the words a quiet button of the ribbon uses (a quiet row of any menu now says why on hover: the reason its command gives, or "(not available yet)"). No row is in the canvas menu (lists none).

**The order of `ids` is the order the window keeps its selection in** (SHAPEOPS-PRIMARY), and the first shape is the one a result takes its text and formatting from: a click selects one shape alone and a Shift-click or a Ctrl-click adds one at the end, so a click selection is in click order and the shape clicked first is first; a rubber band lists the shapes it takes in the page's drawing order, back to front, so the backmost is first, and a Shift-rubber-band adds them after what was selected; Select All is the page's order too; `edit.select {ids}` keeps the order it is given.

**The shapes go to the page they were selected on, and a selection that is not of the page on view is refused**: a shape's `ID` is the page's own, so `edit.select {ids: [1, 2]}` on page 1, `page.select {id: 2}` and `operations.union`, served in one frame by the control channel, would have united page 2's shapes 1 and 2. `selection_target`, which every window command that acts on the selection takes its page and shapes from (the seven here, `format.*`, `format.rotateText`, `arrange.*` and `clipboard.copy`, `.cut` and `.duplicate`), now returns the page the selection was made on and refuses with "the shapes selected are on another page than the one shown" when that is not the page on view, changing nothing; an entry of the Operations menu is quiet with the same words. It refuses and does not drop the selection, since a command must not change what the window holds; a person cannot reach it, as the next frame drops a selection that is not of the page on view. **The panes follow the same rule**: Size & Position, Format Shape and the formatting the Home tab's controls show take the shapes selected only when the selection is of the page on view (`selection_on_view` and `selection_here` in `format.rs`, one place with `selection_target`); with a selection of another page they show nothing of it: their boxes are quiet and blank, Size & Position's title has no shape's name, and no formatting is read. A pane box that cannot be changed takes no keys even while it still holds the focus from the frame before (egui's `add_enabled` greys a text box and leaves its keys on), so a value typed in the frame the page changes reaches neither page.

**An entry is enabled only when `draw::check_shape_ops` says its operation can run on the selection** (two shapes for five of them (Union, Combine, Intersect, Subtract and Join) and one for Fragment, Trim, Offset and Fit Curve; no group, guide, connector, container, list, picture or shape without geometry; no `LockDelete` on a shape the command would delete (Offset and Fit Curve delete none), no `LockVtxEdit` on Subtract's first shape or on a shape Fit Curve changes, no shape on a locked layer), and the Operations button is enabled when any entry is (with every entry quiet the menu does not open and the button's tooltip says why, as the other menus do). A quiet entry's tooltip is the engine's own words ("Union needs two shapes at least (a shape named twice counts once)"), and a command run by name while its entry is quiet is refused with them. **The engine is asked when the selection or the drawing changes, never for a frame:** the answer for each operation is kept for the drawing's generation, its revision, the page and the shapes selected in order (a file that is opened starts its revision at 1 again, so the revision alone would find the old drawing's answers in the new one), and an operation is asked about only when something draws or asks whether it can run: the button asks for the first entry that works, the open menu for the entries it has (a check is one reading of the shapes' geometry, 13 ms on the worst input the engine's tests make, and for Offset and Fit Curve a scan of the types of the rows; `work::Work::shape_op_checks` counts them). **A run that the check let through and its result refuses** (Intersect of squares that do not meet: "no area in common") puts the engine's words in the status bar and leaves the drawing, the undo history and the selection as they were. Each operation is one undo step: Ctrl+Z brings the originals back with their ids and cells, and Ctrl+Y makes it again.

**The Developer tab is off in a new window** and is turned on in **File, Options, Customize Ribbon** (`window.options {tab?, close?}`; `window.developer {on?}` is the command it sends). The dialog lists the ten sections, of which only Customize Ribbon works (the others are quiet, with the tooltip "General (not available yet)"), and its Main Tabs list shows every tab ticked and quiet except the Developer box; **OK sends one `window.developer` if the box was changed**, Cancel and Escape send nothing, and the File view closes behind the dialog. Where the window is too narrow for the list of sections beside the page, the page shows alone. The setting is the window's and is not saved (the dialog's note says it is for this window only, and the next window starts with the tab off); the dialog's layout, its captions and the quiet tabs are ours (R32 says only that the Options dialog's Main Tabs list orders the tabs as the row does). **The reference app was never taken apart.**

## Join and Trim

Join and Trim are the two operations of that work on paths. They are built on the same reading of the operands, the
same frame and rows, the same glue, containers, undo and counts as the five above (**Shape operations**), and on the path library's `try_` forms. **The reference app was
never taken apart**: what the specification marks `unknown` is ours and unverified, and what this
section chooses beyond it is marked **ours**.

| Command | Parameters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `shape.join` | `ids` (two or more), `page`? | `{page, ids, deleted, kept}`: one new shape, in front, with the first shape's text and formatting, holding one section for each chain of the paths whose ends meet; the originals are deleted |
| `shape.trim` | `ids` (one or more), `page`? | one new shape for each stretch of the paths between the places where they cross, touch or meet themselves, in front, with the first shape's formatting and **no text**; the originals are deleted |

The window's Operations menu runs them as `operations.join` and `operations.trim` (below). Each is **one undo step**, a refusal changes nothing and adds no step, the made shapes get
new ids above every one on the page, and `kept` is `null`. Both refuse what the five refuse (a group, a guide, a picture, a connector, a container or a list, a shape with no
geometry, a shape on a locked layer, `LockDelete` on a shape that is deleted, shapes of different containers), and both take shapes that share one container, so that shapes
picked inside a group give shapes that are the group's last members. Join needs two shapes, as the others do; **Trim takes one**: it cuts a shape where it crosses itself.

**What is read of an operand** is the stroke of each shown section as drawn (in the container's coordinates, through the shape's pose), cut into **paths, one for each `MoveTo`** (a *run*,
`draw/shapeops/runs.rs`, ours: R32 takes a section for a path, and a section may hold several). A path is a start and segments, each a straight line or one cubic
Bezier (a quadratic is raised to a cubic; an arc, an ellipse, a spline and a NURBS are the cubics the geometry crate draws them as). It is **closed** when its ends meet within 1E-5.
 A path that draws nothing (no point of it, a control point too, farther than 1E-5 from its start in x or in y) is left out.

**Join** (`draw/shapeops/join.rs`, R32, SHAPEOPS-JOIN). The paths are taken in the order the shapes were named, then the order of the sections, then of the paths in a section. A path
that is closed passes through as a section of its own, in its place. For the others, a chain starts with the first path not yet used. While some unused path has an end within 1E-5
of the chain's tail, the **earliest** such path is attached (turned round if its end is the one that meets), and then the same at the head; a chain whose ends have met is closed and
takes nothing more. **Where three or more ends meet, the earliest pair joins and the rest go to other chains**. One shape comes out even when nothing abuts, with a section for
each chain. The vertex where two paths join is written **once**, and a join moves what it joins by 1E-5 at most; segments in line with each other are **not** merged; a line stays a
`LineTo`, and a curve is one `NURBSTo` cubic (R32 allows curves to come back as cubics within the accuracy). A closed chain is a section of `NoFill` 0, an open one `NoFill` 1, and
the other four flags are 0: the flags of the sections the paths came from are not carried (unlike Combine's). Paths that cross without abutting are not cut: that is Trim's work.
**The library's `join` is not used**: it goes to the nearest end first and bridges a gap with a straight segment, so two lines 0.01 apart would be one path of three segments, where V16
wants two sections, and it closes a path that is alone. Ends are found by a hash of cells 1E-5 wide, each entry looked at charged a step, past 40 million of which the command is
refused in words (so a star of 4,096 lines from one point costs a few steps for each, and a crowd of ends a hair beyond the tolerance of another crowd is refused or finished in
bounded time).

**Trim** (`draw/shapeops/trim.rs`, `ops.rs`, `snap.rs`, SHAPEOPS-TRIM). Every path of every operand, open or closed and whatever its `NoFill`, is cut where it crosses or touches
another path or itself, and each stretch between two neighbouring cuts is one shape. The cutting is the path library's Pathfinder **Outline** (not its `Trim`, which is the illustration
app's operation of removing what a shape in front hides): it cuts where three or more edges of the planar map of all the paths meet, keeps each stretch's own segments (a line stays a line
and a curve is cut exactly where it is crossed), and keeps a stretch that two paths run along **once**, in the place of the earlier path.

* **The order of the pieces** (SHAPEOPS-ORDER, ours): the operands in the order they were named, and each path's pieces in path order **from its first cut**.
  A closed path starts at the first place it is cut after its own start, so the piece that holds its start comes last (the rectangle's right piece, then its left, then the line's
  three). The vectors list pieces as sets and fix no order; this is the order of the library, which the specification's "path order from its start" can be read as. The pieces are
  appended to the container in that order, so the last is frontmost.
* **Which pieces are open**: a path that nothing crosses comes back whole, and a closed one stays closed with `NoFill` 0; **every other piece is open, `NoFill` 1, even where its
  ends meet** (a ring cut at one place is one open piece starting and ending there, and the lobes of a figure of eight are two). The library gives a ring that nothing cut and one cut at
  one place the same way, so they are told apart by the place: a closed piece is whole when no other piece has an end at the place it starts.
* **What touches** (ours): the 1E-5 decides, so before the library is asked, each end of an open path that lies within 1E-5 of a segment of another path
  (or of its own, farther along) is moved onto the nearest point of it, and the library then finds a touch (the library's own reach is a millionth). An end within 1E-5 of the end of
  another open path is two ends that meet and cuts nothing; an end near a joint or a corner goes to it. **Only ends move**: two paths whose middles pass within 1E-5 without crossing, and a
  corner of a ring near a path, are the library's (exact touches are found; near ones may not be).
* **Stretches shorter than 1E-5 are not made** (the library merges junctions closer than its sweep's tolerance and a path of no extent is left out), so crossings that lie closer than that
  to one another along a path are one cut. **Stacked copies**: fifty copies of one square give one closed square, and fifty copies of a line one stretch; thousands of copies on one another are
  refused by the library's limit on pairs of overlapping segments.
* **One shape goes to the library**: every path as a subpath of one shape, with a marker path far from the drawing that is taken out of the answer. The library keeps the windings of every
  shape for each piece of its sweep that lies across it, so many shapes cost the square of their number in memory (20,000 separate segments as 20,000 shapes took 24 GB and were killed); one
  shape costs what the paths do. The marker makes it cut by the planar map of all the paths, whatever they fill, and not by the filled arrangement, in which an edge that two shapes share
  cancels and its ends are not places where three edges meet.
* **The counts** (SHAPEOPS-CAPS, ours): a command makes at most 10,000 shapes, and **more than 10,000 paths are refused before the library is asked** (each path comes back
  as a piece at least, so the result would pass the cap) with "Trim would make more than 10000 shapes"; the library's own limits hold for the rest (`craft_pathops::Limits`, the defaults) and
  say in words that the edges cross or meet in too many places. The snapping is charged in steps (20 million), the search for the ends at the place a closed piece starts in steps (50
  million), and a refusal names them.

**What these cost**, measured by `crates/engine/tests/it/shapeops_join_trim_hostile.rs` and `shapeops_trim_memory.rs` in the test profile (optimised; the times move with the load of the machine,
here shared with other builds; each test holds the whole call to 60 s, far above what it takes and far below a hang, and a refusal changes nothing). Join: 4,096 lines end to end in 0.3 s, a
star of 4,096 lines from one point in 0.5 s, 4,096 copies of one line in 0.4 s, one shape of 90,000 separate segments in 3 to 4 s, two crowds of 2,000 ends 1.5E-5 apart in 0.5 s. Trim: 70 and
70 lines across one another (4,900 crossings, 9,940 pieces) in 3 to 5 s, 100 and 100 refused by the cap in 0.8 s, two combs of 5,000 segments (25 million crossings) refused in 0.3 s, a star
polygon of 2,001 vertices (2 million crossings) refused in 0.03 s, 20 circles that cross in 145 pairs cut into their 580 pieces in 0.4 s, 9,999 separate segments (9,999 pieces) in 4 to 6 s,
more than 10,000 refused at once, a polyline of 20,000 segments shorter than the tolerance in 4 to 6 s, shapes 85 groups deep in milliseconds, and a drawing a trillion inches out or at 1E300 finished or
refused in words (the first near the origin, the second `Degenerate`). About three seconds of the 9,999 pieces is the recalculation of the shapes made, as for a Fragment of 10,000 regions. The
child tests of `shapeops_trim_memory` run under `ulimit -v 3000000`: 9,999 pieces peak at 0.59 GB resident (0.7 GB of address space), 20,000 segments are refused at 0.11 GB and 90,000 (the most the cap on rows lets a command read) at 0.43 GB, 4,096 shapes
of one segment each peak at 0.24 GB, and a Join of 4,096 lines at 0.12 GB.

**What is not here:** Trim's touch of a corner of a ring to a path and of two middles within
1E-5; a container for the many pieces of a Trim.

## Offset and Fit Curve

Offset and Fit Curve are the last two operations of that work on paths. They are built on the same reading of the operands, the
same frame and rows, the same glue, containers, undo and counts as the seven before them (**Shape operations**, **Join and Trim**), on the path library's `try_` forms
(`craft-pathops`, the pin of `Cargo.toml`), and on the work did on an older pin, which was ported and not merged: the library has since got a work meter, so the sweeps of the first
port that counted crossings by hand are gone and the limits below are the library's own, shared out. **The reference app was never taken apart, and the files these commands make are being tested by opening them in it, in LibreOffice Draw and in draw.io**: what the specification marks `unknown` is ours and unverified, and what this section chooses beyond it is marked **ours**.

| Command | Parameters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `shape.offset` | `ids` (one or more), `distance` (above 0, at least 0.0001 and at most 350,000,000, in the cells' own units), `page`? | `{page, ids, deleted, kept, changed, not_fitted}`: for each shown section of each shape named, up to two new shapes in front, one on each side of its path or paths (outside and inside a closed one, left and right of an open one), each holding one path or more, with the line format of **its own original**, `FillPattern` 0 and no text; the originals stay |
| `shape.fit_curve` | `ids` (one or more), `tolerance` (0 or more, in the cells' own units), `flags`? (0, or a sum of 1, 2 and 4), `page`? | the same answer: `changed` lists the shapes whose paths were made of fewer rows, which stay the same shapes with every cell; `not_fitted` lists the shapes the fit left as they were that hold something to fit |

The window runs them as `operations.offset {distance}` and `operations.fitCurve {tolerance, flags?}`, and the Operations menu's rows open their dialogs (below). Each is **one undo step**, a refusal
changes nothing and adds no step, and **a Fit Curve that finds nothing to make smaller is not refused and is no undo step either** (a tolerance of 0 asks for an exact match and changes nothing).
Both refuse what the others refuse (a group, a guide, a picture, a connector, a container or a list, a shape with no geometry, a shape on a locked layer, shapes of different containers), both
take shapes that share one container, and both take **one shape**. What differs from the others is what each locks: **neither deletes an operand**, so `LockDelete` refuses
neither; Fit Curve edits the vertices of every shape, so `LockVtxEdit` on one refuses it and changes none of the others; Offset edits none. **The arguments are in the cells' own units**
(a page of the default scale has inches, a scaled page the units its cells hold: no conversion by the drawing scale is made in the engine); the window's dialog turns the page's
measurement units into them (below).

**Offset** (`draw/shapeops/offset.rs`, SHAPEOPS-OFFSET). The paths are those of each operand's shown sections (read through the shape's own pose into its container's
coordinates), and **each section is worked on near its own centre**, so that the library's tolerance is the same wherever a shape is (two squares 1E12 apart are offset as two near the origin:
the squares at any gap). A section gives one shape for its outer or left sides and one for its inner or right sides; each holds a section for each path of its side, so a shape of two sections
gives four shapes ("each shown path" is a shown section). The copies go to the front in the order of the originals named, each original's outer or left side first, nothing selected
after (SHAPEOPS-ORDER), and **they are in no container or list**, the originals staying where they are. Each copy has the frame of R9 and the rows of R10 (a straight side a `LineTo`, a curved
one a `NURBSTo` cubic), a closed side `NoFill` 0 and an open one `NoFill` 1, no master, no name and no text, the cells of its original's formatting (SHAPEOPS-PROPS) with
`FillPattern` written as 0 on the copy itself, so that a style it is linked to cannot bring a fill back.

* **Closed paths** of a section are one fill by the odd-crossings rule (a ring inside another is a hole, whichever way it runs, and the middle of a pentagram drawn in one ring is one): the
  library normalizes them to boundaries the way each needs, then grows the fill by the distance (the outer side) and shrinks it (the inner side), each corner **mitred** up to the stroker's limit
  of 4 (a corner sharper than about 29 degrees, whose tip would stand more than 4 times the distance from it, is bevelled), the loops that a tight bend would form removed. A ring with a hole keeps
  the hole (it shrinks as the ring grows); **an inner side that vanishes** (a distance that reaches the narrowest half-width) **is not made**, and a region of less than 1E-8 square inch is dropped
  Offset 0.5 of a square of 2 gives the outer square and the inner one, Offset 1 only the outer, Offset 5 only the outer.
* **Open paths** are each their own: the library outlines the stroke of twice the distance with butt caps, which end on the lines through the path's ends square to it, and the **two sides are
  that ring cut at its two caps** (the straight edges that join the points `distance` to each side of the two ends: the library gives one ring, not two paths). The left side runs the way the path
  runs. **A path that crosses itself or doubles back, or bends so hard that its two sides meet, has no two sides** and is refused in words ("Offset cannot make the two sides of a path that ...",
  "has caps that do not meet its sides", "is shorter than the distance is wide"); the same path as a closed ring is one fill, and is offset (the loops are removed there).
* **Accuracy** (SHAPEOPS-PRECISION): the library's offset refits its result to 0.01 whatever it is given, which is 100 times what R46 allows, so the work is done at **1,000 times the size** and
  the sides are scaled back: curved edges are within 1E-4 of the exact offset (a circle of radius 1 offset by 0.25 is within 1E-4 of radius 1.25 and 0.75, as the test samples it) and no vertex of a
  result is nearer than 1E-5 to another.

**The distance** (ours where the specification is silent): a number above 0 and finite, **at least 0.0001** (ours: a result is accurate to 1E-4, so a nearer copy cannot
be told from its original) and **at most 350,000,000** (ours: the library's sweep takes coordinates up to about 7E13 and its tolerance is under 1E-5 for coordinates up to
7E8, so a section of half the size `s` and twice the distance `d` must come to no more than 700,000,000: a square of two inches takes 349,999,999, and one of 1.4E9 is refused with any distance).
0, a negative one and one that is not finite are refused ("Offset needs a distance above 0"), and so is a distance that is not a number, by the parameters (`distance` is required).

**What it costs, counted** (SHAPEOPS-CAPS; ours). The library refuses a call whose sweep would take more work than `Limits::sweep_work` (its work meter: a dry sweep that
counts pieces, crossings and the rest before the real one runs, and is not run below 192 pieces) and each call has that limit to itself, so a command of many calls would have as many limits. The
engine therefore gives each call of a command **its share of one `MAX_SWEEP_WORK` in proportion to the segments it is given**, out of the segments of all the calls of the command (a closed section is
three calls, the rings together, grown and shrunk; an open run is one; a command with one call takes it all), with a floor of 2^22 (about a thousand crossings of two lines) for a call that is nothing
beside the others. The share is also a share of the places where lines cross (3.5 microseconds each, `Limits::real_crossings`), which the library counts before it sweeps, and the pairs of
segments are held to what an offset is held to (524,288); a stroke's outline is held to **65,536 crossings** (ours: a path that crosses itself has no two sides and
is refused after its outline is made, which for an open star of 2,000 vertices took 17 s, and a polyline of thirty thousand sharp bends is under it). A command makes at most **10,000 shapes** and
a side of more than 8,192 paths is refused before any library work (a shape holds 8,192 sections). What it adds in the formatting the copies hold is charged before any is built (500,000 cells and
rows in all, as for Fragment and Trim). A refusal is in words ("the shapes have too many path elements, or their edges cross or meet in too many places, to be worked on in bounded time"), and
changes nothing.

**Fit Curve** (`draw/shapeops/fit.rs`, SHAPEOPS-FITCURVE). Each shape stays the same shape, with its id, name, master link, text, formatting, Shape Data, glue and place in the drawing
order. The paths are read **in the shape's own frame**, where the rows are written (a turned shape is fitted as it is and draws where it did), and the sections whose paths the fit makes of fewer
rows are replaced; a section of rows the fit cannot make smaller keeps its rows exactly (ours: *smaller is rows*, so one `Ellipse` row is not made into a `MoveTo` and
four `NURBSTo`, nor an `ArcTo` into the cubics that draw it), and a section that is hidden, or that the fit leaves, is kept with its flags (`NoFill`, `NoLine`, `NoSnap`, `NoQuickDrag`).
The shape's box is refitted to the new geometry as Subtract's is (a shape that keeps a section of its own, or holds `LockCalcWH`, keeps its frame, and the new rows are
written in it), the pin moving so that nothing moves on the page; an instance of a master gets the master's sections marked deleted and the new ones as its own, and reopens drawing the
same.

* **`flags`** are a sum of 1 (`visSplinePeriodic`: a closed path is fitted as a loop, so the seam where it closes is not forced to be a vertex), 2 (`visSplineDoCircles`: circular arcs for what is
  found to be circular) and 4 (`visSplineAbrupt`: a spline is broken where the direction changes by more than 30 degrees; without it a spline goes across a corner as far as the tolerance
  allows), and nothing else is a flag (8 and more, a negative number and a fraction are refused in words).
* **Circles**: before the library sees a run, the engine looks in it for stretches that a circular arc follows within the tolerance, and writes each as one **`ArcTo`** row (`X`, `Y` and the bow `A`).
  A stretch is at least five points (four lines, or any cubic), at most 256 segments and half a circle (the sign and the sweep past 180 degrees are what readers differ on), its
  bow is more than the tolerance (a stretch a straight line follows is the library's: a line), and every point of it, with the bulge a chord between two points leaves, is within 95 per cent of the
  tolerance of the arc; what the arcs leave is fitted by the library from arc to arc. A polygon of 36 sides on a circle of radius 1 fitted to 0.02 is two half circles (fewer than 36 segments,
  arcs and no spline row, every point within 0.02 of the old path and the old path within 0.02 of the new).
* **One call of the library for the whole command** (ours): every stretch of every run of every shape goes to `craft_pathops::simplify_with` as a subpath of one path, so
  that its counts (`FIT_WORK` over every run of the call, and what it may make against `MAX_ELEMENTS`) bound the command and not each of many calls (a call for each of 4,096 circles, each with a fresh
  work of its own, was 4,096 times the work). What comes back is the same subpaths in the same order, handed each to the stretch it fits; a stretch the library dropped, or whose answer is not
  that stretch's, stays as it was. The first port needed windows of 2,000 segments, retries in halves and a share of the work for each call, because the library of the time handed back a run of
  a few thousand segments as it was; **the library of today's pin fits a sine wave of 7,500, 10,000 and 100,000 points to under a tenth of the rows in one call**, and those workarounds are gone.
* **`not_fitted`** (ours): a shape the fit left as it was and that holds something to fit (a section of more than two rows) is named in the answer, so that a fit
  whose tolerance was too tight for it, or whose work ran out, is not a success that says nothing; with a tolerance of 0 it is empty by design.
* **Counted**: the points looked at for arcs are charged a step each before they are looked at, and a Fit Curve past **40 million** is refused in words ("Fit Curve would look at more than 40000000
  points for circles"); a straight run of 100,000 points costs a few hundred looks and not a hundred thousand. The shapes are changed together, **in the steps of one**: their rows and sizes are
  written, the page is recalculated once, the pins are written, and the page is recalculated once more (a recalculation and a walk of the page for each of 4,096 shapes was the product of the
  shapes and the page: 87 s). Shapes that cover more than **5E13** are refused in words, and a tolerance above that too.

**The window** (`crates/ui-egui/src/operations_dialog.rs`, `operations.rs`). The Developer tab's Operations menu keeps the nine items the reference app's ribbon lists, and **its Offset row is
enabled** (it was quiet before this task): a click opens the **Offset** dialog (`operations.offsetDialog {close?}`), a card with a Distance box (the page's measurement unit, **0.25 inch by default and
6 mm on a metric page**), OK and Cancel. **Fit Curve is in the Draw tab's Operations menu only** (`FitCurveDialog`, the command's id, which lists `FitCurve` and
`FitCurveDialog` as commands that are *not* on the ribbon; ours, a DiaCraft extra beyond the reference app like the menu's place on that tab): its row opens the **Fit
Curve** dialog (`operations.fitCurveDialog {close?}`), a Tolerance box in the page's unit (**a hundredth of an inch by default, a quarter of a millimetre on a metric page: ours**, R43 gives none),
three boxes for the flags (Periodic splines, Circular arcs, Break at abrupt changes, none ticked: ours) and OK and Cancel. **Nothing is sent until OK**, which reads the typed length in the page's unit
as the panes read one (a number with no unit takes the unit; `1 ft` and `2.54 cm` are lengths; a comma between values is refused), carries it through the page's drawing scale as Size & Position's
fields do, and runs `operations.offset {distance}` or `operations.fitCurve {tolerance, flags}`, each of which names the shapes selected and the page they were selected on (refused in words when
that page is not the one shown) and sends `shape.offset` or `shape.fit_curve`, **and clears the selection when it succeeds**. **A refusal stays in the dialog, in words, and the dialog stays open**;
Cancel, Escape and `close: true` change nothing, and Enter is OK while no box has the keyboard. Both rows are enabled exactly when `draw::check_shape_ops` says the operation can run on the
selection, which for these two is a scan of the types of the rows (a shape of 100,000 rows is asked about by looking at its first two) and not a reading of the shapes. The window state has
`offsetDialog` (the text in the box, or `null`) and `fitCurveDialog` (`{tolerance, flags}`, or `null`).

**What these cost**, measured by `crates/engine/tests/it/shapeops_offset_fit_hostile.rs` and `shapeops_offset_memory.rs` in the test profile (optimised; the times move with the load of the machine, here
shared with other builds at a load of 30 to 90 on 32 cores, so each is the time of a loaded machine, and each test holds the whole call to 60 s, far above what it takes and far below a hang): **Offset:** 4,096 lines (8,192 copies) in 3.4 to 5.8 s, 5,000 lines in 50 shapes (the 10,000 copies a command makes) in 4.7 to 5.6 s and one more refused in 0.4 s, a polygon of 1,000, 8,000, 50,000 and 100,000 vertices in 0.4, 3.0 to 3.8, 6 to 9 and 10 to 14 s, a closed star polygon of 301, 501, 1,001 and 2,001 vertices (each joined to the one nearly opposite: 45,000 to 2 million crossings) refused in 0.8 to 1.3 s, 3.6 to 7.7 s, 0.03 s and 0.03 to 0.09 s (the library took 15 s for the one of 1,001 before its crossings were counted against the share), the same stars open (a stroke's outline) refused in 0.02 and 0.05 s (they took 4 to 6 s and 17 s before the cap of 65,536 crossings), a path of 5,000 passes across 5,000 more (25 million crossings, in one section) refused in 1.1 to 2.1 s open and 0.13 s closed, a section of 8,193 open paths refused in 0.04 s and one of 8,192 made in 2 s, two squares 1E12 apart offset in 10 ms. **Fit Curve:** a sine wave of 7,000, 10,000 and 100,000 rows fitted to under a tenth of the rows in 0.25, 0.32 and 2.2 s, 100,000 points of noise that nothing fits left as it was in 3.4 to 4.2 s (the answer's `not_fitted` names it), a circle of 100,000 points made of arcs of up to 256 segments (about 400 of them) with the circles flag in 1.7 to 3.4 s, 4,096 circles of 36 lines each fitted in one call in 4.1 to 5.5 s, 1,000 rectangles that have nothing to fit in 0.07 to 0.19 s. **Memory** (`shapeops_offset_memory`: each scenario in a child under `ulimit -v 3000000`, peak resident memory measured alone): 10,000 copies 0.58 GB, 4,096 lines offset 0.44 GB, 4,096 rectangles 0.64 GB, a polygon of 50,000 vertices 0.35 GB, a star of 501 vertices (refused) 0.26 GB and of 2,001 0.03 GB, the serpentine of 25 million crossings (refused) 0.12 GB, a Fit Curve of a sine wave of 100,000 rows 0.48 GB, of a circle of 100,000 points 0.45 GB and of 4,096 circles 0.83 GB; the largest address space any reached was 0.94 GB. The tests that peak at 500 MB or more are in the `memory-heavy` group of `.config/nextest.toml`.

**What is not here:** Update Alignment Box; Offset of a path that crosses itself (open) or bends so hard that its sides meet, which has no two sides; round and bevelled corners (R38 says mitred); a
