Fit Curve that stays within the tolerance of a path that is not a polyline of at least five points by a circular arc of more than half a circle; the dialogs' captions and defaults are ours,
no source describes them.

## Connection points: double and halve (CPDOUBLE)

**A DiaCraft extra beyond the reference app** (owner, 2026-11-26): a key, a right-click row and a ribbon row that double the connection points of one edge of a shape, or of all its edges, and halve them again, with
every connector kept glued. The reference app has no such command (its Connection Point tool adds, moves and deletes one point at a time), so every rule below is the owner's or DiaCraft's own, marked
**ours**. The design, "Doubling and halving connection points", was approved by the owner with fifteen rulings (old points never move, a doubling adds the middle of every portion, a halving removes only the
newest doubling's points, corner points belong to no edge, a minimum distance between points). **What is built so far** is the query, the parts the edit uses (the references to a shape's `Connections` rows renumbered in every formula of the page and in its `Connect` rows, `draw/conn_refs.rs` on `diacraft_calc::row_refs`, and the marker of the points a doubling made, the row `User.DiaCraftAddedPoints`, read, written and renumbered, `draw/conn_marker.rs`) and the edit, `shape.connection_points`, the files (CPDOUBLE.ODG: VSDX, `.odg` and `.diacraft` read the points, the marker and the glue back as saved) and the window's key, menus
and ribbon rows (`crates/ui-egui/src/edit/conn_edges.rs`). The code is `crates/engine/src/draw/conn_points/` (`edges.rs` reads the outline, `layout.rs` is the arithmetic,
`ends.rs` and `local.rs` read and write the rows, `edit.rs` plans and writes a call), `draw/conn_marker.rs`, `draw/conn_refs.rs` and `crates/engine/src/cmd/conn_points.rs`. No sibling Craft app has an edge or a connection-point doubling to take (checked 2026-11-26), and the arc lengths and
nearest places are kurbo's (`ParamCurveArclen`, `ParamCurveNearest`), so nothing is carved.

| Command | Parameters | Answer and effect |
|---|---|---|
| `shape.connection_edges` (query) | `id`, or `ids` (at most 4,096; not both; an `ID` named twice is told once, in the order first named), `page`? (default: the first page holding all the shapes), `min_gap`? (paper inches, 0.01 to 2, default 3 mm = 0.11811) | `{page, min_gap, units_per_inch, scale_note, shapes: [{id, refused, edges: [{edge, kind, section, rows, steps, length, from, to, path, points, added, newest, gap, adds}], other, points, can_double, can_halve, truncated}]}`: for each shape its edges and where its connection points are, and for each edge what a doubling of it would make under the minimum distance. A query: it changes nothing and is no undo step. Lengths and places are **paper inches on the page** (`units_per_inch` is the factor to the page's drawing units, and `scale_note` says once that a page scale that is zero, negative or not a number was read as 1:1). `kind` is `straight`, `curved` or `closed`; `section` is the reference's spelling (`Geometry1` is the section whose `IX` is 0, or null for a section with no `IX`); `rows` the first and last `IX` of the rows that drew it (the move that began its run is not one of them); `steps` how many steps it draws; `from`, `to` and `path` (at most 32 places along it at equal lengths, for a window to pick and draw it by; a closed edge's are joined last to first) are `{x, y}` on the page; `points` the `IX` of its connection points in their order along it; `added` the points a doubling made, `[{point, generation}]` (1 for the first doubling of the edge, 2 for the next), `newest` the newest generation on the edge (`null` when all its points are originals, so a halving of it has nothing to take); `gap` the smallest gap a doubling would make, in paper inches; `adds` how many points a doubling would make, **0 when it has no room under `min_gap`**. `other` are the rows on no edge (kept as they are), `points` the shape's total, `can_double` whether some edge has room and its doubling fits the cap of 256 points a shape may hold, `can_halve` whether some edge has a point a doubling made, `truncated` whether the shape has more edges than are listed. A shape that cannot be read is told with `refused`, in words, and the rest are still told; an `ID` the page does not hold, a page that is not there, `id` and `ids` together or neither, and a `min_gap` outside its range are refused as parameters |
| `shape.connection_points` (Home, Tools) | `id`, or `ids` (at most 4,096; not both; an `ID` named twice is counted once), `action` (`double` or `halve`), `edge`? (one edge of the one shape named, by the number `shape.connection_edges` gives it), `at`? (`{x, y}`, a place on the page in paper inches: the edge of the shapes named nearest it within `reach` is the one changed, and when none is that near every edge is; not with `edge`), `reach`? (with `at`, inches, more than 0, default 5/72, five screen points at full size), `page`?, `min_gap`? (as the query) | `{page, action, changed, min_gap, scale_note, shapes: [{id, edges: [{edge, kind, before, after, generation}], skipped_edges: [{edge, gap, min_gap}], points_before, points_after, skipped}], reglued: [{connector, end, shape, from, to}], renumbered}`. **One undo step**, labelled "Double connection points" or "Halve connection points". With neither `edge` nor `at` it acts on every edge of every shape named. A **doubling** puts one new point in the middle, by arc length, of every portion of each target edge and moves nothing; a **halving** takes away the points of the newest doubling of each target edge and never an original. `generation` is the one the doubling gave or the halving took, `before` and `after` the edge's points, `skipped` the words of a shape left as it was, `skipped_edges` the edges a doubling had no room on, `reglued` each connector end that went to another point (`to` is `null` for an end glued to the whole shape) and `renumbered` the formulas of other cells that named a row that moved or went and were written again (a connector's end cells and the marker are not counted). **Refused in words, with nothing changed and no undo step:** an `action` other than `double` or `halve` (`set_count` in the words "set_count was dropped: double or halve"), `edge` with several shapes, with `at` or past the last edge, `at` or `reach` that are no numbers, a `min_gap` outside its range, `reach` with no `at`, nothing to halve ("nothing to halve: the edge has no points a doubling made"), no edge with room ("no edge has room: a doubling would put points 1.6 mm apart, under the minimum of 3 mm (Options)") and no shape that can be changed (each reason). The engine's `enabled` reads the session only, so the window's greying of a row is the window's own |

* Our rule (the design's §1). **The outline** is what the shape's `Geometry` sections draw, read as the renderer and the path functions read it: the effective rows (inherited from the master), drawn
  one row at a time (`diacraft_geom::build_row_draws`), in the shape's own frame; a section whose `NoShow` is 1 gives no edge, and `NoFill` and `NoLine` do not matter. **A straight step is an edge of its own** (a `LineTo`, an
  `ArcTo` of bow 0, each piece of a `PolylineTo`, two steps in line are two edges); **the curved steps of one row are one curved edge** (an arc, a Bézier, a spline run, a `NURBSTo`); **a closed curve is one closed edge** (an
  `Ellipse` row, or curved rows from one move that end where they began and turn nowhere: every join, the closing one too, within 1 degree, such as a circle of four arcs; a rounded rectangle is not one, its sides are straight,
  so it has eight edges). The two ends of an open run and each join between edges are **corners**. An edge shorter than a millionth of an inch is no edge. Edges are numbered from 0, the sections in `IX` order and then in the order
  drawn; a closed edge starts where its curve does (an `Ellipse` row's start is its `A`, `B`: DiaCraft's ellipse starts at its right end and runs counterclockwise). `Rounding` is not applied: a straight edge is its row as written.
* Our rule (§2). **A row of the `Connection` section is a point of an edge** when it lies within a thousandth of an inch of it in the shape's own frame (the tolerance within which a glued end lies on its point),
  and on an open edge farther than that from both its ends; it is an ordinary row (no formula in `D`); and it takes connectors (`Type` 0 or 2). A row near two edges is the nearer's, and the
  lower-numbered's of two as near. **Every other row is kept and on no edge** (`other`): a centre point, a point on a corner (a diamond's four vertex points are on no edge), an outward point, an extended row.
* The owner's, 2026-11-26; the design's §3.8. **A doubling puts a new point in the middle of every portion** of an edge (from one point to the next, and from each end of an open edge to the point nearest it, so an
  open edge's N points become 2N + 1 and a closed edge's N become 2N, and an empty closed edge gets two, its start and halfway round), so **the smallest gap it makes is half the shortest portion**. `gap` tells it, `adds` is the
  count when `gap` is at least `min_gap` (a gap of exactly the minimum is room) and 0 when it is not: **all or nothing for an edge**, so the spacing stays even. Lengths are measured along the edge **on the printed page**, by the
  page's drawing scale (`DrawingScale` over `PageScale`): a 2-metre wall drawn at 1:100 is 20 mm on paper and gets 0, 1 then 3 points under 3 mm, and no more. A 1-inch edge with one point in the middle goes 1, 3, 7 under 3 mm
  and then has no room (gaps of 6.35, 3.175 and 1.5875 mm), and 15 under 1.5 mm. Points added by hand, read from a file or a master's are never moved by the rule; it only decides where a doubling may add.
* Our rule (§1.3). **A shape that cannot take points is told, not refused as a call**: a group ("shape 12 is a group: select a shape inside it to change its connection points"), a line, connector or guide ("shape 9 is a
  line or a connector: connection points are put on two-dimensional shapes"), a shape on a locked layer (the words, as a query answers and does not refuse), a shape that draws no outline ("shape 4 draws no outline: it
  has no edge to put connection points on": a text box a file holds with no geometry, a shape whose sections are all hidden or empty). **DiaCraft's own Text tool box holds a rectangle**, so it has four edges and four
  points like the Rectangle.
* The owner's; §3.2. **A doubling puts a new point in the middle, by arc length, of each portion of an edge**: from one point to the next, and from each end of an open edge to the point nearest it, so an open
  edge's N points become 2N + 1 (0 become 1, 1 become 3, 3 become 7) and a closed edge's N become 2N; with no `edge` and no `at` every edge of every shape is doubled the same way. **Nothing moves:** the old points keep their rows,
  formulas and places, and a doubling writes no cell of any connector, no `Connect` row and no other shape's formula. The owner's: **an empty closed edge gets two points**, its start and halfway round, so 0, 2, 4, 8.
  The new points take one more than the newest generation of their edge (1 when all are originals), at most 8 under the cap of 256.
* The owner's; §3.3. **A halving takes the points of the newest generation of each target edge and never an original** (a point from the master, a file, the Connection Point tool or one put in by hand
  after a doubling is an original, and so is every point of a shape whose marker is lost): 7, 3, 1, and then there is nothing to take. A point a person moved along its edge stays added; one moved off every edge belongs to none and stays. A
  shape with a guarded point to take (`GUARD`) is skipped ("connection point 5 of shape 3 is guarded (GUARD) and was not changed"). There is no count set by number.
* Our rule (§3.5, §3.7). **A doubling appends** its rows after the section's last, edge by edge in the order of the edges and along each edge in its order, and renumbers none. **A halving removes** the rows of the points it takes
  and **the rows after them move up**, one for each removed row before them, so the section stays numbered from 0 with no gap. A section keyed by name keeps its names, a new row takes the first free `Row_<n>`, and `ToPart` and
  `Connections.X<n>` count the rows by their places.
* Our rule (§3.1). **The marker** is the `User` row `DiaCraftAddedPoints`, whose `Value` holds `0*(1*Connections.X5+1*Connections.X6+2*Connections.X9)`: each added point by reference, with its generation as the
  factor, and the value 0, so it moves with its row through a renumbering, a copy and a person moving the point, and means nothing to a program that does not know it (**read safely, **: a formula of any other form, one of
  more than 256 terms or 8 KiB, makes every point an original; **a row that two terms name is an original**, whatever generation each gives (a term of generation 0, 256 or 2^32 still names its row) and under any spelling of the row (`Connections.X1` and `Connections.Tally.X` are the one row when row 0 is named `Tally`, and in a section keyed by name a number names the row at that place), so is a row whose one term gives a generation outside 1 to 255, and a term that names a row that is not there is ignored; **a name is read as a reference reads it**: the row of that spelling first, and a row that spells it in another case only when none has it, so rows `Row_5` and `ROW_5` are two rows, a term of one never makes the other an added point, and the marker's reading, a halving and the renumbering of a page all find a term's row that way). A doubling adds a term for each point it makes, a halving drops
  the terms of the points it takes and never maps one to another row, and the row goes with its last term. Change Shape drops the marker of a two-dimensional shape (the new master's points are originals), a duplicate keeps it
  naming its own rows, and the ShapeSheet's row commands keep it right through `sheet_follow` (a row inserted before the added points moves their terms; a row deleted from a section the shape holds whole, or the section, makes the term `REF()`, which makes the marker void and every point an original, which is safe; in a section the shape shares with its master the rows keep their numbers, and the term of the deleted row reads `REF()` there too so the marker is void there as well).
* Our rule (§4.1). **A new point on a straight edge** is worked out from the cells of the edge's two ends, each axis on its own: both ends shares of the box (no formula and 0, `Width`, `Width*<number>`, or a constant share of a relative row) give
  a share written as the masters write one (`Width*0.75`, `Width` for 1, the constant 0 for 0, nine places); both ends plain lengths give the length as a constant in inches; anything else (a control, a scratch cell, a mix) gives
  a formula over the cells of the two ends, `Geometry1.X2+(Geometry1.X3-Geometry1.X2)*0.25` (inside `Width*(...)` for the cells of relative rows). A piece of a `PolylineTo` is read from its constructor (shares when `xType` and `yType` are 0). A cell
  that disagrees with the edge as it is drawn, or a row type this does not read, gives the plain length of the place. The new point follows a resize exactly where it is a share.
* The owner's; §4.2. **A new point on a curved or closed edge** is `X` = `PNTX(POINTALONGPATH(Geometry<s>.Path,<t>,0,<seg>))` and `Y` = `PNTY(...)` of the same, where `<seg>` is the drawn row the place falls in (counted from 1
  over the section's drawn rows, moves left out) and `<t>` the share of that row's length by arc length, to nine places. **The value written is calc's own**, worked out by `evaluate_text` before the write and held within 1E-6 inch of the engine's
  place or the shape is skipped in words, so the cached value and the next recalculation agree, and the point stays on its curve through a resize. The owner's: **a path cell is worked out again only when its section, its shape's
  size or its rounding changes**; a section is followed by formula only when it draws at most 1,024 steps (a curve past it: "the curve of shape 5 draws 12,000 steps, past the 1,024 a point can follow by formula"; a straight edge of such a section
  is doubled, it needs no walk), and the shape's **follow cost** (two walks of the section, each a step a cell the walk reads, three a step drawn and one for 512 multiplications of spline work, a fifth over and 64 for the call, for every path-form point it will hold) is held to 2,000,000 calc
  steps ("its points on curves would cost 2,5xx,xxx calc steps each time the shape is resized ..."). Measured at the counts are in `tests/it/conn_points_costs.rs`: DiaCraft's Ellipse of 256 points costs a resize
  48,475 calc steps (charged 65,016: the charge is a fifth over what a walk reads and draws and the spline work, and 64 for the call, so it is never less than what calc spends), a spline of 1,024 steps with 127 path-form points 1,867,451 (charged 1,930,146, the costliest shape the caps allow), and an edit of another shape works out none of their cells.
* Our rule (§4.3). **The way out and the type of a new point:** `DirX` and `DirY` are constants; when every point of the edge has the same way out the new ones take it (a side whose middle leaves upward gives (0, 1); all nought gives nought),
  otherwise (or with no point) the unit **outward normal** of the edge at the place, away from what the run encloses by the sign of its area, and nothing on an open run. `Type` is the edge's points' when they agree, else 0. A new row holds `X`, `Y`,
  `DirX`, `DirY` and `Type` and no other cell. `Rounding` is not applied: a straight edge is its row as written, so a point near a rounded corner stands off the drawn round (by at most 0.42 of the radius).
* The owner's; §5. **A shape that inherits its points takes the section as its own** when a call changes it: every row it will hold is written as a row of its own with every cell (the formula as it resolves, its value and unit), and
  every inherited row it will not hold is a deleted row (`Del`) of its own, so nothing of the master's shows through; a doubling needs no `Del` row, a halving that takes inherited rows does. A master's later edit no longer reaches the shape. The master is not changed.
  (A marker the master holds is read through to the instance; after a halving to no point that names a row, the stale term names no row and so no point.)
* Our rule (§6). **A halving brings every reference to a row along** (`draw/conn_refs.rs`, `diacraft_calc::row_refs`): the `Connect` rows of the page, the part and the cell together, and every
  formula of every shape of the page (members too) and of the page's sheet that names a row of the shape by `Connections.X<n>` or `Connections.<name>.X`, with no qualifier on the shape's own sheet or `Sheet.<id>!` for it, rewritten **character
  for character** (a string, a quoted name, another shape, another page's qualifier, another section and a trigger are left); one walk of the page for each shape that renumbers a row, none for a doubling. **A connector end on a row that moved up** keeps its
  place and only its number changes. **A connector end on a removed point goes to its successor:** the remaining point nearest it on the same edge (an original or an added one), else the nearest point of the shape that takes connectors; of two as near,
  the one nearer the connector's other end on the page, then the lower row, each end choosing for itself (two connectors on one removed middle point part to its two neighbours); **with no point to take it the end is glued to the whole shape**
  (`ToPart` 3, `ToCell` `PinX`, its cells the `_WALKGLUE` formulas with the places they were as their results, and its trigger naming the shape, which the engine then places on the shape's outline as it places any whole-shape end) and nothing is unglued. **Another formula that names a removed row** is renumbered to its successor, or, when
  the shape would keep no point, **the halving is refused**: "halving would remove the last connection point of shape 5, which the formula of Sheet.9!User.Anchor names". A connector on a locked layer is renumbered too: the lock stops a person editing it, and this keeps its glue.
* Our rule (§9). Every list is bounded before it is made and every loop is charged by the units it walks. **Per shape:** 256 connection rows (counted over the shape, its master and the styles before any is merged:
  "shape 5 has more than 256 connection points, counted over the shape and its master: it is not read", nothing merged), 64 `Geometry` sections, 200,000 rows in a section (the geometry crate's own cap), and 4,096 edges (past it
  the shape is `truncated`, and the edges listed are the first). **Per call, over all its shapes:** 1,000,000 rows of sections merged, 1,000,000 steps drawn, 50,000,000 multiplications of spline work and 1,000,000 arc calls (a
  length worked out for a curved piece, a place found by length, a piece tried against a connection point; a point is tried only against the edges whose box it is in). **A call that spends one stops there: the shape that met the
  limit and every shape after it are `refused` in words** ("the call has drawn the most steps of outline it may (1000000): ask for fewer shapes"), so a list of hostile shapes costs no more than one. The counts are
  `diacraft_engine::draw::conn_points::OutlineWork`, which the tests read; DiaCraft's stock Ellipse draws 15 steps. **The edit adds, per call:** 65,536 rows written (each changed shape's whole own section counts, so 256 shapes of 256 points; past it the call
  is refused in words and nothing is written), 4,096 `Connect` rows renumbered (**one counter with the walk's** `ScanWork`, so the two caps cannot disagree: "more than 4096 connector ends are glued to the points of shape 1"), 4,000,000 formulas and 64 MiB of formula
  text looked at by the halving's walk of the page, and 2,000,000 calc steps for the dry runs of the path formulas; a shape with more than 4,096 edges is skipped by a call on every edge (name an edge), a shape past 256 points after the doubling
  is skipped ("shape 5 would have 263 connection points, past the 256 a connector looks at: it was left as it was"), and **all is read and every budget charged before anything is written**, so a refusal leaves the document as it was. A straight edge's
  formula reads its section's rows once more than the outline did (counted in `OutlineWork::rows`).
* With design calls; §10; **the window**, `crates/ui-egui/src/edit/conn_edges.rs`. **Ctrl+Alt+K doubles and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K halves** the connection points
  (Command+Option+K and Shift+Command+Option+K on a Mac), as the keys of the window command `window.connectionPointsDo` (`action` `double` or `halve`, `target` `pointer`, `all` or `menu`; [Control protocol](control-protocol.md)). **The target:** the key's is the pointer: the edge of a shape
  selected that is nearest the pointer within five screen points (`HIT_REACH`, in inches at the zoom; a tie goes to the earlier edge), else, with the pointer inside a shape, on a shape that is not selected, on the ribbon or off the drawing, **every edge of every shape selected**; the right-click
  rows' is the edge at the click that opened the menu (else every edge), and the ribbon's every edge. **The window decides from what the engine says**, and draws no geometry of its own: it reads the answer of `shape.connection_edges` (`draw::conn_points::query_edges`) for the shapes selected, **keeps it for the drawing's generation, its revision, the page, the
  shapes selected and the minimum distance, and asks again only when one of them changes, never for a frame** (the count is `diacraft_ui_egui::work::Work::connection_edge_queries`; a file opened starts its revision again, so the generation is part of the key), reads at most 256 shapes and 16,384 edges, and picks the edge from the `path` of each (at most 32 places along it). **A program's `at` and
  `reach` pick the same edge** (a test holds it for the window's place and reach, on a rectangle and an ellipse). **Enabled:** Double when the target edge has room under the minimum distance (`adds` above 0) and its shape takes the points (the cap of 256), and for every edge when some shape selected
  can double; Halve when the target edge has a point a doubling made (`newest`), and for every edge when some shape selected has one. A row that cannot run is greyed with the engine's reason as its tooltip ("nothing to halve: the edge has no points a doubling made", "no edge has room: a doubling would put points 1.27 mm apart, under the minimum of 3 mm (Options)"), and **a key that cannot run
  does nothing and says nothing**. **Past the window's caps** (more than 256 shapes selected, more than 16,384 edges, a shape with more edges than the answer lists, a question the engine refused) **both rows stay on**, the call carries the pointer's place as `at` and `reach` for the engine to pick the edge, and the engine's words say what it did. No selection, a connector alone or a group leaves
  both greyed. **The keys stand aside while a shape's text is edited or a menu is open, and for a press that typed a character**, and **take their press even then**: egui lets an extra Alt or Shift match a shortcut, so a press left over went to Ctrl+Shift+K (Small Caps) or Ctrl+K (Link): **before this, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K toggled Small Caps** on a shape selected. AltGr is Ctrl+Alt on Windows, and AltGr+K types ł on the Czech, Hungarian
  and Slovak layouts (read on kbdlayout.info, 2026-11-26): a press that typed it is left to the text; the layouts are named in the key tests (`shortcuts.rs`), with the 26 Mac layouts of that reach the letter K with Command. **The status bar says what changed**: "Connection points doubled on 1 edge of shape 3 (1 to 3)", "... on 4 edges of shape 3 (4 to 12 points in all)", "... on 8 edges of 2 shapes (8 to 24 points in all)", then
  the words of a shape the engine left as it was and how many edges had no room; **the numbers are joined by a word and not an arrow** (the design's example has the arrow): when this was built the window's bundled face had no glyph for U+2192, and a glyph no face has panicked the test harness. The window's faces draw the arrow (Hack stands behind Ubuntu Light), and a glyph no face has is a box in the program, never a panic, so the notice could take the arrow. **The rows:** the shape's right-click menu has a **Connection Points** submenu after Container and before Format Shape (`CanvasConnectionPoints`, with
  `CanvasConnectionPointsDouble` and `CanvasConnectionPointsHalve`; a connector's menu has none), and **Home, Tools, Connection Point** (`ConnectionPointTool`) is a menu of **Double Connection Points** and **Halve Connection Points** (`ConnectionPointsDouble`, `ConnectionPointsHalve`); the captions and ids are ours. View, Connection Points is not turned on by a key (design call).
* **The setting** (§3.8.2). **The minimum distance between doubled points** is a box on the Advanced page of File, Options, under Editing options: a length with a unit (a plain number is millimetres, the unit the box shows), 3 mm at first, from 0.254 mm to 50.8 mm (0.01 in to 2 in), and a distance outside that, or no length, keeps the dialog open with
  the words under the box ("Type a distance from 0.01 in to 2 in (0.254 mm to 50.8 mm)."); OK sends one `window.connectionMinGap {inches}`. **A window setting for now**: it is read by `DiacraftApp::connection_min_gap` and written by `set_connection_min_gap`, not saved and not in a drawing (the settings store has landed, and the distance is not one of its fields yet: making it a field of `InterfacePrefs` is a follow-up); **the default does not follow a
  choice of units** (0.125 in for US customary), because the dialog has none yet. The window sends it as `min_gap` on every call and in every read, and a change reads the answer again with no new selection (it is part of the cache's key). A program that sends no `min_gap` gets 3 mm whatever the window holds.

* **Files (CPDOUBLE.ODG; the design's §11).** **VSDX** writes a shape's `Connection` section as rows of its own (a master's rows it drops as `Del` rows) and the marker as a `User` row, and a save in place differs from the file only in the changed shape's sections and the renumbered cells and `Connect` rows. **`.diacraft`** holds the model and reads back equal. **`.odg`:** a shape the save writes from its rows (a new shape, or a shape of a drawing saved from the model whose outline the writer makes from its rows) lists every connection point as a glue point of its geometry from row 0 (`draw:glue-points`, with `draw:glue-point-leaving-directions` when every row has a way out), a row whose formula is no share of the frame (a point on a curve, a length) from its value, the share of the frame it stands at, and its formula in DiaCraft's data; the style says the rows are its own (`diacraft:glue="own"`) and a connector glued to row *r* names glue point *r* + 4. **A shape of the file** gets a `draw:glue-point` element for each row past the four standard points and the points its geometry lists (the row's number as its `draw:id`, `svg:x` and `svg:y` as centimetres from the frame's centre, an escape direction), keeps the elements whose row is as it was and takes out those a halving took or an edit changed; a shape whose rows are its own has its geometry's list written again; and a shape of another kind than a custom shape, rectangle, ellipse or circle gets none. **The same elements are written whether the file is saved in place or the drawing is written from the model** (a Save As of a drawing that holds no `.odg` to splice into, a `.diacraft` file, a `.fodg` or a drawing saved across the formats, whose model writer keeps the geometry and the glue point elements its file held and gave a row the session added no glue point): the elements of rows that are as they were read stay, the others go, and each new row has one. **A turned or flipped shape has its elements in the page's axes**, where LibreOffice places them, from the box the shape takes up on the page (a whole ellipse's own extent, a frame's box turned): the element is written where the reader's own mapping takes it back to the row, and its way out is the page's own direction (`left`, `right`, `up` or `down` when the turn puts it along an axis, `auto` otherwise). A shape whose geometry lists its points as plain numbers in its view box, and whose first rows are those points in place, is a shape whose rows are its own whatever rows the session added to it (a count of rows alone took it for the other kind after a doubling). **A flip, a turn and a text the session gives a shape of an `.odg` file** are in the file a Save As from the model writes: the geometry its file held is written with the mirrors and the turn of the text the shape has now, a glue point element of the shape is written again for the turn and flips it has (it is in the page's axes), and a flip or a text given to a shape whose geometry is a 3-D extrusion or a fontwork is refused in words, since the reader keeps neither for one; a save into the file refuses a flip in words and writes the elements again for a turn when the rows are a list they can say (it refused a turn when a connector was glued to such a point, and still does when they are not). The marker `User.DiaCraftAddedPoints` rides in DiaCraft's data; a program that drops it leaves every point an original, which is safe, and the points are then the file's own glue points. A whole-shape end of an `.odg` connector on a shape whose rows are its own glue points goes on the middle of a side of its frame, where LibreOffice puts it. Tests: `crates/engine/tests/it/conn_points_files.rs`, `crates/odg/tests/it/write_glue.rs`, `crates/odg/src/write/geometry.rs` and `crates/odg/src/read/connectors.rs` (the placement and its inverse), the fuzz target `odg_write` (op 52, and `model_points` for the model writer); the check against LibreOffice 26.8.2.2 is the ignored tests `write_the_files_for_libreoffice` and `write_the_files_for_libreoffice_fix` and a script.

## What each one does to the document

* **Masters.** `shape.drop` copies the master into the document's masters if the document does not hold it (by the master match rule above: its `UniqueID`, and its `BaseID` where that says it is the same master; for a master of an opened stencil see **Stencil files**) (every master of the built-in stencils has a
  fixed GUID, **ours**: `{D1AC0001-…}` for Basic Shapes, `{D1AC0002-…}` for Basic Flowchart, `{D1AC0004-…}` to `{D1AC0006-…}` for Decorative Shapes, Arrow Shapes and Gane-Sarson, `{D1AC0007-…}` for the Cross-Functional Flowchart Shapes and `{D1AC0008-…}` for the Organization Chart Shapes, numbered from 1 in stencil order: each library has a series of its own: these are the masters' `BaseID`s, and the `UniqueID` is a GUID of its own; `{D1AC0003-…}` is the text 0.2.3 gave a master copied into a drawing when its own `UniqueID` was taken there), then adds an instance that holds only `PinX` and `PinY` (a master dropped beyond the range of eight of the page's drawing scale also gets `Width`, `Height` and `DropOnPageScale` on it: **Dropping a master on a page of another drawing scale**). The rest is inherited; a resize makes the
  instance hold `Width` and `Height` and `Inh` cells with the results that now differ from the master's. Masters stay in the
  document whether or not an instance is left.
* **Basic Shapes** (`crates/engine/src/stencil.rs`): rectangle, square, ellipse, circle, triangle, right triangle, diamond, pentagon,
  hexagon, octagon, parallelogram, trapezoid. Plain mathematics; names, sizes and connection points are **ours**. Each has its geometry as
  formulas of `Width` and `Height`, at least four connection points, and the seven text block cells with their creation formulas.
* **Basic Flowchart** (`crates/engine/src/stencil/flowchart.rs`): eighteen symbols, in the order of the Shapes window. Names are the generic
  ones of the public notation (thirteen from the symbol tables of [Flowchart (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowchart), read
  2026-11-01, which names ISO 5807; the standard itself was not read; delay, display, internal storage, summing junction and or are the
  other symbols general descriptions of ISO 5807 flowcharts list, and the article does not name them). The drawings are plain geometry,
  **ours**; nothing is traced from another application's stencil. The article's annotation symbol is not a master: it has one place to join,
  and a master here has at least four connection points.

  | Id | Name | Size (in) | Drawn as |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `process` | Process | 1.5 × 0.8 | rectangle |
  | `decision` | Decision | 1.5 × 1.0 | diamond; the text block is the inside of it: the largest box a diamond holds, half its width by half its height (0.75 × 0.5 inch at the default size), so that the text stays in the figure. A word wider than the block's usable width breaks inside itself ("a renderer that lets a long word overflow is wrong"), as `Approved?` does in it at 12 point: a longer figure, a smaller size or a shorter word keeps it whole |
  | `terminator` | Terminator | 1.5 × 0.6 | stadium: half circles of radius half the height at the two ends |
  | `data` | Data | 1.5 × 0.8 | parallelogram leaning right, the slant a quarter of the height |
  | `document` | Document | 1.5 × 0.8 | rectangle with a wavy bottom (two circular arcs) |
  | `multiple_documents` | Multiple Documents | 1.5 × 1.0 | three stepped sheets: a document in front, and the two strips that show above and beside it |
  | `predefined_process` | Predefined Process | 1.5 × 0.8 | rectangle with a vertical line a fifth of the height in from each end |
  | `manual_input` | Manual Input | 1.5 × 0.8 | rectangle whose top slopes up to the right from four fifths of the height |
  | `manual_operation` | Manual Operation | 1.5 × 0.8 | trapezoid, wide at the top, slanting in by a quarter of the height |
  | `preparation` | Preparation | 1.5 × 0.8 | elongated hexagon, points at the two ends |
  | `on_page_reference` | On-Page Reference | 0.5 × 0.5 | circle |
  | `off_page_reference` | Off-Page Reference | 0.6 × 0.8 | box ending in a point at the bottom |
  | `database` | Database | 1.0 × 1.2 | cylinder: half-ellipse rims, the front of the top rim a stroke across the fill |
  | `internal_storage` | Internal Storage | 1.0 × 1.0 | rectangle with a vertical and a horizontal line, 0.15 in from the left and the top |
  | `delay` | Delay | 1.2 × 0.8 | rectangle with a half circle for its right end |
  | `display` | Display | 1.5 × 0.8 | a point at the left, a half circle at the right |
  | `summing_junction` | Summing Junction | 0.5 × 0.5 | circle crossed by its two diagonals |
  | `or` | Or | 0.5 × 0.5 | circle crossed by its horizontal and vertical diameters |

  Arcs are `EllipticalArcTo` rows through three points (a circle, or a half-ellipse whose ratio `D` is a formula of the box), so no sign
  convention for a bow is relied on. A slant or a round end is a share of the height, so widening a symbol keeps its angles and its round
  ends (`Width-Height*0.25`); narrowing a terminator, delay or display below its height turns its round ends past each other. A symbol with
  strokes inside its fill (the lines of a predefined process, the front rim of a database, the cross of a summing junction) holds them as
  `Geometry` sections of their own with `NoFill` 1, so that they do not punch the fill (a project rule).
  Connection points are the middle of each side, moved onto the outline where a side is slanted or curved; each lies on the drawn stroke.
* **Glue**: an end glued to connection point `IX` `n - 1` of shape `S` holds `PAR(PNT(Sheet.S!Connections.Xn,
  Sheet.S!Connections.Yn))` in both its cells, and a `Connect` row (`FromPart` 9 for the begin and 12 for the end, `ToPart` 100 plus `IX`). A
  recalculation moves the end with the shape. An end glued to the whole of a shape (`ToPart` 3) in a file, and in a connector made here, holds `_WALKGLUE(...)`, which `calc`
  cannot work out (behaviour `unknown`); the engine puts such an end where says, as the cached value of its
  cells, and the formula stays as the file had it (see Choices).
* **A connector** is a shape with no master, one-dimensional: `Width`, `Angle`, `PinX`, `PinY` and
  `LocPinX` hold the creation formulas, `Height` is 0, and the begin is at (0, `LocPinY`) of its own frame. `EndArrow` is 4. `ObjType` 2 and `GlueType` 2 make it a connector the
  reference application routes again (below). A `User` row
  `DiaCraftRoute` marks a connector as one DiaCraft made; a connector read from a VSDX file has none, and is routed again only (the `.odg` reader gives every
  connector it reads the marker, as one DiaCraft may route again).
  Its label (`TxtPinX`, `TxtPinY`, `TxtAngle`, `TextBkgnd`) follows.
* **The route** is the right-angle rule, named once in `crates/engine/src/draw/route.rs`: Z for ends that face each other,
  L for a corner ahead of both, C for ends that leave the same way, a detour by a standoff of 0.25 otherwise, (rule 6) a bridge in
  place of any of those that would double back on itself, and (rule 7) a way round the boxes of the shapes the ends are glued to, in place of any of those that goes through one; a connector's style
  may make the route one straight leg, or a curve drawn through this one). It is written as `Geometry` rows of constants (`MoveTo`, then `LineTo`) in the
  connector's own frame, **by the command**, after the page is recalculated, and not by a recalculation hook (`crates/engine/src/draw/mod.rs`
  says why). A route has no repeated vertex and no zero-length leg, and no leg that goes out along a line and comes straight back along it
  (which a viewer draws as one line with a second arrowhead on it); the one exception is a connector whose two ends are the same point, which
  is two equal points, since no leg is left to point an arrowhead along. The first row is the begin, at (0, `LocPinY`) of the connector's own
  frame, and the last is the end, at (`Width`, `LocPinY`); `EndArrow` is 4 and there is no `BeginArrow`.
* **Recalculation**. Each command that changes a cell ends by working out **what it changed and what reads it**
  (`calc::changes_between` finds the cells that differ from the document the command began with, and `calc::commit_changed` works out those and
  every cell that reads one of them, again and again), and writes the results under the `Evaluation` origin, so the saved `V` values are right
  for the renderer and the writer. A cell is read by another when its formula names it (`Width`, `Sheet.4!PinX`, `User.Row`), when it calls a
  function that carries a point between frames (`PAR`, `LOC` and the others) and the cell is a pose cell (`PinX`, `PinY`, `LocPinX`,
  `LocPinY`, `Angle`, `FlipX`, `FlipY`) of a shape whose frame it carries between (this is how
  `PAR(PNT(Sheet.4!Connections.X1, ...))` follows shape 4), when a `Connect` row glues its end to a shape, and when it inherits a formula from
  a master that reads it. **A cell that nothing the command changed is read by keeps the value the file saved, byte for byte, whatever this
  evaluator would give for it**, and so does a cell that is worked out and comes out as it was. The route is rewritten from the ends that came
  out. See `crates/calc/src/affected.rs` for what is and is not followed, and `crates/calc/src/index.rs` for how what reads what through other sheets is kept from one command to the next. **A cell passes the change on only if it changed**: the cells that
  read a cell the command wrote are worked out, and the cells that read one of those only if working it out planned a write. A reader that comes out
  as it was, or that `calc` cannot work out (a connector end glued by `_WALKGLUE`), ends the chain: the width and the pin that read such an end keep the
  values the file saved, and are not moved a rounding away from them by a move that did not change the end. **An edit outside the page** (a
  style, the theme, a master's formulas), which `calc` cannot follow cell by cell, works out every formula cell of the page, **measured from the
  document the command began with** (`Changes::since`): the cells of the masters the page's instances use that the edit changed
  are worked out, so an instance that leaves a cell to its master reads the new value through it, and an instance is given a cell it inherits
  and does not hold only where the edit changed what the cell works out to on it and the result is not its master's:
  an instance at its master's size keeps no copy of a master's cell, and one of another size keeps leaving to its master the rows its file
  left there, except a cell the edit changed to another value than its master's.
* The routes an edit writes are read in the same edit; ours. A command routes the connectors it moved again and writes their rows, and the label cells with them, after the recalculation of the edit,
  so a cell that reads a route (a shape tied to a connector by `PNTX(PAR(POINTALONGPATH(Sheet.N!Geometry1.Path, ...)))`, a text that shows its length) held the route the connector had until the edit after, and a full evaluation changed it. `draw/settle.rs` now
  works out, after it writes the routes, the cells that read any cell of each connector's first `Geometry` section (the whole path, as `POINTALONGPATH` does, or one cell of it: `Sheet.N!Geometry1.X2`, the `Y` of the last row, a cell of the connector that reads its own `Geometry1.X3`) or one of the label cells written with them, and what reads those, within the steps left of the edit's routing, and nowhere else: the commit is
  `calc::Changes::only_if_read`, which takes the cells written as holding the values written to them (they are not worked out) and counts as a commit only when something reads them, so an edit on a page that nothing reads a route on makes the commits it made. A route is written whole, so the commit names the section (`calc::Changes::sections`) and not its cells: a reader of one cell is listed under the section as well as under the cell (a reference to a `Geometry` cell only), which finds it whatever row it names, a row the route gained as much as one it lost, and a reader of a row the new route does not have holds what a full evaluation gives (the error of a row that is not there). A tied
  shape follows its connector in the edit that moved it, and one undo takes both back. **The same holds for the other places a route is written after the recalculation:** a leg moved by hand (`connector.edit_path`, with the label cells and `ConFixedCode` it writes) and the
  hops the jump pass gives a connector or takes from it (`draw/jumps.rs`: the connectors a move crosses, `connector.line_jumps`, a delete), each worked out as one commit in the budget a commit has when no edit shares one. Past the steps it has, an edit that is
  not a refit of a group is no refusal (what reads a route holds what it held, as it did before it was worked out here), and a refit of a group, which refuses past its steps, refuses here too.

## Choices that no specification settles (ours)

* A text box is a shape with no master that paints nothing until it is given a fill or a line, and the text block
  of a shape is moved, sized and turned by writing its seven cells as values, the pin carried by the block's turn and flips and the text turned about the pin; see **Text boxes and the text block** above.
* The window: the text box holds the characters only, **the ones the shape shows** (its master's when it holds no text of its own). The fields are shown under them, in order, and not at the places they
  stand in the text: the box is an egui text edit, whose cursor counts the characters it holds, and a field in the middle of them would have to be
  characters it could be typed into. What the box sends has the characters that a file cannot hold (the controls other than a line break and a tab,
  U+FFFE and U+FFFF) taken out first, so a paste that carries them does not make the engine refuse the label and lose it. The box takes at most
  `MAX_TEXT_CHARS` characters. A box that is open on another shape when a new one opens is sent first.
* The window: **the text box lays a right-to-left paragraph out right to left, as the drawing
  does, while it is edited.** The box is egui's text edit and the egui under it is the suite's fork, whose layout shapes right-to-left runs, puts the rows of a line in visual
  order and moves the caret by the screen: **Left and Right move the caret one letter to the left and the right on the screen** whatever the order of the characters in the text,
  **Home and End go to the first and the last character of the row, whichever side of it each is on** (egui's own go to the row's edges on the screen, which differ where a row holds both directions, so the box takes the two keys itself; Ctrl with either is the whole text's), the pointer's hit, a drag and
  Shift with the arrows select by the screen in text of both directions, and an input method's composition is taken as it is in any box. What the box adds is the shape's own
  paragraph format, read by the engine for **the text as it will be once what was typed is sent** (`formatting::editor_paragraphs`: one paragraph for each line feed and one
  more, each with the cells of the run that holds its last character, and typed characters joining the run the commit gives them; at most 4,096
  paragraphs are read): the base direction is the cell `Flags`, **never guessed from the first letter**, so the first word of a paragraph turned right to left is on the right
  whatever it is; alignment 0 puts the rows against the right of the box, 2 against the left and 1 between (a justified paragraph fills the room); the start indent
  (`IndLeft`) is on the right and the stop indent (`IndRight`) on the left, the room of the text being that far in from the box's sides (at least a third of the box stays for
  the text). **Text with no right-to-left paragraph and no right-to-left letter is laid out as the box has always laid it out** (centred, one face and one size), whatever
  its alignment cell says, so that left-to-right editing is not changed. **What the box does not show** (ours: egui has no first-line indent that survives alignment, and one
  job lays the whole text out): the first line's indent, bullets and tab stops; **one direction and one alignment for the whole text** where the paragraphs of a shape agree
  on them the box is exact, and where they differ the direction of each paragraph is its first strong letter's (egui's rule) and the alignment is the first paragraph's. The
  box's line breaks are those of egui's own faces and sizes, which are not the drawing's, so a line can break elsewhere than in the drawing. **Arabic and Hebrew need a face
  with their letters**: Hack and Ubuntu Light have none, so `font_definitions_with` adds, behind the proportional faces, one face for each script from the machine's database
  (the face the drawing falls back on if egui may take it, else the first of a short list of open families that may be taken, by the checks the interface faces pass) and none
  when the machine has none, where the box shows a box for each letter (egui's missing-glyph box, not a panic) as it did before.
* The window; with the double click ours: **typing, F2, the Text tool's click and a double click on a group send the text where the group's `IsTextEditTarget` says.** The cell is found by inheritance and reads TRUE when nothing gives one: the group takes the text itself, as it always did. FALSE sends it to the member on top of the stack, the last in document order that is drawn (a member deleted from its master, or a guide, is passed over), and **the walk goes on through a member that is a group with its own cell FALSE** (a member group with TRUE takes the text itself), at most 8 levels down. The box opens over that member with all its characters selected, and the group stays selected, so typing on a selected class edits its name. The cell is read when the edit begins (a change moves no text that is already there). A group with no member that is drawn takes the text itself. **A group whose `SelectMode` is 0 has no members in the pointer's scene**, and typing on it still reaches its last member: the box is drawn over that member, from the place the engine finds for it (`shape_corners`), and the member's text is what changes. **A member that is selected on its own is typed into whatever its group says**, and **a double click on a member that is selected on its own, with the pointer on it, edits that member** (a second click on a selected group selects the member under the pointer). **The second click of a double click does not go in to the member under it**, so a double click on a group (selected by the first click of the pair, or before it) edits the group's text target and not the member that the second click would have picked: a click, a pause and a double click edit a member that is not the last. No specification says what a double click on a group does, so this is ours, after the typing rule. The edit is one `shape.set_text` of the member and one undo step, and the window state's `editingText` is true while the box is open. **A double click on a shape whose `EventDblClick` calls `OPENGROUPWIN()` (or its old spelling `_OPENGROUPWIN()`) opens no text box** (OPENGROUPWIN; the project rule is that no group window exists): the cell is found by inheritance and looked at, never worked out, and the call stands in for the default; on a **group** nothing opens, nothing is changed, and the status bar says *"Double clicking this group opens a group window, and DiaCraft has no group windows, so nothing was opened."*, and on a shape that is **no group** nothing opens and nothing is said. A cell that calls anything else (`OPENTEXTWIN()`, `DEFAULTEVENT()`), one that does not parse and a shape with none are the default. The reading is `diacraft_engine::draw::double_click::on_double_click`. Tests: `crates/ui-egui/tests/it/group_text.rs`, `crates/engine/tests/it/double_click.rs`.
* The window: a text box that is open is sent before the window runs any command that changes the document or leaves the drawing
  area: every engine command that is not a query, and the window's `page.select`, `edit.select`, `edit.selectAll`, `window.backstage` and `window.tab`; and
  before Save, Save As, New, Open, Export and the close check ask. So Undo with a box open takes back the label (one undo step) and not the step before
  it, a page change sends the label to the page it was typed on, and a close finds the drawing changed. A query (`document.inspect`) and a view command (zoom,
  panels, theme, tool) leave the box open. Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Shift+S work from the box; the other shortcuts are the box's (Ctrl+Z in it
  undoes typing). The title carries the star while a label has been typed and not sent.
* The window: the Save and Export dialogs check the name they were given, and the window adds `.vsdx` or `.png` to a name with no
  type after that. When the file with the type added is there (a file, a folder or a link), the window asks before it writes: Replace or Cancel. A name
  that already had its type was checked by the dialog and is not asked about again.
* The window: `ChangedOnDisk` from `file.save` or from `file.save_as` onto the drawing's own file is a question, not a failure:
  Overwrite (the same command again with `force`), Save As (the Save dialog, then `file.save_as`), or Cancel. A save that was to be followed by New, Open or
  the close is followed only when the file is written, and Cancel ends it.
* The window: the three questions, and the progress card of a file being read, are modals over a shade (`Tokens::scrim`): nothing under
  them takes the pointer, and the shortcuts and drawing keys are held (with the File view open only the shortcuts of New, Open, Save and Save As run, so
  Delete and Ctrl+Z reach no drawing the person is not looking at). Escape is Cancel. A drag that was on when a card came up is dropped.
* The window; L7 of the M3 review: while a file is being read the window takes no edits from the person, rather than asking at the end
  whether the file may replace what was changed meanwhile (which would hold the file back while a question is answered). A program on the control channel is
  not held: what it changes is replaced when the file arrives, as any `file.open` replaces the document.
* **MOVE-1D**: moving a connector moves its ends that are not glued. A glued end stays with its target, since moving it would break the glue. A
  connector with both ends glued has nothing to move: it is not counted in `moved`, and a command that moves nothing at all leaves the document, its
  history and the drawing's unsaved state as they were. `shape.align` moves by the same rule, and ROTATE-1D-1 turns and flips a connector's ends by it.
* Our rule: a member of a group has its pin in the group's frame, which is the page's only for a group that is not turned
  or flipped. `shape.move` carries the distance it is given (a distance on the page) down through the groups the shape is in, the outermost first
  (`Pose::down_vector`), before it adds it to the member's pin (and to the ends of a connector in a group). `shape.resize` carries the box's corner (a
  point of the page) down the same way, and refuses a member of a turned or flipped group, whose box is not square to the page. A group's children are
  not scaled by the group's cells alone: **a group is sized by `shape.resize` as one shape and its members follow it**. `shape.rotate` and `shape.flip` refuse the member of a turned or flipped group too.
* Replaced by: `shape.resize` refused a turned or flipped shape.
* Our rule (`draw/shapes.rs`): `shape.resize` refuses a connector and a member of a turned or flipped group, takes a group, and
  takes a shape that is turned or flipped. `x` and `y` are the place on the page of **the corner of the box that is at (0, 0) of the shape's own
  frame**, and `width` and `height` are along the shape's own axes; for a shape that is neither turned nor flipped that is the lower-left corner and
  the width and height of the box, as had them. The shape keeps its `Angle`, `FlipX` and `FlipY`. The pin follows so that the corner lands where
  it is asked: the local pin is worked out again for the new size (a pin at the middle stays at the middle), and the pin is the corner plus the local
  pin carried by the shape's turn and flips (`Pose::up_vector`). A window finds the corner with `draw::shape_corners`.
* (ours where no specification says: gives the eight handles round a set of selected 2-D shapes and says a corner handle keeps the proportions, and
  that several shapes turned keep their places in relation to each other "as though the page had been turned"; nothing says how each shape comes out of a stretch, so the set follows what one shape's
  handles do, scaled to the set; `draw/scale.rs`). **`shape.resize` with `ids` (and no `id`) makes the joint box of the shapes the box `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`**: the joint box is the smallest box on the page that holds the boxes of
  the shapes (the four corners of each, carried through its turn, its flips and its groups', and for a connector its two ends and nothing else), `x` and `y` the new box's lower-left corner in inches, and
  **every place is carried by the stretch that takes the old box to the new one** (a stretch along each page axis about the old box's lower-left corner, then the move to `x`, `y`), so the shapes keep their order and their gaps in proportion.
  A shape's centre goes where the stretch puts it and its `Width` and `Height` are scaled by the lengths the stretch gives its own two axes (`sx` and `sy` for a shape not turned, `sy` and `sx` for one turned a quarter, and for a
  shape turned by `a` the square roots of `(sx cos a)^2 + (sy sin a)^2` and `(sx sin a)^2 + (sy cos a)^2`: the same factor on both axes scales a shape by it at any angle). **A shape turned by an angle that is not a quarter keeps its
  angle** (a stretch that is not the same on both axes would shear it, which a box cannot say), its flips are kept, and its pin follows from its centre as for one shape (the local pin is worked out again for the new size).
  A connector carries its ends that are not glued by the stretch (a glued end stays with its shape: the connectors glued to a shape that moved or changed size are routed again, as for any edit). A shape named with a group it is
  in is left to the group and a member of a turned or flipped group is refused. The joint box must have a length along each axis (a line along x has no height to stretch: refused in words), and a resize
  to the box the shapes have is no resize and no undo step. At most 4,096 `ids`. **`snap`** snaps the edges of the joint box that the resize moves, as a shape's box is (`snap::snap_resize_set`; the box of a selection is square to the page
  whatever its shapes are, the shapes resized never targets, at most 512 shapes, `keep: "proportions"` keeps the proportions of the joint box: from a corner the opposite corner stays, from a side the opposite side stays and the other axis grows about its middle),
  and the shapes whose own edge is pulled to a guide are held to it as a move holds them. Each kind of target pulls an edge of the joint box from within its own strength, as it pulls a shape's (the grid from
  5 pixels at first; `snap_resize_set` and `snap_resize_ext` are one function for a box square to the page). The result tells how many shapes changed and which were left alone, and the snap.
* Our rule (`draw/scale.rs`). **A group is one shape**: `shape.resize` of a group, by `id` in its own frame or among `ids`, writes its `Width`, `Height` and pin as it does a
  shape's, and **its members follow by their own formulas** (the ties writes: `Sheet.<group>!Width*<factor>`), which the recalculation after the edit works out. A member whose size or place is a number and not a tie is
  carried by the stretch of the group's own frame (the factors the group's size went by), in the same edit: its `PinX`, `PinY`, `Width`, `Height` (by the lengths the stretch gives its own axes, as above) and a `LocPinX` or `LocPinY` that is a
  number, the ends of a line, and a group among them by its own factors in its turn, once its new size is known; **a cell that holds any formula is data and is left as it is**, and **a line among the members is routed again** with the rest of the edit (its route is rows of its own frame, which the stretch changes). The refit rule then makes the group the box of what its members came to when it was that
  box before. At most 20,000 members are carried in one edit (more are refused in words and nothing changes), and groups nest no deeper than `MAX_GROUP_DEPTH`. **Not done:** a group's own constant `Geometry`, `Connection` and `Controls` rows are not scaled
  (a group `shape.group` makes holds none; one of a file that does keeps its numbers), and `shape.size`, the Size & Position pane's command, still refuses a group.
* (the cells' documented meanings: `LockWidth` "keeps width fixed during sizing", `LockHeight` the same for height, `LockAspect` "allows sizing only in proportion"; no
  specification says what a set does with them, so the rest is ours). In a `shape.resize` with `ids`, **a shape with `LockHeight` set keeps its own height and is sized along its width, and one with `LockWidth` the reverse**:
  a shape 2 by 1 inches with `LockHeight` whose joint box is dragged out to 3 by 4 comes to 3 by 1, and with `LockWidth` to 2 by 4. The lock is of the shape's own axis, so a shape turned a quarter keeps the length the page's other axis
  would give it. The shape's middle goes where the stretch puts it, as every shape's does and as a shape with `LockAspect` already did, and the cell of the kept size is **not written**: a group whose `Height` is a formula (a class's, of its text) keeps the formula, and its pin and its
  members go by what the formula works out to once the width is written. **One shape, by `id`** (`shape.resize` with `id` and the window's handles on a single shape, which do not read the locks otherwise) **reads a lock only for a size that is a formula** (a group of compartments holds `LockHeight` and a `Height` of the sum of theirs): a shape with `LockHeight` whose `Height` is a formula is sized along its width and its `Height` is not written, a `LockWidth` over a `Width` formula the reverse, and the pin is held where it is along a kept axis (a text that wraps differently in the new width moves nothing of the shape); a locked size that is a number is written as it always was. **A shape with both locks, or with one of them and `LockAspect`, is left alone**: it is neither sized nor moved, and its box still counts in the joint box the others are stretched from; it is listed in the result's
  `locked`, which lists only the shapes left alone. **A connector with `LockWidth` or `LockHeight` is left alone too**: it has no other axis to size, and a stretch that is not the same on both axes would change its length or its direction. **A shape with `LockAspect` alone is stretched by
  the same factor on both axes**, the geometric mean of the two. When every shape named is left alone the resize is refused in words ("the shapes are locked against sizing (`LockWidth` with `LockHeight`, or either with `LockAspect`, or either on a connector): shape ...") and nothing changes.
  The locks are not read by `shape.resize` with `id`, nor by `shape.size`, nor by the window's handles of one shape, but for a size that is a formula (above: a group of compartments keeps the formula of its height) (a locked shape's grey handle bars, R35, are not drawn either).
* Our rule (`LockRotate` "bars turning a flat shape by handle or quarter-turn command"). **A shape with `LockRotate` set is left alone by `shape.rotate`**: it is neither turned nor moved by a turn of a set, and its box still counts in
  the joint box the others turn about (the middle of the box that is drawn); it is listed in the result's `locked`, and when every shape named is locked the turn is refused in words ("the shape is locked against turning (`LockRotate`): shape ...") and nothing changes. A one-dimensional shape is
  held to it as any other. `rotate_shapes` (the function) leaves the locked shapes and says nothing; `turn_shapes` says which.
* Our rule (`draw/arrange.rs`): `shape.rotate` turns a shape by writing `Angle`, counterclockwise
  (positive is leftward, as the Size & Position window has it), the cell in radians and the command in degrees. `angle` sets it, each shape about its **own pin**.
  `by` adds to it: **one shape turns about its pin, several turn as one about the middle of their joint box** (the box on the page that holds all their boxes; **`about`: {x, y} in inches, with `by`, turns each pin about that point instead**, which is how the window turns a selection about the middle of the box it draws; it is refused beside `angle`), so
  their pins move and their angles all grow by `by` ("several shapes turn as if the page turned"). The pin and the size of a shape
  turned about its own pin are not written. The angle written is kept **from just over -180 up to 180 degrees** (-90 from 0 is written -90 and 270 is written -90
  too; the files hold both signs, and counts 34,207 negative `Angle` cells against 323 larger than pi in size), a value within
  a billionth of a radian of a quarter turn is that quarter exactly (and the same angle: a turn of nothing on a shape whose angle it would have snapped writes
  nothing), and it is written with thirteen places, as the files hold one (`1.5707963267949`), not
  the nine of a length. The cell keeps the unit it had (`DEG`, `RAD`); a formula in it (`30 deg`) is replaced by the number, as a drag replaces one, except
  a `BOUND` or `SETATREF` formula, which passes the number on; a `GUARD`ed cell is an error and nothing changes. A turn to the angle a
  shape has, or by a whole turn, writes nothing, and the command is no undo step. A cell that reads the angle (`TxtAngle` as `-Angle`) is worked out
  again with what reads it. Text turns with the shape and is never mirrored.
* Our rule (no source gives what a flip writes): `shape.flip` is a **mirror of the page picture**, across the vertical line
  (`horizontal`: left becomes right) or the horizontal line (`vertical`) through the middle of the joint box of the shapes named, which for one shape is its own box.
  Each shape's pin is mirrored with it, `FlipX` (`FlipY`) is toggled, and `Angle` changes sign, since `M·R(θ)·F = R(-θ)·M·F` for the mirror `M`: the shape is then the
  mirror of the picture, however it was turned. The box of one shape stays where it is (a pin that is not at the middle moves with the mirror, and one that is does not
  move), flipping twice gives the shape back, and several shapes flip as one, keeping their places in the picture. The cells that turn the text are not touched:
  glyphs are never mirrored, and the net turn of the text is `Angle` minus `TxtAngle` under one flip, so the text of a flipped shape is where it was and
  reads the same way. A flip toggles the cell (it writes 0 and 1, and does not take the cell away).
* **ROTATE-1D-1** (ours, after MOVE-1D): a one-dimensional shape (a connector) is turned or flipped by moving **its ends that are not glued**: with no
  end glued, turned about its pin (one shape, or `angle`: the way the line points, from the begin to the end, is set to the angle) or about the joint box (several turned
  `by`); **with one end glued, the free end turns about the glued end**, so the line turns by the angle and `angle` is reached exactly ("a line takes the angle
  from its begin point"; a set turned `by` still turns its free ends about the joint box); mirrored across the same line as any shape.
  It writes no pose cell: `Angle`, `Width` and the pin follow the ends by their formulas, and a route of ours is made again and its label placed. A glued end stays with its
  target and a connector with both ends glued has nothing to turn or flip, is not counted, and is no undo step. A flip of a file's connector whose route is more than a
  straight line and which has no glued end keeps the rows of its route, which are in its own frame.
* Our rule: `shape.order` reorders the list a shape is in: the page's part, or a group's own members (a shape named with others
  from other lists moves in each list). **Bring to Front and Send to Back go to the end of the shape's band**: a
  shape is put just before the first shape after it with a higher `DisplayLevel` (a lower one, for the back), so that it stays behind every higher band and in front of
  every lower one; with the same band throughout that is the end or the start of the list. `forward` and `backward` move a shape one place, past the next shape that is
  not named and not of a higher band (a lower one, for backward); a block of shapes named moves as one, and one at the end stays. Shapes named together keep the order they
  have among themselves, whatever order they are named in. A shape in the reserved band -32768 has none to keep: it goes to the very front or back, and it stops no other shape.
  `DisplayLevel` is read by inheritance (it may come from a master or a style). **No command writes `DisplayLevel`**: the -32768 that writes for a command that carries
  a shape out of its band does not arise, and the guarded cell is never reached. `moved` counts the shapes named that changed place, and an order that changes
  nothing is no undo step. The writer keeps the order of the page part, and the saved file reads back in it.
* Our rule (the others move to the primary shape without changing spacing): `shape.align` moves every shape named after the first, by the distance on the page
  that puts its left, right, top or bottom edge, or its horizontal or vertical middle (`center` is the middle between left and right, `middle` between top and bottom), where
  the first shape's is. The first shape named, not the lowest `ID`, is the primary one and does not move. A shape's edges are those of **its box on the page**: the bounding box of
  its box carried through its turn, flips and groups (the box, not the drawn curve), and for a connector the box of its ends. The move is a move of `shape.move`'s kind
  (MOVE-1D), done once for all, so a member of a turned group aligns too. One shape named, or shapes that are aligned, is no undo step.
* Our rule: a shape named together with a group it is in is left to the group, which moves, turns or flips it (a member would be moved twice), by
  `shape.rotate`, `shape.flip` and `shape.align`. `shape.rotate` and `shape.flip` refuse a member of a turned or flipped group (its cells are in the group's frame, and a
  turn or a flip of the page is another in it, as for a resize and a group's frame); a group itself turns and flips as a shape, its members with it, and a member of a group that
  is neither turned nor flipped turns, flips and aligns with the page. **The group commands keep this true**: a group made inside a turned or flipped group does not lift the rule for its members, and ungrouping
carries the turn and the flips into the members' own cells, after which they turn and flip like any shape of the page.
* Our rule (`draw/clipboard.rs`): `edit.copy` takes the shapes named, each with everything inside it (a shape named with a group it is in is left to the group), in
  the order of the drawing; at most 50,000 shapes, members counted. **The clipboard is the session's, one for a document**: a new or opened drawing starts with none (a paste is within
  one document, M3 second) and an undo leaves it. It also holds the masters the shapes use, so that a paste after an undo that took a master away (a dropped shape's,
  with the drop) puts it back; otherwise **a paste uses the document's masters by `ID` and never makes a second copy of one** (a master of the document with the same `UniqueID` is that
  master, whatever its `ID`, and so is a built-in master with the same `BaseID`, since a drawing of 0.2.3 holds the built-in masters under another `UniqueID` than this build gives them; matching a stencil's masters to a document's is `stencil.open`'s). A paste gives every shape in the copy, members included, a new `ID`, in the
  order of the copy (above every `ID` on the page and every one the session has given there); puts the copies **on top** of the drawing order, in their order; and makes a
  `Connect` row between the copies where there was one between the shapes. A connector copied with the shapes it is glued to is glued to the copies, by `PAR(PNT(...))` and by
  `_WALKGLUE` alike; **a connector copied without a shape it is glued to has that end a plain point where it was**, and no row (as the delete rule leaves the end of a connector whose shape is
  deleted). A formula in a copy that names a copied shape names its copy; a name that ends in the shape's `ID` ends in the copy's (`Process.4` copied to 9 is
  `Process.9`; ours: no source read says what a copy is called); `UniqueID` is not copied, since it names one shape. Text, runs, fields, formats, style links, `Data1` to `Data3`, `OriginalID` and every cell copy as they are. A
  **member of a group** is copied alone as a shape of the page: its cells are carried out of its groups when it is pasted, so it draws as it did. A member that takes its
  cells from a master group (`MasterShape` and no `Master`) is refused, since it would lose them, and so is a connector in a flipped group. A picture belongs to its page (the `Rel` in
  `ForeignData` is an id in the page part's relationships, which the writer does not add to): **a copy that holds one is pasted on the page it came from only**. The cells that move a copy
  are written as a drag writes them (a formula in `PinX` becomes the number; a `GUARD`ed one is an error), and none is written for a copy that lands where it was.
* Our rule (the reference app's own offset is not given by any source read): `edit.paste` with no `x` and `y` puts the copies a step (a quarter of an inch, in paper inches
  whatever the page's scale) **right and down** of the originals when the page is the one they were copied from, and one more step for each paste of the same copy; on another page the
  first paste is where the originals were, and each later one a step on. With `x` and `y` the middle of the box that holds the copies lands there. `shape.duplicate` offsets by `dx` and
  `dy` (a quarter of an inch right and down by default) and leaves the clipboard, and the count of pastes, alone, so a window that selects the new shapes steps them on by repeating it.
* Our rule (`draw/remap.rs`): in the formula of a cell of a copy, each `Sheet.<id>!` whose `<id>` is the `ID` of a shape copied becomes
  `Sheet.<new>!`, and the rest of the formula is kept character for character. A reference by name (`Process!Width`, a peer by `NameU`) is kept and goes on naming what it named; a
  `Sheet.<id>` after another qualifier (`Pages[Site-2]!Sheet.9!EndY`) is on another page and is kept; text in a string or a quoted name is not a reference. A reference to a shape not
  copied stays with the original **on the page the shapes were copied from**. **On another page it would reach the shape of the new page with that `ID`** (`Sheet.<id>` reaches a shape of
  the page by its `ID`), so a cell of a copy whose formula names a shape not copied is made the constant of its cached value there (as the end of a connector whose shape was not copied is): the glue formula of
  a connector with no `Connect` row, a `BegTrigger`, a `Width` of `Sheet.5!Width*0.5`. **What making a cell its value does** (the same for an ungroup): the formula is taken away, and **the cached error (`E`) with it** (a constant reports none; kept, it would be reported for ever and, on the end of a
  connector, would make skip the connector); the value, unit and the rest of the cell are kept; **a `GUARD`ed cell loses its guard with its formula** (it is a plain constant, as after a drag); **a cell with a formula and no cached value** (malformed) is left as it is, formula and all, since an empty cell would read as 0
  and draw differently. A reference by name is kept on another page too, where it names a peer of that name if there is one. **A member copied alone** (copy, cut or duplicate, pasted on any page) **leaves its
  groups: a formula of it, or of anything in it, that names one of them is made the constant of its cached value too, on the same page as well** (the group may be taken apart or deleted, and a name of it
  would be a `#REF!` that is saved).
* Our rule (`draw/group.rs`): `shape.group` makes a shape of `Type` `Group` whose
  `Shapes` hold the shapes named, with an `ID` above every `ID` of the page. Its frame is the box that holds the members **in the frame they were in** (their four corners
  carried through their poses; for a connector its two ends and **nothing else**: a route that leaves the box of its ends is no part of the frame, as the `.odg` reader and writer have it), so that the group frame rule holds: its `PinX` and `PinY` are the middle of the box, its `Width`
  and `Height` the box's size, its `LocPinX` and `LocPinY` `Width*0.5` and `Height*0.5` (formulas, as a file's), and it holds no angle. It is linked to the root style (so it reads
  `DisplayMode` and the other group properties from it) and has no name (`NAME()` of an unnamed shape is `Sheet.<id>`). It stands in the list in the
  place of the topmost of its members, and the members keep the order they had. The shapes named must be in one list (the page's, or one group's members), two at least once a shape named with a
  group it is in is left to the group; a group goes no deeper than 90 levels (`draw::MAX_GROUP_DEPTH`: the model allows 200, but the reader of a file takes XML 200 elements deep and a level of group costs two, so a drawing nested past about 98 levels could be saved and not read again). Members are carried into the group's frame. Moving, turning, flipping and
  deleting a group carry its members (they are cells of its frame); a glue to a member is by `ID` and survives, and a connector inside the group glued to a shape outside it follows that
  shape (the formula carries its point into the group's frame).
  `shape.ungroup` takes apart each group named, **at most 50,000 members in all** (`draw::MAX_UNGROUP_MEMBERS`: the ids a command takes are capped at 4,096, but one id may name a group of any number of members, so the members are counted before
  any is handled, and more are refused in words) (a shape with no members is left alone; a group named with a group it is in is not taken apart in the same call): the members go to the list the group was
  in, in its place and in their order, carried out through the group's pose, which may be turned and flipped. The group's own cells, and its text, go with it. **A connector glued to
  the group itself is left with that end a plain point where it was** (for the group's shape), and no `Connect` row names a group that is gone. **A formula of a member (or of anything inside one) that names a group that is taken apart** (`Sheet.<group>!Width*0.25`) would be worked out against a shape that is not there and saved naming nothing: such a cell is made the constant of its cached value
  before the group goes (a name of a group that stays is kept). A shape outside the group that names it is another matter, as after a delete: it reads a shape that is not there. A group that is an instance of a master
